High-Yield Practice Problems: Himalayan Stratigraphy & Tethyan Paleontology
Problem 1: Otoceras woodwardi Biozone Significance

Why is the Otoceras woodwardi bed of the basal Lilang Group in Spiti internationally famous in global chronostratigraphy?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The ammonoid Otoceras woodwardi marks the earliest ammonite biozone of the Triassic Period (basal Induan Stage, Griesbachian sub-stage). In Spiti and the adjacent Guryul Ravine in Kashmir, the boundary clay underlying the Otoceras bed preserves the most complete marine record of the Permian-Triassic (P-Tr) mass extinction ($\sim 251.9\text{ Ma}$), recording the catastrophic wipeout of Paleozoic brachiopods and corals.

Problem 2: The Sacred Saligram of the Spiti Shales

What are the sacred Hindu stones known as Saligrams (Shaligrams) found in the Gandaki and Spiti valleys, and what fossil group do they contain?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Saligrams are rounded, black, calcareous-phosphatic concretionary nodules weathered out from the Upper Jurassic Spiti Shales Formation. When cracked open, they reveal beautifully preserved, pyritized or calcified internal molds of ammonites (specifically Virgatosphinctes densiplicatus, Aulacosphinctoides, Blanfordiceras) and belemnites, revered as aniconic representations of Lord Vishnu.

Problem 3: The Fenestella Shales of the Kanawar Group

In which Carboniferous formation of Spiti and Kashmir do we find rock beds packed with the bryozoan Fenestella, and what is its morphology?

Step-by-Step Solution:

In the Po Formation of Spiti (and the Fenestella Shale of Kashmir), Middle Carboniferous shales contain dense colonies of the reticulate marine bryozoan Fenestella plebeia, characterized by a delicate fan-shaped or net-like calcareous skeleton with rectangular mesh apertures bearing zooecial pores.

Problem 4: Kioto Limestone and Megalodon Bivalve

What diagnostic thick-shelled bivalve characterizes the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic Kioto Limestone of Spiti?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The pachyodont bivalve Megalodon (accompanied by Dicerocardium). These massive, thick-walled heart-shaped bivalves formed extensive biostromal carbonate banks across the shallow Tethyan shelf.

Problem 5: Giumal Sandstone vs. Chikkim Formation

Contrast the lithofacies and depositional depth of the Giumal Sandstone with the overlying Chikkim Formation in Spiti.

Step-by-Step Solution:

  • Giumal Sandstone (Early Cretaceous): Shallow-marine, high-energy, greenish-brown glauconitic sandstones and quartzites deposited on an inner shelf.
  • Chikkim Formation (Late Cretaceous): Deep-water, pelagic, white microcrystalline limestones and bluish calcareous shales containing planktonic foraminifera (Globotruncana), reflecting a major oceanic drowning transgression.
Problem 6: Structural Contact between Tethyan Spiti and Higher Himalaya

What major extensional tectonic fault separates the Tethyan sedimentary succession of Spiti from the Higher Himalayan Crystalline basement?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The South Tibetan Detachment System (STDS), also locally designated the Trans-Himadri Fault. This is a regional low-angle, north-dipping normal fault system along which unmetamorphosed Tethyan Paleozoic sediments slipped down to the north during Miocene gravitational collapse of the overthickened Himalayan orogen.

Problem 7: Kuling Group and the Permian Gondwana Cooling

What brachiopod genus dominates the Permian Kuling Group in Spiti, and what paleolatitude does it indicate?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The spiriferid brachiopod Spiriferella rajah and productid Productus. These cold-water to temperate brachiopods reflect the peri-Gondwanan cold marine climate along the southern shore of the Neo-Tethys.

Problem 8: Earliest Trilobites of Spiti

Which famous Lower Cambrian trilobite marks the Parahio River section of the Kunzum La Formation in Spiti?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The redlichiid trilobite Redlichia noetlingi (Order Redlichiida). It possesses a large semicircular cephalon, long genal spines, numerous thoracic segments with pleural spines, and a tiny pygidium, establishing early Cambrian correlation across Asia and Australia.

Indian Stratigraphy & Biostratigraphy / Question 055
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Indian Stratigraphy & Proterozoic Lithostratigraphy

Q055: Vindhyan Supergroup: Semri, Kaimur, Rewa, and Bhander

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 55
Authoritative References: G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 312–316, p. 165); P.K. Mukherjee, A Text Book of Geology (pp. 200–204); Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan, Geology of India (Vol. 1, Ch. 12: Vindhyan Supergroup, pp. 315–342); M.S. Krishnan, Geology of India and Burma (Ch. 7).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Quadripartite Architecture of the Vindhyan Supergroup

The Vindhyan Supergroup represents India's largest and most magnificent Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic intracratonic sedimentary basin (spanning over $100,000\text{ km}^2$ across Central India). Established by J.B. Auden (1933) and reaffirmed by the Geological Survey of India, the Supergroup is universally divided into two primary sub-divisions and four canonical groups (in ascending chronological order):

  • Lower Vindhyan:
    • 1. Semri Group: Basal marine carbonate-volcaniclastic sequence ($\sim 1700-1600\text{ Ma}$). Comprises the Kajrahat Limestone, Porcellanite Formation (acid tuffs), Olive Shales, Fawn Limestone, and Rohtas Limestone. Rich in columnar stromatolites (Collenia, Kussiella) and microfossils.
  • Upper Vindhyan: Dominated by mature clastics, separated from the Semri Group by a regional disconformity:
    • 2. Kaimur Group: Orthoquartzites, quartz arenites, and conglomerates (Dhandraul Quartzite, Scarp Sandstone, Bijaigarh Shale) recording high-energy littoral barrier regimes ($\sim 1150-1000\text{ Ma}$).
    • 3. Rewa Group: Alternating shales and sandstones (Panna Shale, Asan Sandstone, Jhiri Shale, Govindgarh Sandstone). Famous for diamondiferous basal conglomerates derived from the Majhgawan pipe.
    • 4. Bhander Group: The uppermost, thickest, and most widely exposed group ($\sim 900-550\text{ Ma}$). Marks the return of extensive marine carbonate and tidal flat-sabkha sedimentation.
Figure 55.1 (G.B. Mahapatra, p. 165): Stratigraphic classification of the Vindhyan Supergroup showing the ascending sequence: Semri $\to$ Kaimur $\to$ Rewa $\to$ Bhander Group.
2. Detailed Lithostratigraphy of the Uppermost Bhander Group

The Bhander Group terminates the Proterozoic sedimentary history of the Great Vindhyan Basin. It is divided into four constituent formations (in ascending order):

The Ascending Formations of the Bhander Group
$$\mathbf{Ganurgarh \text{ Shale}} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Bhander \text{ Limestone}} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Sirbu \text{ Shale}} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Upper \text{ Bhander Sandstone}}$$
  • Ganurgarh Shale: Reddish-brown, thinly bedded calcareous shales with interbedded siltstones, desiccation cracks, and halite casts indicating tidal flat muds.
  • Bhander Limestone: High-grade calcitic to dolomitic limestone ($50-100\text{ m}$ thick) exhibiting spectacular domal and columnar stromatolites (Baicalia, Maiharia). Forms the premier raw material base for Central India's portland cement industry.
  • Sirbu Shale: Olive-green to purple gypsiferous shales and fine sandstones with abundant ripple marks, mudcracks, and hopper crystal pseudomorphs.
  • Upper Bhander Sandstone: Dark red to pinkish-buff, fine-to-medium grained quartz arenite displaying large-scale tabular cross-bedding and planar lamination, quarried across Rajasthan and MP for world-famous architectural monument stone.
Figure 55.2 (P.K. Mukherjee, p. 202): Comprehensive table of the Vindhyan Supergroup detailing the Semri, Kaimur, Rewa, and Bhander Groups with their diagnostic sub-units.
3. Comparative Matrix of the Four Vindhyan Groups
Group Primary Lithologies Depositional Environment Economic Mineral Products
Bhander Group (Uppermost) Red sandstones, stromatolitic limestones, shales, gypsum. Tidal flat, lagoon, supratidal sabkha. Portland cement limestone, architectural building stones (Red Fort).
Rewa Group Shales, fine sandstones, conglomerates. Shallow shelf, deltaic distributaries. Panna diamond conglomerates, building stones.
Kaimur Group Orthoquartzites, quartz arenites, black shales. High-energy coastal barrier beaches, sand bars. Refractory silica stone, pyrite (Bijaigarh Shale).
Semri Group (Lowermost) Limestones, dolomites, bedded tuffs, glauconitic sandstones. Transgressive shallow marine carbonate platform. High-grade cement limestone (Rohtas, Kajrahat), porcellanite road ballast.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 55
The Vindhyan Supergroup is divisible into four groups viz., Semri Group, Kaimur Group, Rewa Group and
(A) Bijawar group
(B) Bhander group
(C) Gwalior group
(D) None of these
Verified Correct Answer: (B) Bhander group [The four constituent groups of the Vindhyan Supergroup in ascending chronological order are Semri Group, Kaimur Group, Rewa Group, and Bhander Group.]
Correct Option: (B) Bhander group

Detailed Stratigraphic Forensic Analysis:

  • The Vindhyan Supergroup of Central India is universally subdivided across all Indian geological treatises (Auden 1933; Krishnan 1982; Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan 2008; Mahapatra 2019; Mukherjee 2013) into exactly four major lithostratigraphic groups:
    1. Semri Group (Lower Vindhyan)
    2. Kaimur Group (Upper Vindhyan)
    3. Rewa Group (Upper Vindhyan)
    4. Bhander Group (Upper Vindhyan)
  • The Bhander Group represents the fourth, uppermost, and youngest member of this classic quadripartite succession, celebrated for its high-grade cement limestones (Bhander Limestone) and building stones (Upper Bhander Sandstone).
  • Thus, Option (B) Bhander group is the indisputably correct answer.
Incorrect Distractor: (A) Bijawar group

Detailed Refutation:

  • The Bijawar Group is a deformed Paleoproterozoic sequence of quartzites, dolomites, ferruginous beds, and basic lavas that forms the unconformable floor (basement) beneath the Vindhyan Supergroup.
  • The Semri Group rests with angular unconformity upon the Bijawar rocks; hence, Bijawar is an older basement unit, not a constituent of the Vindhyan Supergroup.
Incorrect Distractor: (C) Gwalior group

Detailed Refutation:

  • The Gwalior Group (Par and Morar Formations) is another Paleoproterozoic sedimentary-volcanic succession exposed around Gwalior in northern Madhya Pradesh.
  • It unconformably underlies the Kaimur Group of the Vindhyan Supergroup, making it an older basement series rather than a member of the Vindhyan Supergroup.
Incorrect Distractor: (D) None of these

Detailed Refutation:

  • Because Option (B) Bhander group is the exact canonical fourth group, Option (D) is incorrect.

High-Yield Practice Problems: Vindhyan Stratigraphy & Sedimentary Petrology
Problem 1: Stromatolite Biostratigraphy of Bhander Limestone

Which branching columnar stromatolite taxon characterizes the Neoproterozoic Bhander Limestone and correlates it with the Riphean of Russia?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Bhander Limestone is characterized by the branching columnar stromatolite Baicalia baicalica and Maiharia maiharensis. In Riphean biostratigraphy, Baicalia is the diagnostic index form for the Middle to Upper Riphean ($\sim 1000-700\text{ Ma}$), establishing global biostratigraphic correlation for the Bhander Group.

Problem 2: Halite Pseudomorphs as Evaporite Indicators

Explain the step-by-step mechanism of hopper-crystal halite pseudomorph formation in the Sirbu Shale.

Step-by-Step Solution:

  1. Under hyper-saline, arid conditions on supratidal sabkha mudflats, brine evaporates, precipitating skeletal cubic "hopper" crystals of halite ($\text{NaCl}$) within the soft mud.
  2. During episodic marine flooding or rainstorms, less saline water dissolves the soluble halite crystal, leaving a hollow cubic mold in the mud.
  3. Inflowing silt or mud deposits immediately fill the cavity, casting a perfect cubic pseudomorph preserved on shale bedding planes.
Problem 3: Architectural Durability of the Upper Bhander Sandstone

Why has the Upper Bhander Sandstone survived centuries of environmental exposure in Mughal monuments (e.g., Red Fort, Fatehpur Sikri) without crumbling?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Upper Bhander Sandstone is a super-mature quartz arenite consisting of $>95\%$ monocrystalline quartz grains bonded by syntaxial silica cement in optical continuity with the host grains (secondary quartz overgrowths), with a microscopic coating of hematite providing the warm red color. The absence of unstable feldspars and soluble carbonate cements renders it virtually impervious to chemical weathering and acid rain.

Problem 4: The Great Eparchean Hiatus at the Base of the Semri

The basal conglomerate of the Semri Group rests upon the Bundelkhand Granite ($\sim 2500\text{ Ma}$). What is the duration of the missing geological time interval represented by this unconformity if the Semri initiated at $\sim 1700\text{ Ma}$?

Step-by-Step Solution:

$$\text{Hiatus} = 2500\text{ Ma} - 1700\text{ Ma} = 800\text{ Ma}$$

Final Answer: The basal nonconformity represents an enormous erosional hiatus of approximately $800\text{ million years}$.

Problem 5: Carbon Isotope Excursion ($\delta^{13}\text{C}$) in the Bhander Limestone

Modern chemostratigraphy shows that the Bhander Limestone exhibits strongly positive carbon isotope ratios ($\delta^{13}\text{C} \approx +4.0\text{ to } +6.0\text{ \textperthousand}$). What global biogeochemical condition does this indicate?

Step-by-Step Solution:

High positive $\delta^{13}\text{C}_{\text{carb}}$ values indicate high global rates of organic carbon burial in anoxic sediments (preferentially sequestering light $^{12}\text{C}$ into buried biomass, leaving the ocean reservoir enriched in heavy $^{13}\text{C}$). This massive burial of organic carbon corresponds to the Neoproterozoic oxygenation event preceding the radiation of multicellular life.

Problem 6: Origin of Porcellanite in the Semri Group

What is the petrogenetic origin of the banded "porcellanite" beds in the Semri Group?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Porcellanites are dense, chert-like, microcrystalline silicified rocks that formed by the devitrification and diagenetic alteration of airborne felsic volcanic ash and rhyolitic tuffs deposited in a shallow marine basin during syn-sedimentary Paleoproterozoic volcanism.

Problem 7: Great Boundary Fault Juxtaposition

Along the northwestern margin of the Vindhyan basin in Rajasthan, which specific Vindhyan group is brought into direct thrust contact against pre-Vindhyan schists by the Great Boundary Fault?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Bhander Group (specifically the Upper Bhander Sandstone and Sirbu Shale) is folded into steep marginal synclines and faulted directly against the Aravalli-Bhilwara metamorphic basement by the Great Boundary Fault.

Problem 8: Modern Terminal Age of the Vindhyans

Recent discoveries of Ediacaran trace fossils and discs in the Bhander Group place the terminal sedimentation close to which global chronostratigraphic boundary?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The uppermost Bhander Group extends to approximately $540-550\text{ Ma}$, placing the cessation of Vindhyan sedimentation immediately at the Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary (the Precambrian-Cambrian transition).

Indian Stratigraphy & Biostratigraphy / Question 056
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Principles of Stratigraphy & Basin Analysis

Q056: Chronostratigraphic Correlation: Establishing Time-Equivalence

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 56
Authoritative References: Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (4th Ed., Pearson, Ch. 15: Stratigraphic Correlation, pp. 518–534, Fig. 15.2); International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS), International Stratigraphic Guide (A. Salvador, Ed., 2nd Ed., 1994); North American Commission on Stratigraphic Nomenclature (NACSN), North American Stratigraphic Code (2005); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 13).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Fundamentals of Stratigraphic Correlation

In stratigraphy and basin analysis, correlation is the demonstrative process of establishing geometric, lithological, paleontological, or temporal correspondence between geographically separated stratigraphic units. The International Stratigraphic Guide rigorously separates correlation into three distinct categories:

  • Chronostratigraphic Correlation (Time Correlation): The specific scientific procedure of demonstrating that separated rock bodies, lithofacies, or physical events were deposited or occurred at the exact same geological time / identical absolute age. It establishes true chronocorrelation across diverse depositional realms (e.g., correlating deep pelagic shales with coastal barrier sandstones that formed synchronously).
  • Lithostratigraphic Correlation: The matching of rock strata based strictly on their lithological similarity, petrographic properties, and geometric position without regard to their age. Crucially, lithostratigraphic units (formations, members) are frequently diachronous (time-transgressive) due to marine transgressions and regressions (Walther's Law).
  • Biostratigraphic Correlation: The matching of strata based on identical fossil content and biozone boundaries (assemblage zones, taxon-range zones, concurrent-range zones).
Figure 56.1 (Sam Boggs Jr., Fig. 15.2): Fundamental dichotomy in stratigraphy: Lithostratigraphic boundaries (transgressive beach sandstones, dashed red) migrate diachronously across time horizons, whereas Chronostratigraphic isochrons (bentonite ash beds, solid blue) cut across lithologies at true constant time lines.
2. Primary Geoscientific Tools for Establishing Chronostratigraphic Age Equivalence

Establishing that distant rock bodies share the same age requires identifying isochronous marker surfaces (time horizons) that were deposited virtually instantaneously across wide geographic areas:

Mathematical Statement of Chronostratigraphic Equivalence
$$\text{Unit } A(\mathbf{x}_1) \sim \text{Unit } B(\mathbf{x}_2) \iff t_1 = t_2 \quad \left(\text{Instantaneous Time Horizon: } \frac{dt}{dx} \to 0\right)$$

Contrasted with diachronous lithofacies migration: $\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{v_{\text{transgression}}} \neq 0$.

  • 1. Volcanic Ash Beds (Bentonites / Tonsteins): Airborne plinian volcanic eruptions disperse pyroclastic ash across entire continents and ocean basins within days. High-precision CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb dating on sanidine/zircon crystals provides absolute chronostratigraphic datum surfaces with sub-permil accuracy ($\pm 20,000\text{ years}$).
  • 2. Magnetostratigraphic Polarity Reversals: Earth's geomagnetic field reverses synchronously worldwide. A magnetic chron boundary (e.g., the Matuyama-Brunhes reversal at $0.78\text{ Ma}$) represents an absolute global chronostratigraphic isochron.
  • 3. Chemostratigraphic Isotopic Excursions: Rapid, planetary-scale carbon ($\delta^{13}\text{C}$), oxygen ($\delta^{18}\text{O}$), or strontium ($^{87}\text{Sr}/^{86}\text{Sr}$) excursions (e.g., the PETM hyperthermal negative carbon isotope excursion at $56\text{ Ma}$).
  • 4. Microfossil Datum Planes (FADs and LADs): First Appearance Datums (FAD) and Last Appearance Datums (LAD) of planktonic organisms (foraminifera, calcareous nannoplankton).
Figure 56.2 (Sam Boggs Jr., p. 524): Textbook principles of chronostratigraphic correlation, defining how isochronous surfaces establish time equivalence across distant basins.
3. Detailed Comparison: Litho- vs. Bio- vs. Chronostratigraphic Correlation
Correlation Category Fundamental Basis Units Correlated Temporal Validity Primary Limitations
Chronostratigraphic Correlation Age Equivalence (Same Geological Time) Erathem, System, Series, Stage, Chronozone. Strictly Isochronous (True Time Equivalent). Requires radiometric dates, ash beds, or magnetic reversals.
Lithostratigraphic Correlation Lithologic composition, rock type, and stratigraphic position. Group, Formation, Member, Bed. Frequently Diachronous (Time-Transgressive). Misleads age interpretation due to lateral facies shifts (Walther's Law).
Biostratigraphic Correlation Similar fossil content and taxon assemblage ranges. Biozone (Range Zone, Interval Zone, Assemblage Zone). Approximately isochronous within the resolution of the biochron ($0.5-2\text{ Ma}$). Fossil preservation bias; provincialism and facies control on living taxa.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 56
_____ is the process of establishing which sedimentary strata are the same age at distant geographical areas by means of their stratigraphic relationship.
(A) Chronostratigraphic correlation
(B) Lithostratigraphic correlation
(C) Biostratigraphic correlation
(D) Stratigraphic correlation
Verified Correct Answer: (A) Chronostratigraphic correlation [The process of establishing that strata in geographically separated areas were deposited at the exact same geological age is by formal definition chronostratigraphic correlation.]
Correct Option: (A) Chronostratigraphic correlation

Detailed Stratigraphic Forensic Analysis:

  • In formal stratigraphic nomenclature (Boggs Jr. 2012, Ch. 15; Salvador 1994, International Stratigraphic Guide), correlation that specifically establishes that rock bodies in distant geographic regions share the exact same age (temporal equivalence) is designated as Chronostratigraphic correlation (or chronocorrelation / time correlation).
  • It utilizes isochronous horizons—such as tephra ash falls (bentonites), paleomagnetic reversals, and isotope chemostratigraphy—to tie disparate facies together along lines of equal time.
  • Therefore, Option (A) Chronostratigraphic correlation is the textbook-verified, precise scientific term.
Incorrect Distractor: (B) Lithostratigraphic correlation

Detailed Refutation:

  • Lithostratigraphic correlation matches strata based solely on physical rock characteristics (lithology, grain size, mineralogy) and geometric position.
  • Lithostratigraphic units are famously diachronous (time-transgressive). For example, a basal sandstone in a transgressive sea grows progressively younger in the direction of the shoreline; tracing that sandstone across a basin does not establish strata of the same age. Hence, (B) is false.
Incorrect Distractor: (C) Biostratigraphic correlation

Detailed Refutation:

  • Biostratigraphic correlation establishes similarity in fossil content and biozones.
  • While biostratigraphy is a crucial tool used to achieve time correlation, biostratigraphic correlation in itself specifically denotes fossil assemblage matching, which can occasionally be facies-controlled or diachronous (due to migration rates). The overarching process of establishing *same age* is chronostratigraphic correlation.
Incorrect Distractor: (D) Stratigraphic correlation

Detailed Refutation:

  • Stratigraphic correlation is the broad umbrella term encompassing all forms of geological correlation (litho-, bio-, chrono-, chemo-, and seismic).
  • Because the question specifically asks for the process of establishing strata of the same age, the specific and exact term required is Chronostratigraphic correlation.

High-Yield Practice Problems: Correlation Methods & Geochronology
Problem 1: Transgressive Shoreface Velocity Calculation

A transgressive quartz sandstone unit has a basal age of $505.0\text{ Ma}$ at location A and $501.0\text{ Ma}$ at location B, situated $200\text{ km}$ inland. Calculate the rate of shoreline migration in $\text{mm/year}$ and determine whether this formation is isochronous or diachronous.

Step-by-Step Solution:

$$\Delta t = 505.0 - 501.0 = 4.0\text{ Ma} = 4.0 \times 10^6\text{ years}$$ $$\text{Distance } D = 200\text{ km} = 2.0 \times 10^8\text{ mm}$$ $$v_{\text{migration}} = \frac{D}{\Delta t} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^8\text{ mm}}{4.0 \times 10^6\text{ yr}} = 50\text{ mm/year} = 5.0\text{ cm/year}$$

Final Answer: The shoreline migrated at $50\text{ mm/year}$. Because the age of the sandstone differs by $4.0\text{ million years}$ between locations, the formation is strongly diachronous (time-transgressive).

Problem 2: Bentonite Ash Bed Correlation

Why do altered volcanic ash beds (bentonites / tonsteins) provide the gold standard for chronostratigraphic correlation across differing sedimentary facies?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Volcanic ash plumes from explosive plinian eruptions are carried across the stratosphere and settle out over marine basins, deltas, and lakes within a matter of days or weeks (essentially instantaneous in geological time: $dt \to 0$). The resulting thin clay-rich bentonite layer cuts across all environmental boundaries, providing a literal physical time plane containing radiometrically datable zircons and sanidines.

Problem 3: Walther's Law of Facies Application

State Walther's Law of Facies and explain how it prevents erroneous chronostratigraphic correlations.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Walther's Law states: "Facies that occur in conformable vertical succession must have been formed in laterally adjacent depositional environments at the same time." This warns stratigraphers that vertical changes in rock type (e.g., sandstone $\to$ shale $\to$ limestone) represent lateral shifts of environmental belts over time, meaning lithostratigraphic contacts cannot be assumed to be horizontal time planes.

Problem 4: Magnetostratigraphic Reversal Resolution

How does magnetostratigraphic correlation establish time equivalence without requiring body fossils?

Step-by-Step Solution:

When volcanic rocks cool below their Curie temperature ($T_c$) or magnetic minerals settle in sediments, they align with Earth's magnetic dipole field. Geomagnetic field polarity reversals (Normal vs. Reverse chrons) occur globally at the exact same instant ($<5,000\text{ years}$ transition duration). By matching the unique bar-code pattern of normal and reversed polarity zones to the global geomagnetic polarity timescale (GPTS), strata are chronocorrelated worldwide.

Problem 5: Carbon Isotope Chemostratigraphic Correlation ($\delta^{13}\text{C}$)

In a Precambrian basin devoid of index fossils, how can a negative carbon isotope excursion establish chronostratigraphic equivalence with another continent?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The oceanic carbon reservoir has a residence time of $\sim 10^5\text{ years}$, which is much longer than the ocean mixing time ($\sim 1,000\text{ years}$). Therefore, catastrophic carbon perturbations (such as the Shuram negative $\delta^{13}\text{C}$ excursion of the Ediacaran) alter the isotopic composition of seawater synchronously worldwide. Carbonate rocks precipitating from seawater preserve this identical isotopic curve, allowing global chronocorrelation.

Problem 6: Seismic Reflection Clinoforms as Time Lines

In seismic stratigraphy, do seismic reflections represent lithological boundaries or chronostratigraphic time horizons?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Seismic reflections are generated at acoustic impedance contrasts ($Z = \rho v$) which coincide with bedding planes, stratal unconformities, and hiatuses. Because stratal surfaces were once continuous depositional surfaces (paleo-seafloors) formed over a single increment of time, seismic reflections represent chronostratigraphic time-surfaces, cutting across diachronous lithofacies boundaries.

Problem 7: GSSP (Golden Spike) Definition

What is a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) in chronostratigraphy?

Step-by-Step Solution:

A GSSP (popularly termed a "Golden Spike") is an internationally agreed-upon, physically designated reference point in a specific geological rock outcrop that defines the lower boundary of a formal chronostratigraphic Stage (and hence Series and System). It is anchored to a primary marker event (e.g., FAD of a microfossil or magnetic reversal).

Problem 8: Graphic Correlation Method of Shaw (1964)

What is Alan Shaw's graphic correlation technique and what does the Slope of the Line of Correlation (LOC) indicate?

Step-by-Step Solution:

In Shaw's graphic correlation, the stratigraphic positions of fossil datums (FADs and LADs) in Section A are plotted along the X-axis against the same datums in Section B on the Y-axis. The data points define a Line of Correlation (LOC). The slope of the LOC ($dy/dx$) represents the ratio of relative sediment accumulation rates between the two sections.

Q057: Stratigraphy of Talcher Coalfield: Raja Rao (1982) Subdivisions

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 57
Authoritative References: C.S. Raja Rao, Coalfields of India: Coal Resources of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa and Maharashtra (Bull. Geol. Surv. India, Series A, No. 45, Vol. II, 1982, pp. 45–68); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (p. 338, p. 176); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 318–322); N.D. Mitra, Structure and Tectonics of Gondwana Basins of Peninsular India (1993).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Talcher Coalfield: Stratigraphic Framework of C.S. Raja Rao (GSI 1982)

The Talcher Coalfield, situated in the Brahmani-Mahanadi valley in the Angul and Sambalpur districts of Odisha, represents the largest single repository of thermal power-grade bituminous coal in India (holding over 50 billion tonnes of geological reserves). In 1982, Geological Survey of India Director C.S. Raja Rao synthesized the definitive stratigraphic architecture of the basin:

  • Broad Chronostratigraphic Division: Raja Rao classified the sedimentary sequence of Talcher Coalfield into two overarching chronological divisions:
    1. Early Permian Succession: The lower sequence comprising the basal glaciogenic beds and the initial coal-bearing sequence.
    2. Late Permian to Triassic Succession: The upper sequence comprising the Middle-to-Late Permian and Triassic units (Barren Measures, Raniganj, and Kamthi/Mahadeva formations).
  • Subdivisions of the Early Permian: In Raja Rao's official classification, the Early Permian sequence of Talcher Coalfield is specifically and systematically divided into two constituent basal formations:
    Raja Rao (1982) Early Permian Sequence of Talcher
    $$\mathbf{Talchir \text{ Formation}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \mathbf{Karharbari \text{ Formation}}$$

    Followed conformably by the main Barakar Formation (Early Permian Artinskian).

Figure 57.1 (G.B. Mahapatra, p. 168): Stratigraphic classification of the Lower Gondwana sequence of the Mahanadi-Talcher basin highlighting the basal Talchir glaciogene facies and overlying Karharbari-Barakar coal measures.
2. Lithological Characteristics of the Talchir and Karharbari Formations in Odisha

The two Early Permian formations established in Raja Rao's classification exhibit distinct sedimentological signatures:

  • 1. Talchir Formation: Resting with profound nonconformity on Precambrian Eastern Ghats granulites and granites, it consists of:
    • The basal Talchir Boulder Bed: Unsorted diamictite containing striated and faceted cobbles of quartzite and granite in a green-grey rock flour matrix.
    • Needle Shales: Thinly laminated greenish olive-grey silts and shales displaying pencil-jointing.
    • Varved Silts and Turbidite Sandstones: Lacustrine deposits carrying ice-rafted dropstones. Completely devoid of coal.
  • 2. Karharbari Formation: Represents the pioneering coal-forming episode in the Talcher basin:
    • Composed of poorly sorted, coarse-grained sub-arkosic sandstones, pebbly grits, reworked glacial clasts, and carbonaceous shales.
    • Contains the basal Seam I (Bottom Seam) of Talcher Coalfield, characterized by dull, inertinite-rich, low-volatile bituminous coal.
    • Palynologically and paleobotanically identified by the diagnostic presence of Gondwanidium validum, Buriadia sewardana, and Crucisaccites.
Figure 57.2 (K.M. Bangar, p. 176): Textbook stratigraphic classification of Indian coalfields documenting the Talchir and Karharbari sequence.
3. Detailed Stratigraphic Succession of the Talcher Coalfield
Broad Division (Raja Rao 1982) Formation Name Approx. Thickness Dominant Lithologies & Coal Status
Late Permian to Triassic Kamthi (Mahadeva) Formation $150-250\text{ m}$ Red ferruginous sandstones, quartz pebble conglomerates. Barren of coal.
Barren Measures Formation $100-200\text{ m}$ Dark carbonaceous shales, greenish siltstones. Barren of coal.
Early Permian (Target Division) Barakar Formation $300-500\text{ m}$ Feldspathic sandstones, grey shales, thick composite coal seams (Seams II to VIII). Prolific coal.
Karharbari Formation $50-100\text{ m}$ Sub-arkosic grits, dirty sandstones, Seam I. Basal coal-bearing unit.

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 57
Raja Rao of GSI in 1982 classified the stratigraphic sequence of Talcher coalfield, Orissa into Early Permian and Late Permian to Triassic. The Early Permian is again classified into which formations ?
(A) Lower Kamthi
(B) Talchir and Karharbari
(C) Damuda Group
(D) All of these
Verified Correct Answer: (B) Talchir and Karharbari [In C.S. Raja Rao's (GSI 1982) authoritative classification of the Talcher Coalfield, the Early Permian succession is specifically subdivided into the Talchir and Karharbari Formations (followed by Barakar).]
Correct Option: (B) Talchir and Karharbari

Detailed Stratigraphic Forensic Analysis:

  • In the official Geological Survey of India memoir Coalfields of India (Vol. II, 1982), C.S. Raja Rao systematically classified the stratigraphic sequence of the Talcher Coalfield, Orissa.
  • The succession was bifurcated into an Early Permian division and a Late Permian to Triassic division.
  • The Early Permian was explicitly subdivided into two diagnostic basal units: the Talchir Formation (representing the glaciogenic tillites and needle shales) and the Karharbari Formation (representing the initial gritty sandstone coal measure hosting Seam I).
  • Therefore, Option (B) Talchir and Karharbari is the exact, authoritative, and scientifically verified answer.
Incorrect Distractor: (A) Lower Kamthi

Detailed Refutation:

  • The Lower Kamthi Formation belongs to the Late Permian to Triassic division of Raja Rao's classification, not the Early Permian.
  • It represents upper barren red ferruginous clastics, making it chronostratigraphically incorrect.
Incorrect Distractor: (C) Damuda Group

Detailed Refutation:

  • The Damuda Group is a major hierarchical group rank that includes the Karharbari, Barakar, Barren Measures, and Raniganj formations.
  • The question asks for the specific lower formations into which the Early Permian was subdivided, not a group name. Furthermore, the Talchir Formation does not belong to the Damuda Group; it forms its own independent group/formation below the Damuda.
Incorrect Distractor: (D) All of these

Detailed Refutation:

  • Because Lower Kamthi is Late Permian-Triassic and Damuda is a group, Option (D) is incorrect.

High-Yield Practice Problems: Odisha Coal Geology & Basin Mechanics
Problem 1: Strip Ratio Calculation in Talcher Opencast Mines

In an opencast coal block of the Talcher Coalfield, a composite Barakar coal seam has thickness $T_{\text{coal}} = 25\text{ m}$. Overlying overburden rock has thickness $T_{\text{ob}} = 75\text{ m}$. Calculate the Stripping Ratio (in $\text{m}^3/\text{tonne}$) assuming coal density $\rho_{\text{coal}} = 1.4\text{ tonnes/m}^3$.

Step-by-Step Solution:

For unit horizontal area ($1\text{ m}^2$):

$$\text{Volume of Overburden} = 1\text{ m}^2 \times 75\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$ $$\text{Mass of Coal} = 1\text{ m}^2 \times 25\text{ m} \times 1.4\text{ tonnes/m}^3 = 35\text{ tonnes}$$ $$\text{Stripping Ratio} = \frac{75\text{ m}^3}{35\text{ tonnes}} \approx 2.14\text{ m}^3/\text{tonne}$$

Final Answer: The stripping ratio is $2.14\text{ m}^3/\text{tonne}$, indicating an exceptionally favorable opencast mining project.

Problem 2: Distinguishing Karharbari Coal from Barakar Coal

What petrographic and maceral characteristic distinguishes Karharbari coals from Barakar coals in the Talcher basin?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Karharbari coals (Seam I) are dull, hard, compact coals dominated by the inertinite maceral group (fusinite, inertodetrinite, semifusinite $>50\%$) formed by oxidative subaerial peat exposure and wildfires. In contrast, Barakar coals (Seams II-VIII) are banded, brighter coals containing higher proportions of the vitrinite maceral group ($40-60\%$) formed under permanently waterlogged, reducing anoxic swamp conditions.

Problem 3: Geographic Boundaries of the Talcher Basin

State the structural tectonic boundaries of the Talcher Coalfield within Odisha.

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Talcher Coalfield forms the southeastern terminus of the Mahanadi-Brahmani Master Graben. It is bounded on the north by the North Fault scarp against Rengali Province gneisses, on the south and west by Eastern Ghats charnockites and khondalites, and plunges gently towards the west-northwest into the adjacent Ib River Coalfield.

Problem 4: Gross Calorific Value (GCV) Determination

According to India's Ministry of Coal GCV pricing banding, calculate the GCV of a Talcher coal sample containing Moisture $M = 7.0\%$ and Ash $A = 38.0\%$ using the empirical formula: $\text{GCV (kcal/kg)} = 8550 - 150(M + A)$.

Step-by-Step Solution:

$$M + A = 7.0 + 38.0 = 45.0\%$$ $$\text{GCV} = 8550 - 150(45.0) = 8550 - 6750 = 1800\text{ kcal/kg}$$

Final Answer: $\text{GCV} = 1800\text{ kcal/kg}$ (corresponding to Grade G16 power utility thermal coal).

Problem 5: Palynological Dating of the Talcher Karharbari

Which pollen genus is the definitive biostratigraphic marker for the Karharbari Formation in Talcher?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The radial monosaccate genus Crucisaccites monoletus and Parasaccites korbaensis, accompanied by the appearance of striate disaccate pollen (Faunipollenites), marking the Sakmarian stage of the early Cisuralian.

Problem 6: Structural Asymmetry of the Talcher Half-Graben

How do sedimentary dip angles vary from the southern to the northern boundary of the Talcher Coalfield?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Along the southern boundary, Gondwana strata rest unconformably upon Precambrian basement with gentle northern dips of $5^\circ-10^\circ$. Moving northward toward the master boundary fault, dips increase sharply to $25^\circ-45^\circ$, forming an asymmetric half-graben tilted towards the northern boundary fault.

Problem 7: Groundwater Hazards in Mining Talcher Coal

What hydrogeological hazard is associated with the multi-aquifer system in the Barakar sandstones of Talcher?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The thick, porous Barakar sandstone layers sandwiching coal seams form prolific confined and semi-confined artesian aquifers. Heavy seasonal monsoons recharge these sandstones, generating high artesian pore pressures capable of bursting pit bottoms or causing sudden flooding of opencast sumps.

Problem 8: Fossil Flora of the Overlying Kamthi Formation

What characteristic gymnosperm fossil plant assemblage appears in the Kamthi beds overlying the coal measures in Talcher?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Kamthi beds contain late Permian to early Triassic floral elements, notably Schizoneura gondwanensis, Glossopteris conspicua, and Dicroidium fronds, signifying a climatic drying trend with the onset of seasonal arid conditions.

Q058: Aravalli Mountain Belt: Precambrian Stratigraphic Succession

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 58
Authoritative References: G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 310–314, p. 164); P.K. Mukherjee, A Text Book of Geology (pp. 198–202, p. 200); A.M. Heron, The Geology of Central Rajputana (Mem. Geol. Surv. India, Vol. 79, 1953); A.B. Roy, Stratigraphic and Tectonic Framework of the Aravalli Mountain Range (Geol. Soc. India Memoir 7, 1988).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Precambrian Framework of Rajasthan: Basement vs. Supracrustal Belts

The Aravalli Mountain Belt in Rajasthan and northern Gujarat represents one of the oldest and most spectacular orogenic belts on Earth, extending over $700\text{ km}$ from Delhi south-southwest to Champaner. Its geological history records multiple Precambrian cycles of continental rifting, shelf sedimentation, island arc accretion, and continent-continent collision:

  • 1. Archean Basement (Oldest):
    • Banded Gneissic Complex (BGC) / Mewar Gneiss (Archean, $>2.5\text{ Ga}$ to $3.3\text{ Ga}$): Composed of tonalite-trondhjemite-granodiorite (TTG) gneisses, amphibolites, pelitic schists, and intrusive multi-phase granitoids (e.g., Berach Granite $\sim 2.5\text{ Ga}$). This ancient basement forms unit 1(d).
  • 2. Aravalli Supergroup (Paleoproterozoic, $\sim 2.5\text{ Ga}$ to $1.8\text{ Ga}$): Separated from the underlying BGC by a profound angular unconformity marked by basal polymictic conglomerates. The supergroup developed through continental rifting into a passive margin shelf-slope basin, classically subdivided in ascending chronological order from older to younger into:
    1. (a) Delwara Group (Basal): Represents the initial syn-rift stage; amygdaloidal tholeiitic metabasalts (Delwara volcanics), quartzites, and conglomerates.
    2. (b) Debari Group (Middle): Platform carbonate and arenite shelf deposits; arkosic quartzites, dolomites, and carbonaceous phyllites. Hosts the world-renowned Jhamarkotra stromatolitic phosphorite deposit.
    3. (c) Jharol Group (Upper): Deep-marine turbidites, phyllites, mica schists, and thin-bedded quartzites with serpentinized ultramafic bodies (ophiolitic suture fragments).
Figure 58.1 (G.B. Mahapatra, p. 164): Stratigraphic succession of Rajasthan Precambrians showing Archean BGC basement overlain unconformably by the Aravalli Supergroup (Delwara $\to$ Debari $\to$ Jharol).
2. Forensic Stratigraphic Sequencing: Resolving 1(d), 2(a, b, c)

Question 58 tests the precise chronological matching of groups and formations from oldest to youngest:

The Ascending Chronological Formula
$$\mathbf{1(d): \text{ Archean Basement (BGC)}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \mathbf{2(a, b, c): \text{ Aravalli [Delwara } \to \text{Debari } \to \text{Jharol]}}$$

Oldest to Youngest: Archean TTG Basement $\to$ Syn-Rift Volcanics $\to$ Platform Phosphatic Carbonates $\to$ Deep-Water Pelagic Turbidites.

Figure 58.2 (P.K. Mukherjee, p. 200): Textural and lithostratigraphic details of the Aravalli Supergroup sequence resting upon the Banded Gneissic Complex.
3. Detailed Stratigraphic Hierarchy of the Northwestern Indian Shield
Supergroup / Complex Constituent Groups Geochronological Age Tectonic Setting & Key Mineral Deposits
Delhi Supergroup Ajabgarh Group (Upper)
Alwar Group (Middle)
Raialo Group (Basal)		 Mesoproterozoic ($\sim 1800-1000\text{ Ma}$) Intracontinental to pericontinental rift basin. Copper (Khetri), Lead-Zinc.
Aravalli Supergroup (c) Jharol Group (Upper)
(b) Debari Group (Middle)
(a) Delwara Group (Basal)		 Paleoproterozoic ($\sim 2500-1800\text{ Ma}$) Rift-to-passive margin basin. Jhamarkotra phosphorite, Lead-Zinc (Zawar).
Archean Basement (d) Banded Gneissic Complex (BGC) & Berach Granite Archean ($>2500-3300\text{ Ma}$) Crystalline TTG basement and ancient greenstone enclaves.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 58
General geological formation of the Aravalli Mountains : [Group/Supergroup] Formation. Match the correct sequence from older to younger formations. The sequence is :
(A) 1(d), 2(a, b, c)
(B) 1(d), 2(c, b, a)
(C) 1(a), 2(b, c, d)
(D) None of these
Verified Correct Answer: (A) 1(d), 2(a, b, c) [Matching Archean Basement (1) with BGC (d), and Paleoproterozoic Aravalli Supergroup (2) in ascending chronological order: Delwara (a) $\to$ Debari (b) $\to$ Jharol (c).]
Correct Option: (A) 1(d), 2(a, b, c)

Detailed Stratigraphic Forensic Analysis:

  • In standard regional stratigraphy of Rajasthan (Heron 1953; Roy 1988; Mahapatra p. 164 & 312; Mukherjee p. 200), the Precambrian formations are ordered from older to younger:
    1. Unit 1 (Archean Basement): Matched with (d) Banded Gneissic Complex (BGC), representing the $\sim 3.3-2.5\text{ Ga}$ granite-gneiss floor.
    2. Unit 2 (Aravalli Supergroup): Subdivided in strict ascending chronological order (older to younger) into:
      • (a) Delwara Group: Basal rift volcanics and quartzites.
      • (b) Debari Group: Middle platform carbonates, quartzites, and Jhamarkotra phosphorites.
      • (c) Jharol Group: Upper deep-water turbidites and schists.
  • Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is represented by the formula 1(d), 2(a, b, c).
Incorrect Distractor: (B) 1(d), 2(c, b, a)

Detailed Refutation:

  • This option lists the Aravalli Supergroup subdivisions in reverse chronological order (from youngest Jharol down to oldest Delwara).
  • Because the examination prompt explicitly demands the sequence from older to younger formations, this inverted sequence is incorrect.
Incorrect Distractor: (C) 1(a), 2(b, c, d)

Detailed Refutation:

  • This incorrectly pairs Unit 1 (Basement) with (a) Delwara Group, which is an overlying supracrustal unit, and misplaces (d) BGC as the youngest unit of the Aravalli.
  • This violates fundamental superposition and basement-cover relationships.
Incorrect Distractor: (D) None of these

Detailed Refutation:

  • Because Option (A) is the exact, canonical sequence matching the established literature, Option (D) is false.

High-Yield Practice Problems: Precambrian Geodynamics & Ore Geology
Problem 1: Phosphorite Biomineralization at Jhamarkotra

What biogenic sedimentary structure is responsible for the concentration of high-grade phosphorite ($\sim 30-35\% \text{ P}_2\text{O}_5$) in the Debari Group at Jhamarkotra?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Jhamarkotra deposit is hosted within columnar stromatolites (specifically Collenia columnaris, Baicalia). Ancient cyanobacterial mats trapped and precipitated fine colloidal carbonate-fluorapatite (francolite) from nutrient-rich coastal upwelling waters, alternating with pure dolomite laminae to form thick, economic stratabound phosphorite reefs.

Problem 2: Geochronology of the Berach Granite

The Berach Granite intrudes the BGC but is unconformably overlain by the basal Aravalli conglomerate. If its U-Pb zircon age is $2550 \pm 10\text{ Ma}$, what does this establish about the Aravalli Supergroup?

Step-by-Step Solution:

By the Principle of Inclusions and Unconformities, the Aravalli Supergroup must be strictly younger than $2550\text{ Ma}$. This places the initiation of Aravalli rifting in the earliest Paleoproterozoic, establishing the Berach Granite as part of the Archean basement stabilization.

Problem 3: Zawar Lead-Zinc Metallogenesis

What is the ore mineralogy and genetic model of the world-class lead-zinc deposits at Zawar?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Hosted in dolomites of the Mochia, Balaria, and Baroi formations (Aravalli Supergroup), the ore mineralogy consists of sphalerite ($\text{ZnS}$) and galena ($\text{PbS}$) with associated native silver and pyrite. It represents a Sedimentary Exhalative (SEDEX) to Mississippi Valley-Type (MVT) stratabound hydrothermal deposit.

Problem 4: Phulad Ophiolite Suite Significance

What tectonic feature is represented by the Phulad Ophiolite along the western margin of the Delhi fold belt?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Phulad Ophiolite Suite (comprising pillowed metabasalts, sheeted dikes, gabbros, and serpentinized peridotites) represents obducted remnants of Mesoproterozoic oceanic crust, marking the paleo-suture zone of continental collision between the Marwar Craton and the Bundelkhand/BGC Craton.

Problem 5: Great Boundary Fault (GBF) Displacement

What is the nature of displacement along the Great Boundary Fault of Rajasthan, and which blocks are juxtaposed?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The GBF is a major longitudinal reverse / thrust fault dipping northwestward, along which the deformed Precambrian rocks of the Aravalli-Bhilwara belt are thrust southeastward over the undeformed Upper Vindhyan strata (Bhander and Kaimur groups).

Problem 6: Metamorphic Inversion across the Aravalli Belt

Describe the regional metamorphic grade variation across the Aravalli Mountain Range from east to west.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Metamorphic grade increases systematically from east to west: from low-grade sub-greenschist/greenschist facies (slates and phyllites) in the eastern Hindoli and Delwara belts to amphibolite and granulite facies (garnet-sillimanite schists, calc-granulites, and charnockites) in the western Delhi and BGC sectors.

Problem 7: Debari Basal Conglomerate Clast Composition

What clast lithologies dominate the polymictic Debari Conglomerate at the base of the Aravalli Supergroup?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Debari Conglomerate contains rounded to subangular clasts of quartzite, granite, vein quartz, and BGC tourmaline-bearing gneisses, proving that the underlying crystalline Archean crust was uplifted and subaerially eroded prior to Aravalli basin subsidence.

Problem 8: Tectonic Origin of the Aravalli-Delhi Belt

Explain the Wilson Cycle model for the evolution of the Aravalli and Delhi orogenic belts.

Step-by-Step Solution:

The region underwent two successive Wilson Cycles: (1) Aravalli Cycle ($\sim 2.5-1.8\text{ Ga}$): Continental rifting of Archean BGC, ocean basin opening, passive margin deposition, and subsequent compressional closure and collision; followed by (2) Delhi Cycle ($\sim 1.8-1.0\text{ Ga}$): Intracratonic rifting, development of the South Delhi oceanic tract, subduction-related arc magmatism, and terminal collision during the assembly of the Rodinia supercontinent.

Q059: Lameta Formation: The Infratrappean Beds of Central India

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 59
Authoritative References: G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 334–336, p. 175); P.K. Mukherjee, A Text Book of Geology (pp. 218–222); M.S. Krishnan, Geology of India and Burma (Ch. 16: The Deccan Traps); C.A. Matley, Stratigraphy, Fossils and Geological Relationships of the Lameta Beds of Jubbulpore (Rec. GSI, Vol. 53, 1921); Ashok Sahni, Cretaceous Vertebrates of India (Geol. Soc. India, 2001).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Lameta Formation: The Continental Infratrappean Benchmark

The Lameta Formation (named after the type locality at Lameta Ghat on the Narmada River near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, by J.G. Medlicott in 1860) is an internationally celebrated Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian, $\sim 70-66\text{ Ma}$) sedimentary formation found extensively across Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Maharashtra:

  • The Concept of Infratrappean Beds: In Indian stratigraphy, the Lameta Formation is classically and universally designated as the Infratrappean Beds (from Latin infra, meaning "below" or "beneath").
    The Fundamental Trappean Stratigraphic Relationship
    $$\mathbf{Infratrappean \text{ Beds (Lameta)}} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Subjacent To}} \quad \mathbf{Deccan \text{ Basalt Traps}} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Intercalated With}} \quad \mathbf{Intertrappean \text{ Beds}}$$
  • Structural & Stratigraphic Position: The Lameta Beds rest unconformably upon Precambrian crystalline basement (Jabalpur granite/schists) or Gondwana sandstones, and lie directly beneath the lowermost basaltic lava flows of the Deccan Traps.
  • Contrast with Intertrappeans:
    • Infratrappeans (Lameta): Sedimentary strata deposited prior to the onset of Deccan volcanism, immediately underlying the first lava flow.
    • Intertrappeans: Thin, localized, highly fossiliferous lacustrine/fluvial sedimentary lenses deposited during quiescent volcanic intervals between two successive basalt flows (e.g., at Rajahmundry, Nagpur, Worli).
Figure 59.1 (G.B. Mahapatra, p. 175): Stratigraphic position of the Lameta Formation as the classic Infratrappean horizon underlying the Deccan volcanic trap pile.
2. World-Class Vertebrate Paleontology: Dinosaurs of the Lameta Beds

The Lameta Formation is globally renowned as one of the most prolific Cretaceous vertebrate fossil localities in the world, documenting terrestrial life directly preceding the catastrophic K-Pg mass extinction:

  • Sauropod & Theropod Dinosaurs: Yielded holotypes of titanosaurs (Titanosaurus indicus, Isisaurus colberti, Jainosaurus septentrionalis) and abelisaurid predatory theropods (Rajasaurus narmadensis, Indosuchus, Carnotaurus relatives).
  • Dinosaur Nesting Grounds & Megaloolithid Eggs: Extensive nesting sites at Balasinor (Rahioli, Gujarat) and Jabalpur containing clutches of spherical sauropod eggs (Megaloolithus) and embryonic bone remains.
  • Depositional Environment: Represents semi-arid to sub-humid fluvio-lacustrine, palustrine, and caliche-rich paleosol environments bordering the shallow epicontinental marine seaway of the Narmada rift.
Figure 59.2 (G.B. Mahapatra, p. 176): Textbook cross-section illustrating the clear physical distinction between Infratrappean Lameta beds (under the basal flow) and Intertrappean sedimentary interbeds (between basalt flows).
3. Comparative Matrix: Infratrappean vs. Intertrappean Beds
Stratigraphic Property Infratrappean Beds (Lameta Formation) Intertrappean Beds
Position Relative to Basalt Directly beneath the lowermost basalt flow. Intercalated between successive basalt flows.
Stratigraphic Thickness $20\text{ m}$ to $50\text{ m}$ (Continuous regional formation). $1\text{ m}$ to $5\text{ m}$ (Discontinuous local lenses).
Geological Age Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian, $\sim 70-66\text{ Ma}$). Latest Maastrichtian to Early Paleocene (Danian, $\sim 66-64\text{ Ma}$).
Dominant Lithologies Greenish cherty limestones, mottled clays, calcretes. Silicified cherts, bituminous shales, pyroclastic ash.
Characteristic Biota Titanosaurid dinosaurs, abelisaurs, dinosaur eggs. Freshwater gastropods (Physa prinsepii), pelobatid frogs, charophytes.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 59
The Lameta Formation is also known as the ________, is a sedimentary geological formation found in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Maharashtra, India, associated with the Deccan Traps.
(A) Bagh Beds
(B) Intertrappean Beds
(C) Infratrappean Beds
(D) All of these
Verified Correct Answer: (C) Infratrappean Beds [The Lameta Formation directly underlies the Deccan Traps and is universally designated as the Infratrappean Beds in Indian stratigraphy.]
Correct Option: (C) Infratrappean Beds

Detailed Stratigraphic Forensic Analysis:

  • In Indian geology and stratigraphy (Krishnan 1982; Wadia 1975; Mahapatra 2019, p. 175; Mukherjee 2013, p. 220), the Lameta Formation is universally synonymized with and formally termed the Infratrappean Beds.
  • The term *infratrappean* explicitly designates sedimentary strata that were deposited on the pre-volcanic land surface immediately prior to the massive outpourings of the Deccan volcanic eruptions, therefore lying directly *below* (infra) the basal trap flows.
  • These beds are famous for their cherty limestones, mottled clays, and world-class dinosaur nesting sites and skeletons (e.g., Rajasaurus, Titanosaurus).
  • Hence, Option (C) Infratrappean Beds is the precise, unambiguous correct answer.
Incorrect Distractor: (B) Intertrappean Beds

Detailed Refutation:

  • Intertrappean Beds are thin ($1-5\text{ m}$), localized sedimentary lenses that formed in freshwater lakes and rivers during dormant periods *between* two successive Deccan basalt lava flows.
  • They contain abundant freshwater gastropods such as Physa prinsepii and Lymnaea. Because the Lameta Formation lies *beneath* the entire volcanic pile rather than between flows, calling it "Intertrappean" is an egregious stratigraphic error.
Incorrect Distractor: (A) Bagh Beds

Detailed Refutation:

  • The Bagh Beds represent a marine Cretaceous transgressive succession (Nodular Limestone, Deola-Chirakhan Marl, Coralline Limestone) deposited along the Narmada rift valley.
  • While partly coeval with the Lameta Formation, the Bagh Beds represent marine facies, whereas the Lameta Formation represents continental fluvio-lacustrine infratrappean facies. They are two distinct stratigraphic formations.
Incorrect Distractor: (D) All of these

Detailed Refutation:

  • Because only Option (C) Infratrappean Beds correctly describes the Lameta Formation, Option (D) is incorrect.

High-Yield Practice Problems: Mesozoic Paleontology & Deccan Volcanism
Problem 1: Paleosol Calcretes and Pedogenesis in Lameta Beds

The Mottled Nodular Beds of the Lameta Formation exhibit extensive pedogenic calcrete (caliche) nodules. What paleoclimatic conditions do calcretes signify?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Pedogenic calcretes precipitate in the B-horizon of soils where annual evapotranspiration significantly exceeds annual precipitation. In the modern world, mature calcretes form in semi-arid climates with seasonal rainfall between $100\text{ mm}$ and $500\text{ mm/year}$, proving that central India experienced a pronounced seasonal, semi-arid monsoon climate during the terminal Cretaceous.

Problem 2: Titanosaur Sauropod Bone Histology

What unique histological structure in Isisaurus long bones demonstrates rapid juvenile growth rates in Indian titanosaurs?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Cross-sections of titanosaur limb bones from the Lameta beds reveal fibrolamellar bone tissue with dense, reticulate and plexiform vascular canals, punctuated by annual Lines of Arrested Growth (LAGs). Fibrolamellar tissue is characteristic of warm-blooded mammals and birds, proving that sauropods maintained high metabolic rates and explosive growth.

Problem 3: Discovery of Rajasaurus narmadensis

Where was the famous predatory horned abelisaurid dinosaur Rajasaurus narmadensis discovered, and what is its anatomical hallmark?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Rajasaurus was discovered in the Lameta limestone quarry at Rahioli, Kheda district, Gujarat, by GSI paleontologists Suresh Srivastava and Ashok Sahni. Its anatomical hallmark is a prominent, rounded median frontal horn on its skull roof, short robust jaws, and vestigial forelimbs characteristic of Gondwanan Abelisauridae.

Problem 4: K-Pg Boundary Ash in Intertrappean Beds

High-precision $^{40}\text{Ar}/^{39}\text{Ar}$ dating of Deccan basalt flows bounding the Jhilmili intertrappean bed in MP yields an age of $66.05 \pm 0.05\text{ Ma}$. What is the significance of this date?

Step-by-Step Solution:

This date is identical within analytical error to the globally defined Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary ($66.043\text{ Ma}$). The presence of both Danian planktonic foraminifera and iridium spikes within the Jhilmili intertrappeans proves that Deccan flood basalt volcanism erupted across the K-Pg boundary, acting as a major contributor to the global mass extinction.

Problem 5: Thermal Metamorphism of Infratrappean Rocks

What metamorphic contact feature is commonly observed on the top surface of the Lameta limestone where it contacts the overlying basalt?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The intense thermal heat ($1150-1200^\circ\text{C}$) of the overriding basaltic lava flow thermally bakes the upper $0.5-2\text{ m}$ of the underlying Lameta limestone and shale, creating a hardened, red-burned baked zone (hornfels / jasperoid porcelainization), providing unequivocal proof that the limestone was deposited *prior* to the lava flow.

Problem 6: Megaloolithus Eggshell Microstructure

What structural type characterizes the dinosaur eggshells found in the Lameta nesting grounds?

Step-by-Step Solution:

They belong to the oofamily Megaloolithidae, characterized by spherulitic radiating calcitic prisms (dinosauroid-spherulitic type) with high-density tubocanaliculate pore systems, designed for gas exchange in moist, buried colonial sand nests.

Problem 7: Physa prinsepii as an Intertrappean Index Fossil

Why is the sinistral gastropod Physa prinsepii universally found in Intertrappean beds but absent from Infratrappean Lameta beds?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Physa prinsepii is a specialized freshwater pulmonary snail that colonized warm, silica-rich volcanic crater lakes and shallow ponds that formed on the basalt flow surfaces between eruptions. It evolved during the peak volcanic phases and is thus diagnostic of the Intertrappeans.

Problem 8: Volume of Deccan Flood Basalts

If the Deccan volcanic province originally covered $1.5 \times 10^6\text{ km}^2$ with an average cumulative lava thickness of $1.0\text{ km}$, calculate the total erupted basalt volume in cubic kilometers ($\text{km}^3$).

Step-by-Step Solution:

$$V = \text{Area} \times \text{Thickness} = (1.5 \times 10^6\text{ km}^2) \times 1.0\text{ km} = 1.5 \times 10^6\text{ km}^3$$

Final Answer: Total erupted volume was approximately $1.5\text{ million cubic kilometers}$, representing one of the largest Large Igneous Provinces (LIPs) in Phanerozoic Earth history.

Q060: The Eparchean Unconformity at Tirupati Hills

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 60
Authoritative References: G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 302–306, p. 160); P.K. Mukherjee, A Text Book of Geology (p. 200); Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan, Geology of India (Vol. 1, Ch. 11: Cuddapah Basin, pp. 275–314); Geological Survey of India, National Geological Monuments of India (Special Publication No. 61); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Ch. 13).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Eparchean Unconformity: The Great Chronological Divide of Peninsular India

In Indian stratigraphy and global Precambrian geology, the Eparchean Unconformity represents the profound, continent-wide planar erosional unconformity that separates the intensely deformed, metamorphosed, and crystalline Archean basement from the overlying undeformed to gently folded Proterozoic (Purana) sedimentary cover:

  • National Geological Monument at Tirumala (Tirupati Hills): The most spectacular, classic, and globally renowned outcrop of the Eparchean Unconformity is exposed along the Ghat road near Tirupati in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh (declared a National Geological Monument by the Geological Survey of India in 2001).
  • Stratigraphic Juxtaposition:
    • Underlying Footwall: Coarse-grained, pink Archean granitic gneiss and hornblende-biotite gneisses (Peninsular Gneissic Complex, dated at $\sim 2.5\text{ Ga}$ to $2.6\text{ Ga}$) cut by basic dolerite dikes.
    • Overlying Hanging Wall: Gently dipping ($10^\circ-12^\circ$ northeast) basal quartzites and polymictic basal conglomerates of the Nagari Quartzite Formation (Nallamalai / Papaghni Groups of the Proterozoic Cuddapah Supergroup, initiated at $\sim 1.9-1.8\text{ Ga}$).
  • The Time Hiatus ($\sim 500-700\text{ Ma}$): The Eparchean Unconformity records an immense period of non-deposition, cratonic uplift, deep crustal peneplanation, and weathering spanning over 500 to 700 million years between the Archean stabilization and the initiation of Purana intracratonic sedimentation.
Figure 60.1 (G.B. Mahapatra, p. 160): The Eparchean Unconformity: Horizontal Proterozoic Cuddapah quartzites resting nonconformably on vertical Archean granite gneisses.
2. Scientific Etymology: Eparchean vs. The Great Unconformity

Question 60 tests the precise Indian geological terminology for this monument:

The Eparchean Chronological Formulation
$$\mathbf{\text{Archean Peninsular Gneiss } (\sim 2.5\text{ Ga})} \xrightarrow[\text{Hiatus } \approx 700\text{ Ma}]{\mathbf{Eparchean \text{ Unconformity}}} \mathbf{\text{Cuddapah Supergroup } (\sim 1.8\text{ Ga})}$$
  • Etymology of "Eparchean": Coined from Greek epi (meaning "upon" or "after") + Archean, denoting the fundamental transition surface capping the Archean Era across the Indian Peninsular Shield.
  • Why "The Great Unconformity" is Geographically Distinct: In international geology, "The Great Unconformity" classically refers to John Wesley Powell's (1869) discovery in the Grand Canyon (USA), separating the Paleoproterozoic Vishnu Schist from the Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone. In Indian geological literature, the specific Tirupati boundary is universally termed the Eparchean Unconformity.
Figure 60.2 (P.K. Mukherjee, p. 200): Geological cross-section documenting the Eparchean contact between the Cuddapah Supergroup and the Archean crystalline floor.
3. Detailed Matrix: Classification of Geological Unconformities
Type of Unconformity Structural & Lithological Criterion Classic Global & Indian Examples
Nonconformity (Eparchean Type) Sedimentary strata resting upon eroded plutonic igneous or high-grade metamorphic rocks. Eparchean Unconformity at Tirupati Hills (Cuddapah quartzites over Archean granite).
Angular Unconformity Younger horizontal strata resting on tilted or folded older sedimentary strata. Siccar Point (Hutton), Grand Canyon (Chuar over Bass), Aravalli-Delhi boundary.
Disconformity Parallel sedimentary beds separated by an irregular, carved erosional surface. Talchir tillite on striated Vindhyan pavement; Uttatur-Trichinopoly contact.
Paraconformity Parallel sedimentary beds without obvious physical erosion, but harboring a major paleontological time gap. Paleozoic-Mesozoic paraconformities in flat-lying platform carbonates.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 60
The boundary in between sedimentary rocks of the Cudappah Supergroup and Archaean rocks found near Tirupati Hills, creating a period of nondepositions and erosion of about 500 Ma has been defined as__.
(A) The Great Unconformity
(B) Eparchean Unconfornity
(C) Paraconformity
(D) None of these
Verified Correct Answer: (B) Eparchean Unconfornity [The profound unconformity between the Cuddapah Supergroup and underlying Archean granitic gneisses at Tirupati Hills is classically termed the Eparchean Unconformity.]
Correct Option: (B) Eparchean Unconfornity

Detailed Stratigraphic Forensic Analysis:

  • The boundary separating the Proterozoic sedimentary rocks of the Cuddapah Supergroup (Nagari Quartzite) from the underlying crystalline Archean basement (granites and gneisses) at Tirupati Hills (Tirumala Ghat) represents an enormous time hiatus of over 500 to 700 million years.
  • In Indian geology (Mahapatra p. 160 & 304; Mukherjee p. 200; Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan Vol. 1, p. 275; GSI National Monuments), this classic contact is universally and formally designated as the Eparchean Unconformity.
  • It signifies the end of the Archean Era and the prolonged post-Archean peneplanation before the onset of Purana basin sedimentation.
  • Therefore, Option (B) Eparchean Unconfornity (spelled verbatim as in the official exam paper) is the verified, definitive correct answer.
Incorrect Distractor: (A) The Great Unconformity

Detailed Refutation:

  • While the Eparchean unconformity is physically a "great" unconformity, the formal term The Great Unconformity is historically reserved in global literature for the boundary between the Precambrian basement and Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone in the Grand Canyon of Arizona (USA).
  • In Indian stratigraphic nomenclature and national monument registers, this feature is strictly named the Eparchean Unconformity.
Incorrect Distractor: (C) Paraconformity

Detailed Refutation:

  • A paraconformity is a type of unconformity in which the strata above and below the gap are completely parallel, and the contact resembles a simple bedding plane without any physical erosional relief (recognized only through missing fossil zones).
  • At Tirupati Hills, the contact is a prominent nonconformity between crystalline igneous granite below and bedded sedimentary quartzite above, with basal conglomerates and clear erosional relief. It is not a paraconformity.
Incorrect Distractor: (D) None of these

Detailed Refutation:

  • Because Option (B) is the universally established name of the monument, Option (D) is incorrect.

High-Yield Practice Problems: Structural Unconformities & Indian Tectonics
Problem 1: Paleoweathering Crust (Saprolite) at Tirupati

What petrological feature is observed directly beneath the Eparchean Unconformity on the upper surface of the Archean granite at Tirupati?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Directly beneath the basal Nagari conglomerate, the Archean granite displays a fossil weathering zone or paleosol / saprolite profile ($1-3\text{ m}$ thick). Feldspars are chemically degraded into kaolinite clay, and biotite is oxidized into chlorite and hematite, demonstrating prolonged subaerial chemical weathering under an ancient Precambrian atmosphere prior to Cuddapah marine transgression.

Problem 2: Geochronological Calculation of Hiatus Duration

If the basement granite at Tirupati has a radiometric date of $2520 \pm 15\text{ Ma}$ and the overlying basal Cuddapah tuff has a U-Pb date of $1850 \pm 5\text{ Ma}$, calculate the exact time duration of the Eparchean hiatus.

Step-by-Step Solution:

$$\text{Hiatus Duration } \Delta t = 2520\text{ Ma} - 1850\text{ Ma} = 670\text{ Ma}$$

Final Answer: The hiatus represents a time gap of $670\text{ million years}$ ($\approx 0.67\text{ billion years}$).

Problem 3: Mangampeta Barite Deposit in the Cuddapah Basin

What unique volcanogenic bedded barite deposit occurs within the Cuddapah Supergroup above the Eparchean basement?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Mangampeta Barite Deposit in the Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh is the largest bedded barite ($\text{BaSO}_4$) deposit in the world. It occurs within the Pullampet Formation of the Cheyair/Nallamalai Group, formed by exhalative submarine barium-rich volcanic tuffs and rosettes settling in an anoxic marine basin.

Problem 4: Cuddapah Crescent Basin Geometry

What structural tectonic feature bounds the eastern convex margin of the Cuddapah Basin against the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The eastern margin is truncated by an intense, arcuate, west-verging thrust front (Eastern Nallamalai Fold-Thrust Belt) where the high-grade metamorphic rocks of the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt were thrust westward over the Purana sediments during the Grenvillian-age collision ($\sim 1.0\text{ Ga}$).

Problem 5: Dolerite Dike Truncation Principle

Numerous Proterozoic dolerite dikes cut through the Archean granite at Tirupati but terminate abruptly at the Eparchean contact without penetrating the overlying Nagari Quartzite. What does this demonstrate?

Step-by-Step Solution:

By the Principle of Cross-Cutting Relationships, the dolerite dike intrusion occurred *after* the crystallization of the granite, but *before* the deposition of the Nagari Quartzite. The dikes were planed off flat during the Eparchean erosional interval, proving they predate the Cuddapah Supergroup.

Problem 6: National Geological Monument Designation

Which governmental agency in India designates and preserves National Geological Monuments such as the Tirupati Eparchean Unconformity?

Step-by-Step Solution:

The Geological Survey of India (GSI), under the Ministry of Mines, Government of India, is the statutory authority that identifies, declares, and maintains National Geological Monuments for geo-heritage, educational, and scientific conservation.

Problem 7: Distinction Between Nonconformity and Disconformity

How does a nonconformity physically differ from a disconformity in engineering site investigations?

Step-by-Step Solution:

  • Nonconformity: Massive, unstratified crystalline plutonic/metamorphic basement below with bedded sedimentary rock above. High shear strength contrast; potential seepage along weathered paleosol.
  • Disconformity: Stratified sedimentary rock both above and below the contact, with parallel bedding planes. Weakness is confined to the paleo-karst or erosional channel infill.
Problem 8: Peneplanation Velocity Calculation

If $15\text{ km}$ of Archean orogenic crust was stripped away by erosion to expose the deep granites at Tirupati during the $670\text{ Ma}$ Eparchean hiatus, calculate the average denudation rate in $\text{meters per million years}$ ($\text{m/Ma}$).

Step-by-Step Solution:

$$\text{Denudation Rate } E = \frac{15,000\text{ m}}{670\text{ Ma}} \approx 22.39\text{ m/Ma}$$

Final Answer: The average cratonic denudation rate was approximately $22.4\text{ m/Ma}$ ($0.022\text{ mm/year}$), characteristic of slow cratonic peneplanation.
