Comprehensive Textural & Structural Framework of Igneous Rocks
Texture / Structure Primary Petrographic Definition Cooling Regime & Environment Nucleation vs Growth Kinetics Canonical Rock Types
Phaneritic Texture Individual mineral grains macroscopic ($>1\text{ mm}$), clearly distinguishable with naked eye Plutonic (Abyssal, deep crustal batholiths & stocks) Low undercooling ($\Delta T$); Low nucleation ($I$), High growth rate ($Y$) Granite, Diorite, Syenite
Ophitic Texture Laths of plagioclase completely enclosed poikilitically in large single pyroxene plates Hypabyssal (Subvolcanic dikes, sills, minor intrusions) Cotectic crystallization; high plagioclase nucleation followed by rapid augite growth Dolerite (Diabase)
Holocrystalline Texture $100\%$ crystalline mineral framework; entirely devoid of uncrystallized glassy base Plutonic to Hypabyssal (slow to moderate cooling) Complete crystallization achieved before temperature drops below glass transition ($T_g$) Gabbro, Peridotite, Granodiorite
Pillow Structure Interlocking, bulbous, convex-up sack-like lobes with chilled glassy rinds and radial fractures Extrusive (Subaqueous / Submarine seafloor volcanism) Instantaneous thermal quenching in water ($1200^\circ\text{C} \to 4^\circ\text{C}$); ductile crust budding Spillite (Spilite), Submarine Basalt
Porphyritic Texture Large, conspicuous crystals (phenocrysts) embedded in a finer groundmass Two-stage cooling (slow plutonic incubation followed by rapid ascent/eruption) Early low $\Delta T$ phenocryst growth followed by sudden high $\Delta T$ groundmass nucleation Rhyolite, Andesite porphyry, Basalt
Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Crystal Size Distribution (CSD) Theory & Residence Time

In a porphyritic granite pluton, Crystal Size Distribution (CSD) analysis of plagioclase phenocrysts yields a linear slope $s = -0.12\text{ mm}^{-1}$ in a plot of $\ln(n)$ versus crystal size $L$. If the linear crystal growth rate is experimentally determined as $G = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ mm/s}$, calculate the average magma residence time ($\tau$) in years ($1\text{ year} \approx 3.15 \times 10^7\text{ s}$).

Step-by-Step CSD Derivation:
In steady-state CSD theory (Marsh, 1988), the population density slope $s$ is related to growth rate $G$ and residence time $\tau$ by: $$s = -\frac{1}{G \cdot \tau}$$
Rearranging for residence time $\tau$: $$\tau = -\frac{1}{G \cdot s} = \frac{1}{(1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ mm/s}) \times (0.12\text{ mm}^{-1})} = \frac{1}{1.2 \times 10^{-11}\text{ s}^{-1}} \approx 8.33 \times 10^{10}\text{ seconds}$$
Converting seconds to years: $$\tau = \frac{8.33 \times 10^{10}\text{ s}}{3.1536 \times 10^7\text{ s/year}} \approx \mathbf{2,642\text{ years}}$$
Interpretation: The plagioclase phenocrysts resided in the cooling granitic magma chamber for approximately 2,640 years prior to final consolidation.
Problem 2: Petrographic Discrimination of Basaltic Textures

Compare and contrast the microscopic definitions and cooling regimes of: (a) Ophitic; (b) Subophitic; (c) Intergranular; and (d) Intersertal textures.

Textural Continuum in Mafic Rocks:
1. Ophitic: Plagioclase laths are completely enclosed poikilitically within large, optically continuous clinopyroxene plates. (Slowest cooling among hypabyssal dolerites; thick sill cores).
2. Subophitic: Plagioclase laths are only partially enclosed by pyroxene crystals, with parts of the laths projecting outside. (Moderate cooling rates; medium-width dikes).
3. Intergranular: Plagioclase laths form an interlocking lattice, and the angular interstitial spaces are completely filled by small, polygonal, granular pyroxene and iron-oxide crystals without any glass. (Rapid cooling; dike margins).
4. Intersertal: The angular wedges between plagioclase laths are occupied by brown amorphous volcanic glass (tachylite) or cryptocrystalline devitrified material. (Very rapid cooling / subaqueous flow tops).
Problem 3: Chemical Stoichiometry of the Spilitization Reaction

Submarine basalts undergo hydrothermal metasomatism (spilitization) on the ocean floor. Write the balanced chemical reaction representing the albitization of an anorthite plagioclase component in the presence of dissolved sodium and silica in seawater, producing secondary calcite.

Stoichiometric Reaction:
$$\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\ (\text{Anorthite}) + 2\text{Na}^+ + 4\text{SiO}_{2\text{ (aq)}} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \longrightarrow 2\text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{Albite}) + \text{CaCO}_3\ (\text{Calcite})$$
Geochemical Significance: Calcic plagioclase ($\text{An}_{50\text{--}70}$) is unstable in the presence of heated, circulating seawater ($T \approx 200\text{--}350^\circ\text{C}$). Seawater donates $Na^+$ while leaching $Ca^{2+}$, transforming the basalt into a spilite dominated by albite, chlorite, epidote, and calcite amygdules.
Problem 4: Geopetal Younging Criteria in Submarine Pillow Basalts

A structural geologist mapping an overturned Archean greenstone belt encounters deformed pillow lavas. Explain how the cross-sectional geometry of individual pillows indicates the original stratigraphic "way-up" (younging direction).

Geopetal Criteria:
1. Convex Upper Surface: As hot lava buds from a feeder tube, buoyancy and surface tension cause the top surface of the pillow to expand smoothly upward, forming a broad, convex-upward dome.
2. Cuspidate V-shaped Base (Pedicle): The soft, plastic bottom of the expanding pillow sags under gravity into the triangular cusp or indentation formed between the two underlying, pre-existing pillows, producing a downward-pointing tail or "keel" (V-shaped pedicle).
3. Vesicle Zonation: Gas vesicles are concentrated near the top margin of the pillow due to buoyant upward gas migration before quenching.
Deduction: The smooth rounded curve points to stratigraphic TOP (younger); the pointed V-shaped cusp points to stratigraphic BASE (older).
Problem 5: Thermal Profiling of a Dolerite Dike Chilled Margin

A vertical dolerite dike of thickness $w = 10\text{ meters}$ intrudes cold country rock ($T_0 = 20^\circ\text{C}$). The magma enters at its liquidus temperature ($T_m = 1180^\circ\text{C}$). Using Jaeger's (1968) thermal contact solution, calculate the immediate contact temperature ($T_c$) at the dike wall and describe the resulting texture.

Thermal Contact Derivation:
Assuming equivalent thermal properties (heat capacity and thermal conductivity) for the magma and host rock, the initial contact temperature ($T_c$) immediately upon intrusion is: $$T_c = \frac{T_m + T_0}{2} = \frac{1180 + 20}{2} = \frac{1200}{2} = \mathbf{600^\circ\text{C}}$$
Textural Evolution Across the Dike:
- At the immediate wall ($x = 0$): Quenched instantly from $1180^\circ\text{C}$ to $600^\circ\text{C}$ ($\Delta T = 580^\circ\text{C}$). Extreme undercooling produces an aphanitic to glassy chilled margin (tachylite).
- At the dike interior ($x = 5\text{ m}$): Cooling is slow, controlled by heat conduction through the country rock. Low undercooling allows complete crystal growth, developing classic coarse ophitic texture.
Problem 6: Poikilitic vs. Ophitic: Terminological Demarcation

Both poikilitic and ophitic textures describe mineral grains enclosed within larger host crystals. Explain the precise mineralogical restriction that distinguishes an ophitic texture from general poikilitic texture.

Taxonomic Distinction:
- Poikilitic Texture (General Term): A generic petrographic texture where relatively small, randomly oriented crystals of any mineral phase (chadacrysts) are enclosed within a much larger host crystal of a different mineral (oikocryst). Examples: Olivine enclosed in hornblende, or quartz enclosed in biotite.
- Ophitic Texture (Specific Restrictive Variety): A specialized variety of poikilitic texture strictly restricted to mafic rocks where the enclosed chadacrysts are specifically prismatic laths of plagioclase feldspar, and the enclosing oikocryst is specifically clinopyroxene (augite).
Problem 7: Grain Size Boundaries in Crystalline Rocks

State the internationally accepted metric grain size thresholds defining: (a) Fine-grained (aphanitic); (b) Medium-grained; (c) Coarse-grained; and (d) Pegmatitic crystalline rocks according to the IUGS Subcommission on the Systematics of Igneous Rocks.

IUGS Grain Size Scales:
- Fine-grained (Aphanitic): Average grain diameter $< 1.0\text{ mm}$ (individual crystals cannot be distinguished with the naked eye; e.g., basalt, rhyolite).
- Medium-grained: Average grain diameter between $1.0\text{ mm}$ and $5.0\text{ mm}$ (typical of hypabyssal rocks; e.g., dolerite, microgranite).
- Coarse-grained (Phaneritic): Average grain diameter between $5.0\text{ mm}$ and $30.0\text{ mm}$ (typical of plutonic rocks; e.g., granite, gabbro).
- Very Coarse / Pegmatitic: Giant crystals exceeding $> 30.0\text{ mm}$ (often $> 5\text{--}10\text{ cm}$), crystallized from volatile-rich, water-saturated residual pegmatitic melts.
Problem 8: Glass Formation and the Glass Transition Temperature ($T_g$)

Why do high-silica rhyolitic magmas readily form natural glass (obsidian) upon subaerial cooling, whereas low-silica basaltic magmas rarely form pure glass except when quenched underwater?

Melt Polymerization and Rheology:
1. Polymerization and Viscosity: Rhyolitic magma ($SiO_2 \approx 72\text{--}75\text{ wt}\%$) has a fully polymerized, three-dimensional network of bridging oxygens ($NBO/T \approx 0$), resulting in an astronomical viscosity ($\eta \approx 10^7\text{ to } 10^9\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$). During subaerial cooling, high viscosity impedes the diffusion of ions to crystal growth sites, freezing the disordered liquid structure into glass even under moderate subaerial cooling rates.
2. Basaltic Depolymerization: Basaltic magma ($SiO_2 \approx 48\text{--}50\text{ wt}\%$) is rich in network-modifying cations ($Mg^{2+}, Fe^{2+}, Ca^{2+}$) with high non-bridging oxygens ($NBO/T \approx 0.6\text{--}0.8$), giving it an extremely low viscosity ($\eta \approx 10\text{--}100\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$). Rapid ionic diffusion allows crystals to nucleate and grow rapidly; pure glass can only form when basalt is violently quenched in cold water ($dT/dt > 100^\circ\text{C/s}$).

Q078: Ultra-Alkalic Rocks: Ijolite Petrography & Foidolite Magmatism

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 78
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 2: Classification of Igneous Rocks / Foidolites, p. 28; Ch. 19: Alkaline Igneous Rocks); Anthony Hall, Igneous Petrology (Longman, Ch. 11: Alkaline Rocks); Daniel S. Barker, Igneous Rocks (Prentice-Hall); R.W. Le Maitre, Igneous Rocks: A Classification and Glossary of Terms (IUGS).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition of Ultra-Alkalic Rocks & the IUGS Foidolite Suite

In igneous petrology, alkaline rocks are defined as magmas whose molecular alkali-to-alumina ratio $\frac{\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{K}_2\text{O}}{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}$ or alkali-to-silica ratio is unusually high, such that minerals deficient in silica—most notably feldspathoids (foids: nepheline, leucite, kalsilite, sodalite)—appear in the norm or mode.

The designation ultra-alkalic (or hyper-alkaline) is reserved for extraordinary plutonic rocks where silica deficiency is so profound that true feldspars (plagioclase and alkali feldspar) are completely excluded from the mineral assemblage. In the standard IUGS QAPF classification (Le Maitre, 2002; Winter, 2014, p. 28), these rocks plot in Field 15 (Foidolites), where feldspathoids comprise greater than $60\%$ (and frequently $100\%$) of the light felsic minerals.

Figure 78.1 — IUGS QAPF Classification & Field 15 (Foidolites): Authentic textbook diagram from J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 2). Highlighting the ultra-alkalic, feldspar-free Foidolite field containing the Urtite-Ijolite-Melteigite series.
2. Petrography of the Urtite-Ijolite-Melteigite Series

The classic plutonic suite of feldspar-free, nepheline-clinopyroxene rocks is known as the Ijolite Series (named after the type locality at Iivaara / Ijola, Kuusamo, Finland). The rocks are classified strictly on the basis of their Color Index ($M'$), representing the modal percentage of dark mafic minerals:

The Three Members of the Ijolite Series

  • Urtite ($M' = 0\text{--}30\%$): Leucocratic end-member, consisting predominantly of nepheline ($>70\text{--}90\%$) with minor green aegirine-augite. (Named from Lujaur-Urt, Kola Peninsula).
  • Ijolite ($M' = 30\text{--}70\%$): The quintessential mesocratic ultra-alkalic rock, consisting of approximately equal proportions of nepheline ($30\text{--}70\%$) and sodic clinopyroxene (aegirine or aegirine-augite, $30\text{--}70\%$). Feldspars are completely absent! Common accessory minerals include titanium-rich black andradite garnet (melanite), fluorapatite, titanite (sphene), perovskite, and primary magmatic calcite.
  • Melteigite ($M' = 70\text{--}90\%$): Melanocratic end-member, dominated by aegirine-augite ($>70\%$) with subordinate interstitial nepheline ($10\text{--}30\%$). (Named from Melteig, Fen complex, Norway).
Mineralogical Archetype of Ijolite:
$$\mathbf{\text{Ijolite}} = \mathbf{\text{Nepheline (30--70\%)}} + \mathbf{\text{Aegirine-Augite (30--70\%)}} + \text{Melanite Garnet} + \text{Apatite} \quad [\mathbf{\text{Feldspar = 0\%}}]$$
3. Geodynamic Setting, Carbonatite Association & Fenitization

Ijolites never occur as isolated regional batholiths; instead, they are diagnostic components of alkaline-carbonatite ring complexes emplaced within intra-continental rift valleys (e.g., East African Rift, Kola Alkaline Province in Russia, Fen Complex in Norway, and the Amba Dongar complex in Gujarat, India).

Petrogenesis and Liquid Immiscibility

  • Primary Carbonated Mantle Melting: Primary carbonated nephelinite magmas are generated by extremely low degrees of partial melting ($F < 2\text{--}5\%$) of deep, volatile-metasomatized sub-continental lithospheric mantle (SCLM) at depths $> 100\text{ km}$ ($P > 3.0\text{ GPa}$) in the presence of high $CO_2$ and $H_2O$.
  • Silicate-Carbonatite Unmixing: As the primary nephelinitic melt ascends and decompresses into crustal chambers, it intersects a two-liquid miscibility gap, unmixing into an ultra-alkaline silicate melt (crystallizing as ijolite) and a conjugate carbonate-rich liquid (crystallizing as carbonatite: sovite/alvikite).
  • Fenitization (Alkali Metasomatism): The extreme alkali enrichment of ijolitic and carbonatitic intrusions generates intense hydrothermal exsolution of sodium-potassium-rich fluids. These reactive fluids invade surrounding granitic and gneissic country rocks, leaching silica and quartz while metasomatically replacing host minerals with aegirine, sodic amphibole (riebeckite/arfvedsonite), and alkali feldspar—a process termed fenitization.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 78
Which of the following is an ultra-alkalic rock ?
(A) Adamellite
(B) Rhyodacite
(C) Trondhjemite
(D) Ijolite
CORRECT ANSWER: (D)
Ijolite: An ultra-alkalic, feldspar-free plutonic rock composed essentially of nepheline (30–70%) and sodic pyroxene (aegirine-augite), plotting in the Foidolite field of the IUGS QAPF classification.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Adamellite — INCORRECT

Adamellite is the classic European petrographic synonym for Quartz Monzonite (IUGS Field 8). It is a subalkaline, quartz-bearing granitoid consisting of roughly equal proportions of alkali feldspar and plagioclase with 5–20% quartz. It is completely subalkaline to calc-alkaline and contains abundant silica, making it the diametric opposite of an ultra-alkalic rock.

(B) Rhyodacite — INCORRECT

Rhyodacite is a subalkaline, volcanic intermediate-to-felsic rock compositional equivalent to granodiorite. It is characterized by phenocrysts of plagioclase, quartz, and biotite/hornblende in a fine-grained, silica-oversaturated groundmass ($SiO_2 \approx 66\text{--}72\%$). It belongs to typical calc-alkaline subduction arc suites.

(C) Trondhjemite — INCORRECT

Trondhjemite is a leucocratic variety of tonalite belonging to the famous Archean TTG suite (Tonalite-Trondhjemite-Granodiorite). It consists almost entirely of sodic plagioclase (oligoclase) and quartz, with $<10\%$ K-feldspar and minor biotite. It is strongly subalkaline, metaluminous to peraluminous, and completely devoid of feldspathoids.

(D) Ijolite — CORRECT

Ijolite is the classic, textbook archetype of an ultra-alkalic plutonic rock (Winter, 2014, p. 28, 412). It is a foidolite composed exclusively of nepheline and aegirine-augite with total exclusion of feldspars. Its agpaitic index, extreme silica-undersaturation, and association with carbonatites firmly establish it as ultra-alkalic.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Agpaitic Index ($AI$) and Peralkalinity Quantitative Calculation

A geochemical analysis of an ultra-alkalic plutonic rock yields the following molar concentrations: $\text{Na}_2\text{O} = 0.142\text{ mol}$, $\text{K}_2\text{O} = 0.038\text{ mol}$, and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 0.125\text{ mol}$. Calculate the Agpaitic Index ($AI$) and classify the rock as peralkaline, metaluminous, or peraluminous.

Step-by-Step Calculation:
The Agpaitic Index ($AI$, or Peralkalinity Index) is defined as the molar ratio of total alkalis to alumina: $$AI = \frac{\text{Molar }(\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{K}_2\text{O})}{\text{Molar }\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}$$
Substituting the molar values: $$AI = \frac{0.142 + 0.038}{0.125} = \frac{0.180}{0.125} = \mathbf{1.44}$$
Classification:
- Since $\mathbf{AI = 1.44 > 1.0}$, the rock is strictly Peralkaline (Agpaitic).
- Surplus sodium beyond that needed to form feldspars and feldspathoids ($(\text{Na}+\text{K}) > \text{Al}$) forces the crystallization of sodic mafic minerals, namely aegirine ($\text{NaFe}^{3+}\text{Si}_2\text{O}_6$) and arfvedsonite, characteristic of ijolites.
Problem 2: Color Index ($M'$) Classification in the Ijolite Series

Point-counting modal analysis of three foidolitic plutonic thin sections from a carbonatite complex yielded the following modal percentages:
- Sample A: $82\%$ Nepheline, $14\%$ Aegirine-augite, $4\%$ Melanite garnet.
- Sample B: $48\%$ Nepheline, $42\%$ Aegirine-augite, $6\%$ Melanite, $4\%$ Apatite.
- Sample C: $18\%$ Nepheline, $74\%$ Aegirine-augite, $8\%$ Titanite + Magnetite.
Classify Samples A, B, and C into their specific members of the Ijolite Series.

Color Index ($M'$) Derivation:
$M'$ is the sum of all dark, mafic, and accessory minerals ($100 - \text{Felsic Foids}$):
- Sample A: $M' = 14\% + 4\% = 18\%$. Since $M' < 30\%$, it is classified as Urtite (leucocratic foidolite).
- Sample B: $M' = 42\% + 6\% + 4\% = 52\%$. Since $M'$ is between $30\%$ and $70\%$, it is classified as Ijolite sensu stricto.
- Sample C: $M' = 74\% + 8\% = 82\%$. Since $M' > 70\%$, it is classified as Melteigite (melanocratic foidolite).
Problem 3: Liquid Immiscibility: Silicate-Carbonatite Unmixing

Explain why ijolite and carbonatite rocks are intimately associated in space and time within alkaline complexes, citing experimental phase equilibria in the system $\text{Na}_2\text{O}\text{--}\text{CaO}\text{--}\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\text{--}\text{SiO}_2\text{--}\text{CO}_2$.

Experimental Petrologic Mechanism:
1. Miscibility Gap: Freestone & Hamilton (1980) and Kjarsgaard & Hamilton (1988) demonstrated that at crustal pressures ($0.2\text{--}0.5\text{ GPa}$) and temperatures of $850\text{--}1050^\circ\text{C}$, a primary $CO_2$-saturated nephelinitic melt enters a wide two-liquid immiscibility field.
2. Phase Separation: The homogeneous melt splits into two conjugate, immiscible liquids: - An alkali-aluminosilicate liquid enriched in $SiO_2, Al_2O_3, Na_2O$, which crystallizes as ijolite.
- A conjugate alkaline-carbonatitic liquid enriched in $CaO, CO_2, P_2O_5$, and LREE, which crystallizes as carbonatite (calciocarbonatite/sovite).
3. This explains why ijolites form concentric ring dikes and plugs directly enclosing central carbonatite cores.
Problem 4: Chemical Impossibility of Quartz and Nepheline Coexistence

Demonstrate thermodynamically why quartz and nepheline can never coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium in any primary igneous rock.

Thermodynamic Reaction:
Nepheline is a silica-undersaturated feldspathoid. In the presence of free silica (quartz), it undergoes instantaneous, spontaneous reaction to form albite feldspar: $$\text{NaAlSiO}_4\ (\text{Nepheline}) + \text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz}) \rightleftharpoons \text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{Albite})$$
The standard Gibbs free energy of this reaction is strongly negative ($\Delta G^\circ_{298} \approx -26.5\text{ kJ/mol}$) across all magmatic temperatures and pressures. Therefore, free quartz consumes nepheline to form albite until one of the reactants is completely exhausted. Rocks containing nepheline (like ijolite) have zero modal or normative quartz.
Problem 5: Fenitization Halo Metasomatic Mass Balance

Describe the mineralogical transformations that occur when a granitic country rock containing quartz ($30\%$), microcline ($40\%$), and oligoclase ($30\%$) undergoes intense fenitization by fluids exsolved from an ijolitic intrusion.

Metasomatic Progression:
1. Desilication: High-pH alkaline hydrothermal fluids dissolve quartz entirely: $$\text{SiO}_{2\text{ (solid)}} + 2\text{OH}^- \longrightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SiO}_4^{2-\text{ (aqueous)}}$$
2. Aegirine Formation: Sodium and ferric iron metasomatically replace host mafic minerals and quartz: $$\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{Na}^+ + 2\text{SiO}_2 \longrightarrow \text{NaFe}^{3+}\text{Si}_2\text{O}_6\ (\text{Aegirine})$$
3. Alkali Feldspar Recrystallization: Oligoclase is albitized, and potassium feldspar recrystallizes into perthitic orthoclase/microcline. The resulting rock is a fenite: a quartz-free rock composed of perthite, albite, and radiating needles of aegirine.
Problem 6: Melanite Garnet: The Diagnostic Accessory Phase of Ijolite

In thin section, ijolite typically contains dark brown to opaque dodecahedral garnet crystals. Identify this garnet variety, write its chemical formula, and explain why titanium enters its crystal lattice.

Mineralogical Characterization:
- Mineral Variety: Melanite (or Schorlomite when $TiO_2 > 10\text{ wt}\%$), a titanium-rich variety of the ugrandite garnet Andradite.
- Chemical Formula: $\text{Ca}_3(\text{Fe}^{3+}, \text{Ti})_2(\text{SiO}_4, \text{Fe}^{3+}\text{O}_4)_3$, ideally $\text{Ca}_3\text{Fe}_2^{3+}\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}$ with up to $5\text{--}15\text{ wt}\% TiO_2$.
- Titanium Incorporation: In silica-undersaturated, alkaline ijolitic magmas, the low activity of silica ($a_{\text{SiO}_2}$) impedes the formation of sphene/titanite or ilmenite. Instead, $Ti^{4+}$ substitutes into the octahedral $Y$-site and tetrahedral $Z$-site of andradite via coupled substitutions ($\text{Ti}^{4+} + \text{Fe}^{3+} \rightleftharpoons \text{Si}^{4+} + \text{Al}^{3+}$), yielding the deep black/brown melanite garnet.
Problem 7: Amba Dongar Alkaline-Carbonatite Complex, Gujarat

The Amba Dongar complex in the Chhota Udaipur alkaline sub-province of Gujarat represents India's most famous carbonatite-alkaline ring complex. Identify the spatial distribution of ijolites and carbonatites within this ring structure and its relation to Deccan volcanism.

Indian Regional Geology:
- Tectonic & Temporal Context: Emplaced at $\sim 65\text{ Ma}$, Amba Dongar is intimately associated with the terminal rifting stage of the Deccan Traps flood basalt province (Reunion hotspot interaction with the Narmada-Tapi rift zone).
- Ring Architecture: The complex forms a prominent ring dike system cutting Cretaceous Bagh Sandstones. The central volcanic diatreme depression consists of carbonatite breccia and large ring dikes of calciocarbonatite (sovite) and ankeritic carbonatite.
- Ijolite Occurrence: Ijolitic and nephelinitic plutonic bodies occur as peripheral intrusions and ring segments intimately associated with extensive fenitization of the surrounding Bagh Sandstones. It hosts world-class hydrothermal fluorite mineralization.
Problem 8: CIPW Norm Calculation: Differentiating Silica Saturation

Given the following CIPW normative mineral percentages for two igneous rocks, determine which one is an ultra-alkalic rock and explain why:
- Rock X: $Q = 14.5\%, Or = 28.0\%, Ab = 32.5\%, An = 15.0\%, Hy = 6.0\%, Mt = 2.5\%$.
- Rock Y: $Ne = 42.0\%, Di = 44.0\%, Ol = 8.0\%, Ap = 3.5\%, Mt = 2.5\%$.

Normative Analysis:
- Rock X: Contains $14.5\%$ normative Quartz ($Q$) and abundant normative feldspars ($Or + Ab + An = 75.5\%$). It is a silica-oversaturated, calc-alkaline rock (Quartz Monzonite / Adamellite).
- Rock Y: Contains $42.0\%$ normative Nepheline ($Ne$) and zero normative quartz or feldspars ($Or = Ab = An = 0\%$). The entire felsic norm is nepheline, accompanied by dominant normative Diopside ($Di = 44\%$). This normative composition corresponds precisely to an ultra-alkalic foidolite (Ijolite).

GEO - 2/21 • Petrology & Textural Analysis

Q079: Myrmekitic Texture: Vermicular Quartz-Plagioclase Intergrowth

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 79
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 3: Textures of Igneous Rocks, pp. 44–46); Anthony Hall, Igneous Petrology; G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (p. 119); F.J. Turner & J. Verhoogen, Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology; L.G. Collins, Hydrothermal Differentiation and Myrmekite.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Petrographic Definition & Microstructural Anatomy of Myrmekite

The term myrmekite (derived from the ancient Greek myrmex, meaning "ant") was introduced by F. Becke (1899) to describe the uncanny resemblance of this intergrowth to subterranean ant tunnels or worm-like burrows under high-power petrographic microscopy.

Myrmekitic texture consists of an intimate intergrowth of vermicular (worm-like, cylindrical, or tubular) quartz rods hosted inside a convex, cauliflower-shaped or wart-like lobe of plagioclase feldspar (typically oligoclase, $\text{An}_{10\text{--}30}$) that projects directly into an adjacent grain of potassium feldspar (microcline or orthoclase).

Figure 79.1 — Petrographic Architecture of Myrmekitic Texture: Authentic textbook diagram from J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 3). Illustrating the lobate plagioclase bulb with vermicular quartz rods advancing into adjacent microcline K-feldspar.

Three Diagnostic Optical Criteria of True Myrmekite

  • Host Mineralogy: The host matrix is strictly sodic plagioclase (oligoclase or albite), never K-feldspar. (In contrast, graphic texture hosts quartz in a K-feldspar matrix!).
  • Morphology & Tapering of Quartz: The quartz rods are tubular and branching, showing a diagnostic tapering geometry: they are thickest near the central interior of the plagioclase lobe and become progressively thinner and more delicate toward the outer lobate margin entering the K-feldspar.
  • Optical Extinction: Under cross-polarized light, all vermicular quartz tubes within a single plagioclase lobe extinguish simultaneously, proving they represent a single, interconnected, branching crystallographic skeleton of quartz.
2. Petrogenesis of Myrmekite: Metasomatic Replacement vs. Exsolution

The origin of myrmekite has been one of the most vigorously debated topics in petrology, with three primary scientific mechanisms recognized:

1. The Becke-Phillips Metasomatic Replacement Model (Dominant Mechanism)

During late-magmatic cooling, deuteric auto-metasomatism, or fluid-assisted retrograde metamorphism, intergranular fluids rich in $Ca^{2+}$ and $Na^+$ attack primary potassium feldspar (microcline), replacing it with calcic/sodic plagioclase. Because anorthite requires fewer silica atoms per formula unit than K-feldspar, an abundance of free silica is released:

Stoichiometric Replacement Reaction:
$$2\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{K-feldspar}) + \text{Ca}^{2+} \longrightarrow \text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\ (\text{Anorthite in Plagioclase}) + \mathbf{4\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Vermicular Quartz})} + 2\text{K}^+$$

For every mole of anorthite created to replace two moles of microcline, exactly four moles of free $\text{SiO}_2$ are expelled locally, precipitating in situ as vermicular quartz rods within the expanding plagioclase front!

2. Schwantke's Molecule Subsolidus Exsolution Hypothesis

A. Schwantke (1909) proposed that high-temperature ternary feldspars incorporate a defect component termed Schwantke's molecule: $\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_6\text{O}_{16}$ (or $\text{Ca}_{0.5}\Box_{0.5}\text{AlSi}_3\text{O}_8$). Upon subsolidus cooling, this unstable solid solution breaks down:

$$\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_6\text{O}_{16} \longrightarrow \text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\ (\text{Anorthite}) + 4\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz})$$

3. Deformation-Induced Myrmekite in Ductile Shear Zones

Simpson & Wintsch (1989) demonstrated that in mylonitic granites and ductile shear zones, asymmetric myrmekite develops preferentially on K-feldspar grain boundaries facing the principal compressive stress axis ($\sigma_1$), where strain energy accelerates potassium leaching and plagioclase nucleation.

3. Petrographic Discrimination from Other Common Intergrowth Textures

It is vital in optical mineralogy not to confuse myrmekitic texture with other intergrowth phenomena:

  • Graphic Texture: A primary magmatic eutectic cotectic intergrowth where angular, wedge-shaped quartz crystals resembling ancient cuneiform or runic writing are embedded in a potassium feldspar (microcline) host (e.g., in granitic pegmatites).
  • Granophyric Texture: A microscopic, spherulitic, plumose, or delicate skeletal intergrowth of quartz and alkali feldspar formed by rapid eutectic crystallization in shallow, subvolcanic granitic porphyries.
  • Perthitic Texture: Subsolidus exsolution lamellae, blebs, or strings of sodic plagioclase (albite) enclosed within a potassium feldspar host.
  • Antiperthitic Texture: Exsolution blebs or oriented inclusions of potassium feldspar enclosed within a plagioclase host.
  • Corona / Reaction Rim: A concentric sheath of one or more secondary minerals completely surrounding a core mineral grain (e.g., orthopyroxene rim around olivine), formed by solid-state reaction with surrounding matrix phases.
  • Trachytic Texture: Subparallel fluidal flow-alignment of tiny tabular laths of sanidine/alkali feldspar microlites in volcanic rocks.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 79
This texture results from the inter-growth of quartz and plagioclase (usually oligoclase). The inter-growth of quartz is in the form of worm-like rods within the plagioclase. It is found in some granite and metamorphic rocks. It is termed as :
(A) Graphic texture
(B) Myrmekitic texture
(C) Corona texture
(D) Trachytic texture
CORRECT ANSWER: (B)
Myrmekitic texture: An intergrowth of vermicular (worm-like) quartz rods within a plagioclase host (typically oligoclase), forming lobate warts invading adjacent potassium feldspar in granites and metamorphic gneisses.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Graphic texture — INCORRECT

Graphic texture is a primary cotectic magmatic intergrowth of quartz and potassium feldspar (microcline), where quartz occurs as angular, cuneiform, runic wedges resembling ancient Hebrew or Babylonian characters. It does not consist of worm-like rods in a plagioclase host.

(B) Myrmekitic texture — CORRECT

Myrmekitic texture is the exact, unambiguous scientific term defined by an intergrowth of vermicular (worm-like) rods of quartz hosted within plagioclase (specifically oligoclase). It is universally found in granites, charnockites, and high-grade metamorphic gneisses at contacts with K-feldspar grains (Winter, 2014, p. 45; Bangar, p. 77; Mahapatra, p. 119).

(C) Corona texture — INCORRECT

Corona texture (reaction rim / kelyphitic rim) consists of concentric shells or mantles of one mineral (e.g., pyroxene, amphibole, spinel) surrounding an earlier-crystallized core mineral (such as olivine or garnet). It is a metamorphic or magmatic reaction rim, entirely lacking vermicular quartz-plagioclase intergrowths.

(D) Trachytic texture — INCORRECT

Trachytic texture is a volcanic flow-alignment texture occurring in intermediate to felsic lavas (especially trachytes), characterized by closely packed, subparallel, sub-aligned microscopic tabular laths of sanidine microlites.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Stoichiometric Volume Balance of Becke's Myrmekite Reaction

Consider the metasomatic replacement of microcline by pure anorthite according to Becke's reaction: $$2\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{Microcline}) + \text{Ca}^{2+} \longrightarrow \text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\ (\text{Anorthite}) + 4\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz}) + 2\text{K}^+$$ Given the molar volumes: $V_m(\text{Microcline}) = 108.9\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$, $V_m(\text{Anorthite}) = 100.8\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$, and $V_m(\text{Quartz}) = 22.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$. Calculate the theoretical volume percentage of vermicular quartz in the resulting myrmekite.

Step-by-Step Volumetric Derivation:
1. Calculate volume of products generated per mole of anorthite: $$V(\text{Anorthite}) = 1 \times 100.8\text{ cm}^3 = 100.8\text{ cm}^3$$
$$V(\text{Quartz}) = 4 \times 22.7\text{ cm}^3 = 90.8\text{ cm}^3$$
$$\text{Total Volume of Myrmekite} = V(\text{Anorthite}) + V(\text{Quartz}) = 100.8 + 90.8 = 191.6\text{ cm}^3$$
2. Calculate volume percentage of quartz: $$\text{Vol}\%\ \text{Quartz} = \frac{V(\text{Quartz})}{\text{Total Volume}} \times 100\% = \frac{90.8}{191.6} \times 100\% \approx \mathbf{47.39\%}$$
Petrological Note: Because natural myrmekite plagioclase is oligoclase ($\sim \text{An}_{20}\text{Ab}_{80}$) rather than pure anorthite, the albitic component ($NaAlSi_3O_8$) releases zero free quartz during replacement ($KAlSi_3O_8 + Na^+ \to NaAlSi_3O_8 + K^+$). Consequently, the actual modal percentage of quartz in natural oligoclase myrmekite is lower, typically $10\text{ to } 22\text{ vol}\%$.
Problem 2: Quartz Content vs. Plagioclase Anorthite Content ($An\%$) Correlation

F. Becke (1908) observed empirically that the volume fraction of vermicular quartz ($X_Q$) in myrmekite increases linearly with the anorthite content ($An$) of the host plagioclase. Explain why this relationship constitutes definitive proof of the metasomatic replacement hypothesis over simple cotectic crystallization.

Theoretical Proof:
- The Chemical Stoichiometry: In metasomatic replacement, albite ($\text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_8$) has the exact same $Si:Al$ ratio ($3:1$) as potassium feldspar ($\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8$). Therefore, replacing K-feldspar by albite releases zero quartz ($\Delta \text{Si} = 0$). Only the anorthite component ($\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8$, $Si:Al = 1:1$) releases excess silica ($2\text{ moles } \text{SiO}_2$ per mole of $Al$).
- Linear Proportionality: The volume of quartz precipitated must therefore be strictly proportional to the mole fraction of anorthite: $$X_Q \propto \frac{\text{An}}{100}$$
- If myrmekite were formed by eutectic magmatic crystallization, the quartz-plagioclase cotectic ratio would be dictated by the liquidus phase diagram and would not vary linearly with solid-solution anorthite content across different post-solidus metamorphic zones.
Problem 3: Kinetic Meaning of Tapering Quartz Rods

In thin section, the vermicular quartz rods of myrmekite systematically taper, becoming thinnest at the lobate convex margin facing the potassium feldspar and thickest toward the interior base of the plagioclase. Deduce the direction of growth and explain the physical cause of this geometry.

Growth Vector & Diffusion Kinetics:
1. Growth Vector: The plagioclase lobe advances into the potassium feldspar; hence, the outer convex margin represents the active, younger reaction front, while the base is the older, established core.
2. Physical Cause of Tapering: At the advancing reaction front, plagioclase nucleates rapidly, creating tiny, nascent quartz nuclei. As the reaction front moves forward, silica continues to diffuse down chemical potential gradients toward existing quartz conduits. The older portions of the tubes at the base continue to thicken by sustained syntaxial precipitation of silica over time, whereas newly formed tubes at the tip have had minimal time to grow, producing the diagnostic tapered morphology.
Problem 4: Deformation-Induced Myrmekite as a Kinematic Shear Sense Indicator

In a mylonitized granite from a ductile shear zone, K-feldspar porphyroclasts display myrmekite lobes developed almost exclusively on the edges facing the shortening quadrant ($\sigma_1$), while quartz ribbons occupy the pressure shadows ($\sigma_3$). Explain the stress-induced mechanism driving this asymmetric growth.

Mechanochemical Mechanism (Simpson & Wintsch, 1989):
1. Stress Concentration: In ductile shear zones, compressive differential stress is focused on the high-angle boundaries of rigid K-feldspar porphyroclasts facing the shortening direction ($\sigma_1$).
2. Strain-Enhanced Dissolution: High elastic strain energy at these compressive edges elevates the chemical potential of $KAlSi_3O_8$, accelerating the breakdown and dissolution of K-feldspar into intergranular fluids.
3. Myrmekite Nucleation: Influx of $Ca^{2+}$-bearing fluids replaces the dissolving K-feldspar with lower-volume plagioclase and quartz (myrmekite), relieving compressive stress. The asymmetric distribution of myrmekite lobes on porphyroclast margins provides a reliable microstructural indicator of finite shear strain and shear sense.
Problem 5: Schwantke's Molecule and Exsolution Thermodynamics

Write the formula of Schwantke's molecule and calculate the moles of free silica generated when 0.05 moles of Schwantke component exsolve from a high-temperature orthoclase solid solution.

Calculation:
Schwantke's molecule is written as $\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_6\text{O}_{16}$ (or vacancy notation $\text{Ca}_{0.5}\Box_{0.5}\text{AlSi}_3\text{O}_8$).
The exsolution breakdown reaction is: $$\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_6\text{O}_{16} \longrightarrow \text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\ (\text{Anorthite}) + 4\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz})$$
For $0.05\text{ moles}$ of Schwantke's molecule: $$\text{Moles of Quartz} = 0.05 \times 4 = \mathbf{0.20\text{ moles of SiO}_2}$$
$$\text{Moles of Anorthite} = 0.05 \times 1 = \mathbf{0.05\text{ moles of Anorthite}}$$
Problem 6: Graphic vs. Myrmekitic Textures: Summary Comparison

Contrast Graphic and Myrmekitic textures across four criteria: (a) host mineral; (b) quartz geometry; (c) primary vs. secondary origin; and (d) geological environment.

Fourfold Contrast:
- (a) Host Mineral: Graphic texture hosts quartz in K-feldspar (microcline); Myrmekite hosts quartz in plagioclase (oligoclase).
- (b) Quartz Geometry: Graphic quartz forms angular, cuneiform, runic prisms resembling alphabet characters; Myrmekite quartz forms rounded, tubular, vermicular (worm-like) rods.
- (c) Genesis: Graphic texture is a primary magmatic simultaneous eutectic cotectic intergrowth; Myrmekite is a late-stage secondary metasomatic replacement or subsolidus exgrowth.
- (d) Geological Environment: Graphic texture is characteristic of granitic pegmatites; Myrmekite is found in plutonic granites, charnockites, and metamorphic gneisses.
Problem 7: Symplectite vs. Myrmekite in Metamorphic Rocks

In high-pressure granulites and retrogressed eclogites, fine vermicular intergrowths termed "symplectites" are common. Explain how a symplectite differs conceptually and mineralogically from myrmekite.

Petrological Distinction:
- Myrmekite (Specific Texture): A strictly defined intergrowth restricted to quartz + plagioclase replacing K-feldspar.
- Symplectite (Broad Textural Family): A generic metamorphic texture describing the fine-grained, vermicular, worm-like intergrowth of any two or more minerals formed during rapid, diffusion-controlled subsolidus reaction or decompression breakdown. Examples include: 1. Omphacite breakdown in eclogites: $\text{Omphacite} \to \text{Diopside} + \text{Albite symplectite}$.
2. Garnet decompression in granulites: $\text{Garnet} + \text{Quartz} \to \text{Orthopyroxene} + \text{Cordierite symplectite}$.
Problem 8: Optical Petrography: Identifying Myrmekite under Cross-Polarized Light

Describe the optical diagnostic features you would use under cross-polarized light (XPL) to positively verify myrmekitic texture in a granite thin section during a professional geological examination.

Step-by-Step Optical Verification:
1. Locate K-Feldspar Margins: Search for microcline grains displaying diagnostic cross-hatched (tartan/gridiron) twinning or orthoclase displaying Carlsbad twinning.
2. Identify Convex Plagioclase Lobes: Look for hemispherical, wart-like lobes of plagioclase projecting into the microcline margin. Verify polysynthetic albite twinning in the plagioclase.
3. Observe Quartz Rods: Within the plagioclase lobe, observe clear, colorless, high-relief vermicular rods with lower refractive index than plagioclase.
4. Extinction Test: Rotate the microscope stage: the entire network of quartz vermicules within a single lobe extinguishes simultaneously, while the host plagioclase extinguishes at a different angle, and the surrounding microcline displays its own distinct extinction position.

Q080: Charnockite Composition: Hypersthene Granulite & Holland's Series

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 80
Authoritative References: G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (Ch. 8: Petrology / Metamorphic Rocks, pp. 140–142); John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 21: Granulite Facies, pp. 468–475); Sir Thomas H. Holland (1900, Memoirs of the Geological Survey of India, Vol. 28, Pt. 2: "The Charnockite Series"); B.L. Sreenivas & R. Srinivasan, Precambrian Geology of South India.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Historical Discovery & Mineralogical Definition of Charnockite

The rock name Charnockite holds a historic and honored position in Indian and international petrology. It was introduced in 1893 and comprehensively established in 1900 by Sir Thomas H. Holland, Director of the Geological Survey of India (GSI).

Holland named the rock in memory of Job Charnock, the founder of modern Kolkata (Calcutta). In 1892, Holland discovered that Job Charnock's monumental tombstone in St. John's Churchyard, Kolkata (erected in 1695), was carved from a distinctive, dark, greasy, hypersthene-bearing granitic rock that had been quarried and transported from St. Thomas Mount at Pallavaram, near Chennai (Madras), Tamil Nadu.

Figure 80.1 — Essential Mineralogy & Granulitic Fabric of Charnockite: Authentic textbook scan from G.B. Mahapatra (A Text-Book of Geology, p. 140). Showing the essential granoblastic mineral assemblage of hypersthene orthopyroxene, perthitic potassium feldspar, and quartz, along with its characteristic greasy, waxy dark luster.

Mineralogical Definition of Charnockite (sensu stricto)

According to both Holland's classical definition and the modern IUGS Subcommission on the Systematics of Metamorphic/Igneous Rocks:

Charnockite (sensu stricto) = Hypersthene Granite
$$\mathbf{\text{Essential Minerals}} = \mathbf{\text{Hypersthene (Orthopyroxene)}} + \mathbf{\text{Potassium Feldspar (Microperthite)}} + \mathbf{\text{Quartz}} \pm \text{Oligoclase/Andesine}$$

Megascopic Diagnostic Features

  • Color & Luster: Despite containing over $70\text{ wt}\% \text{SiO}_2$ (an acidic, felsic chemistry), charnockite displays an anomalously dark greenish-grey, bluish-grey, or greasy dark brown to black coloration with a diagnostic greasy, waxy, or vitreous luster.
  • Cause of Dark Coloration: Under high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, this greasy dark appearance is produced by dense networks of submicroscopic exsolution lamellae, micro-fracture fillings of carbonic and ferruginous fluids, and submicron-scale acicular inclusions of rutile and ilmenite inside quartz and feldspar crystals.
  • Fabric: Typically exhibits a medium-to-coarse granoblastic equigranular (granulitic) texture, frequently displaying coarse metamorphic gneissose foliation.
2. Holland's Charnockite Series & Petrographic Classification

Sir Thomas Holland recognized that charnockites do not occur in isolation but form a complete, cogenetic consanguineous differentiation suite spanning from acid to ultrabasic compositions, all unified by the constant presence of orthopyroxene (hypersthene):

The Four Divisions of the Charnockite Series (Holland, 1900)

  1. Acid Division (Charnockite sensu stricto): The hypersthene granite ($SiO_2 > 70\%$). Dominated by quartz, microcline/orthoclase microperthite, and pleochroic hypersthene, with subordinate oligoclase.
  2. Intermediate Division (Enderbite / Mangerite): Quartz diorite or monzonite equivalents ($SiO_2 \approx 60\text{--}70\%$). In Enderbite (Tilley, 1936), plagioclase (antiperthitic andesine/oligoclase) vastly exceeds K-feldspar ($Plag \gg Kfs$).
  3. Basic Division (Norite / 2-Pyroxene Granulite): Basaltic/gabbroic equivalent ($SiO_2 \approx 48\text{--}55\%$). Composed of calcic plagioclase (labradorite), hypersthene, and clinopyroxene (augite/diopside), with or without garnet; quartz and K-feldspar are absent.
  4. Ultrabasic Division (Pyroxenite / Bahite): Ultramafic end-member ($SiO_2 < 45\%$). Composed entirely of hypersthene, diopside, hornblende, and magnetite, with zero feldspar.
3. Metamorphic Petrogenesis: Granulite Facies & Carbonic Fluid Influx

While Holland originally interpreted charnockites as an igneous plutonic suite, modern petrology conclusively proves that they are high-grade regional metamorphic rocks formed under Granulite Facies conditions ($T \approx 750\text{--}900^\circ\text{C}$, $P \approx 6\text{--}10\text{ kbar}$, depths of $20\text{--}35\text{ km}$ in the lower continental crust).

Dehydration Breakdown of Hydrous Minerals

At granulite facies temperatures, hydrous phyllosilicates (biotite and hornblende) become thermodynamically unstable in the presence of quartz and undergo vapor-absent dehydration melting or breakdown, forming anhydrous orthopyroxene:

Biotite Dehydration Reaction:
$$\text{K}(\text{Mg,Fe})_3\text{AlSi}_3\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2\ (\text{Biotite}) + 3\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz}) \rightleftharpoons 3(\text{Mg,Fe})\text{SiO}_3\ (\mathbf{\text{Hypersthene}}) + \text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\mathbf{\text{K-feldspar}}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

The "Incipient Charnockite" Phenomenon at Kabbaldurga (Karnataka)

In a landmark paper, Janardhan, Newton & Smith (1979) documented the genesis of "incipient charnockite" at Kabbaldurga quarry in the Dharwar Craton. Foliated, grey amphibolite-facies Peninsular Gneiss containing biotite and hornblende is transformed along fracture-controlled patches and veins into coarse, unfoliated, greasy dark charnockite.

Fluid inclusion studies confirmed that this dehydration was driven by an active influx of mantle-derived, juvenile, high-density $CO_2$-rich fluids. The massive influx of $CO_2$ flushed out water, reducing the water activity ($a_{H_2O} < 0.35$). Because $a_{H_2O}$ was depressed, the biotite dehydration curve was drawn down to lower temperatures, precipitating hypersthene + K-feldspar + quartz in situ.

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 80
What is the composition of Charnockite ?
(A) Hypersthene + K-feldspar + Quartz
(B) Hornblende + K-feldspar + Quartz
(C) Sillimanite + K-feldspar + Quartz
(D) Epidote + Plagioclase + Quartz
CORRECT ANSWER: (A)
Hypersthene + K-feldspar + Quartz: Charnockite (sensu stricto) is canonically defined as a hypersthene granite, characterized by the essential anhydrous mineral assemblage of orthopyroxene (hypersthene), potassium feldspar (perthitic microcline), and quartz.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Hypersthene + K-feldspar + Quartz — CORRECT

This is the exact, canonical definition established by Sir Thomas Holland (1900) and maintained in all international metamorphic and igneous classifications (Winter, 2014, p. 468; Mahapatra, p. 140). The defining diagnostic mineral that separates charnockite from all ordinary granites is the orthopyroxene hypersthene, coexisting with potassium feldspar (perthite) and quartz under high-grade granulite facies conditions.

(B) Hornblende + K-feldspar + Quartz — INCORRECT

An assemblage of hornblende + K-feldspar + quartz represents an ordinary hornblende granite or amphibolite-facies granitic gneiss. It lacks the defining orthopyroxene (hypersthene). In fact, charnockite forms when hornblende breaks down and dehydrates into hypersthene.

(C) Sillimanite + K-feldspar + Quartz — INCORRECT

This aluminous, pelitic granulite assemblage is diagnostic of Khondalite (a quartz-manganese-garnet-sillimanite schist/gneiss named after the Khond tribes of Odisha and Eastern Ghats), or a metapelitic restite. It represents a metamorphosed aluminous clay/shale, not the quartzofeldspathic hypersthene rock charnockite.

(D) Epidote + Plagioclase + Quartz — INCORRECT

This hydrous, low-to-medium grade assemblage is characteristic of greenschist or epidote-amphibolite facies metabasites and epidote tonalites. Epidote is completely unstable at granulite facies temperatures and pressures, breaking down at $T > 550\text{--}650^\circ\text{C}$ long before charnockite forms.

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
The Complete Charnockite Series (Holland, 1900) & Granulite Suites
Division / Rock Name Igneous Equivalent $\text{SiO}_2\text{ (wt\%)}$ Essential Mineral Assemblage Diagnostic Features
Acid: Charnockite (sensu stricto) Hypersthene Granite $> 70\%$ Hypersthene + K-Feldspar (Perthite) + Quartz $\pm$ Oligoclase Greasy dark brownish-green luster; high silica; granoblastic
Acid-Intermediate: Enderbite Hypersthene Tonalite $65\text{--}70\%$ Hypersthene + Plagioclase (Antiperthite) + Quartz ($Plag \gg Kfs$) Sodic, plagioclase-dominated; low K-feldspar
Intermediate: Mangerite / Jotunite Hypersthene Monzonite / Monzodiorite $55\text{--}65\%$ Hypersthene + Plagioclase + K-Feldspar + Clinopyroxene $\pm$ Quartz Mesocratic; roughly equal plagioclase and alkali feldspar
Basic: Basic Charnockite (Norite) Hypersthene Gabbro (Two-Pyroxene Granulite) $48\text{--}55\%$ Hypersthene + Clinopyroxene (Augite) + Calcic Plagioclase $\pm$ Garnet Melanocratic; dark grey-black; anhydrous mafic granulite
Ultrabasic: Bahite (Pyroxenite) Orthopyroxenite $< 45\%$ Hypersthene + Diopside + Hornblende + Magnetite (Feldspar-free) Ultramafic; dense; dark green-black
Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Stoichiometric Biotite Dehydration Reaction & Gibbs Free Energy

Write the balanced chemical reaction for the breakdown of pure phlogopite biotite in the presence of quartz to form enstatite and K-feldspar. Given standard free energies of formation ($\Delta G^\circ_f$): Phlogopite = $-5,835\text{ kJ/mol}$, Quartz = $-856.3\text{ kJ/mol}$, Enstatite = $-1,460.8\text{ kJ/mol}$, K-feldspar = $-3,742.9\text{ kJ/mol}$, and $H_2O\text{ (steam)} = -228.6\text{ kJ/mol}$. Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy of the reaction ($\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$) at 298.15 K.

Step-by-Step Thermodynamic Derivation:
The balanced dehydration reaction is: $$\text{KMg}_3\text{AlSi}_3\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2\ (\text{Phl}) + 3\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Qtz}) \longrightarrow 3\text{MgSiO}_3\ (\text{En}) + \text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{Kfs}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
1. Calculate $\sum \Delta G^\circ_f(\text{Reactants})$: $$\sum \Delta G^\circ_f(\text{reactants}) = -5,835 + 3(-856.3) = -5,835 - 2,568.9 = -8,403.9\text{ kJ}$$
2. Calculate $\sum \Delta G^\circ_f(\text{Products})$: $$\sum \Delta G^\circ_f(\text{products}) = 3(-1,460.8) + (-3,742.9) + (-228.6) = -4,382.4 - 3,742.9 - 228.6 = -8,353.9\text{ kJ}$$
3. Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$: $$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \sum \Delta G^\circ_f(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta G^\circ_f(\text{reactants}) = -8,353.9 - (-8,403.9) = \mathbf{+50.0\text{ kJ/mol}}$$ Physical Interpretation: At 298 K, $\Delta G^\circ > 0$, meaning hydrous biotite + quartz is stable at surface conditions. Because the reaction produces steam ($\Delta S_{\text{rxn}} \gg 0$), the $-T\Delta S$ term dominates at high temperature ($T > 750^\circ\text{C}$), driving $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}$ negative and precipitating hypersthene charnockite.
Problem 2: Thermodynamic Effect of Water Activity ($a_{H_2O}$) on Charnockitization

The equilibrium constant for the biotite dehydration reaction is given by $\ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT}$. If the solid phases are pure minerals ($a_{\text{solids}} = 1$), express the equilibrium temperature ($T_{\text{eq}}$) as a function of water activity ($a_{H_2O}$). Explain why $CO_2$ flushing induces "incipient charnockite" formation at Kabbaldurga.

Thermodynamic Fluid Activity Derivation:
The equilibrium constant expression is: $$K = \frac{a_{\text{En}}^3 \cdot a_{\text{Kfs}} \cdot a_{H_2O}}{a_{\text{Phl}} \cdot a_{\text{Qtz}}^3} = a_{H_2O}$$
$$\Delta G^\circ(T) = -R T \ln(a_{H_2O}) \implies \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = -R T \ln(a_{H_2O})$$
Solving for equilibrium temperature $T$: $$T = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ - R \ln(a_{H_2O})}$$
Kabbaldurga Mechanism: Influx of juvenile, mantle-derived $CO_2$ dilutes intergranular metamorphic pore fluids, drastically lowering water activity from $a_{H_2O} \approx 1.0$ down to $a_{H_2O} \approx 0.2\text{--}0.3$. Because $\ln(a_{H_2O})$ becomes a large negative number, the denominator increases, lowering the equilibrium dehydration temperature by $100\text{--}150^\circ\text{C}$. Consequently, ambient amphibolite-facies gneisses at $\sim 700^\circ\text{C}$ are instantly dehydrated into hypersthene charnockite without requiring any addition of heat!
Problem 3: Optical Mineralogy: Hypersthene Pleochroic Formula

State the diagnostic optical properties of hypersthene under the petrographic microscope, including its axial character, extinction angle, and characteristic pleochroic colors along its three vibration axes ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$).

Optical Properties of Hypersthene (Ferroan Enstatite):
- Crystal System: Orthorhombic ($P_{bca}$).
- Extinction: Parallel (straight) extinction ($0^\circ$) to prismatic $\{110\}$ cleavage in longitudinal sections.
- Cleavage: Two sets of distinct prismatic cleavages intersecting at approximately $87^\circ$ and $93^\circ$ in basal cross-sections.
- Optic Sign: Biaxial Negative ($2V \approx 50\text{--}80^\circ$).
- Diagnostic Pleochroism: The most famous pleochroism in petrology:
- $\alpha\ (X) = \mathbf{\text{Pink to brownish-red / salmon pink}}$
- $\beta\ (Y) = \mathbf{\text{Pale yellow to greenish-yellow}}$
- $\gamma\ (Z) = \mathbf{\text{Pale green to emerald green}}$
Problem 4: Petrographic Discrimination: Charnockite vs. Enderbite

A granulite facies rock contains $25\%$ quartz, $15\%$ hypersthene, $55\%$ antiperthitic plagioclase ($\text{An}_{32}$), and only $5\%$ microcline. Classify this rock into Holland's terminology and modern IUGS nomenclature.

Classification Derivation:
- Felsic Ratio: Quartz ($Q = 25\%$), Plagioclase ($P = 55\%$), Alkali Feldspar ($A = 5\%$).
- In the QAP classification, $P / (P + A) = \frac{55}{55 + 5} = \frac{55}{60} = \mathbf{91.7\%}$. This plots directly in Field 5 (Tonalite / Quartz Diorite).
- Taxonomic Designation: Because plagioclase vastly predominates over K-feldspar ($P \gg A$) and the mafic mineral is hypersthene, the rock is an Enderbite (Tilley, 1936), the plagioclase-dominant member of the Charnockitic suite, distinct from Charnockite sensu stricto where $A \ge P$.
Problem 5: Physical Cause of the Greasy Luster and Dark Color

Why do acid charnockites ($SiO_2 > 70\%$) appear dark olive-green or greasy dark brown in hand specimen, whereas common calc-alkaline granites of identical silica content appear light pink, white, or light grey?

Solid-State Physics and Optical Scattering:
1. Submicroscopic Inclusions: Charnockites formed at deep lower crustal levels under high confining pressures ($>7\text{ kbar}$). Slow cooling under anhydrous conditions caused $Fe$ and $Ti$ dissolved in the feldspar and quartz lattices at high temperature to precipitate as billions of submicron-scale needles of ilmenite ($\text{FeTiO}_3$) and rutile ($\text{TiO}_2$).
2. Micro-Fracture Hydrocarbon/Fluid Films: Intergranular grain boundaries and micro-cracks host high-density carbonic fluid inclusions and thin films of graphite/chlorite/iron-oxides.
3. Rayleigh & Mie Scattering: These submicroscopic inclusions scatter and absorb light across all visible wavelengths, completely destroying the normal white specular reflection of feldspars and imparting a dark, greasy, waxy appearance.
Problem 6: The Charnockite-Khondalite Terrain of the Eastern Ghats (EGMB)

In the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt (EGMB) of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, charnockites are intimately intercalated with khondalites. Contrast the protoliths and metamorphic environments of these two iconic Indian rock types.

Regional Tectonometamorphic Contrast:
- Khondalite (Metasedimentary Protolith): Formed by ultra-high temperature granulite metamorphism of highly weathered, kaolinite-rich aluminous pelitic sediments (lithomargic clays and bauxitic soils) deposited in passive margins. Mineralogy: Garnet (almandine-pyrope) + Sillimanite + Quartz + K-feldspar $\pm$ Graphite.
- Charnockite (Meta-igneous / Ortho-gneiss Protolith): Formed by deep crustal granulite metamorphism and dehydration of calc-alkaline igneous granitoids, tonalites, and diorites under high-density $CO_2$ conditions. Mineralogy: Hypersthene + K-feldspar + Quartz $\pm$ Plagioclase.
- Geodynamic Setting: Both were fused and metamorphosed together during Proterozoic collisional orogenies (Grenvillian / Kuunga orogenies, ~1000–900 Ma) when India docked against East Antarctica.
Problem 7: Geothermobarometry of the Garnet-Orthopyroxene Pair

In garnet-bearing charnockites, the exchange of iron and magnesium between garnet and hypersthene: $$\frac{1}{3}\text{Mg}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}\ (\text{Pyrope}) + \text{FeSiO}_3\ (\text{Ferrosilite}) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{3}\text{Fe}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}\ (\text{Almandine}) + \text{MgSiO}_3\ (\text{Enstatite})$$ is used as a geothermometer (Harley, 1984). If the distribution coefficient is $K_D = \frac{(Fe/Mg)_{\text{grt}}}{(Fe/Mg)_{\text{opx}}} = 3.25$, explain how $K_D$ responds to increasing metamorphic temperature.

Thermodynamic Response:
- The exchange reaction is endothermic in the forward direction. Consequently, as metamorphic temperature ($T$) increases, thermal agitation overcomes the energy barrier that selectively partitions $Fe^{2+}$ into the smaller 8-coordinated garnet dodecahedral site.
- Therefore, with increasing temperature, $K_D$ decreases systematically toward unity ($K_D \to 1.0$).
- A high $K_D$ value ($3.25$) reflects retrograde cooling or lower granulite facies ($T \approx 700\text{--}750^\circ\text{C}$), whereas peak ultra-high temperature (UHT) granulites ($T > 950^\circ\text{C}$) yield lower $K_D$ values ($K_D \approx 1.8\text{--}2.2$).
Problem 8: Retrograde Metamorphism: Uralitization of Hypersthene

During exhumation and hydration of a charnockite terrain, hypersthene is often partially replaced along cracks and margins by green amphibole (hornblende) and secondary biotite. Name this texture and write the general hydration reaction.

Retrograde Reaction & Nomenclature:
- Textural Name: Uralitization (when pyroxene is replaced by fibrous amphibole) or kelyphitic / corona rim.
- Hydration Reaction: Influx of aqueous fluids ($H_2O$) during cooling and crustal uplift reverses the prograde dehydration: $$\text{Hypersthene} + \text{Plagioclase} + \text{K-feldspar} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Hornblende} + \text{Biotite} + \text{Quartz}$$
- Significance: Identifies retrograde amphibolite-facies overprinting of pristine anhydrous granulite facies charnockites.

Q081: Antiperthite Texture: Subsolidus Feldspar Exsolution

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 81
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 6: Feldspar Phase Equilibria, pp. 91–98, Fig. 6-16); Anthony Hall, Igneous Petrology; G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 119–120); Deer, Howie & Zussman, An Introduction to the Rock-Forming Minerals (3rd Ed., Mineralogical Society, pp. 385–412).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Microstructure & Crystallographic Architecture of Antiperthite

The term antiperthite describes an intimate subsolidus intergrowth texture in which a host crystal of plagioclase feldspar (typically oligoclase, andesine, or albite) contains oriented, bleb-like, rod-like, rectangular, or irregular inclusions of potassium feldspar (orthoclase or microcline).

It is the exact crystallographic and structural mirror-image of perthite:

The Fundamental Perthite–Antiperthite Distinction:
$$\mathbf{\text{Perthite}} = \mathbf{\text{Potassium Feldspar Host}} \quad \text{containing exsolved blebs/lamellae of } \mathbf{\text{Plagioclase (Albite)}}$$
$$\mathbf{\text{Antiperthite}} = \mathbf{\text{Plagioclase Host}} \quad \text{containing exsolved blebs/inclusions of } \mathbf{\text{Potassium Feldspar (Kfs)}}$$
$$\mathbf{\text{Mesoperthite}} = \text{Roughly equal proportions } (\sim 50:50) \text{ of mutually intergrown K-feldspar and Plagioclase}$$
Figure 81.1 — The Ternary Feldspar Solvus and Subsolidus Exsolution: Authentic textbook diagram from J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 6, Fig. 6-16). Illustrating the subsolidus miscibility gap (solvus) across the $Ab\text{--}Or\text{--}An$ system where homogeneous high-temperature feldspars unmix into perthite (K-rich host) or antiperthite (Na-Ca-rich host).

Optical Identification Under the Polarizing Microscope

  • Host Grain: Displays continuous polysynthetic albite twinning ($\{010\}$ plane) or combined Carlsbad-albite twinning across the entire grain.
  • Exsolved Inclusions: Appear as tiny, discrete, rectangular, bleb-like, or flame-shaped islands of K-feldspar scattered throughout the plagioclase host. Under cross-polarized light (XPL), the K-feldspar inclusions extinguish at a distinctly different angle from the host plagioclase and often display subtle gridiron/tartan twinning (microcline) or remain untwinned with lower refractive index ($n < 1.525$).
2. Thermodynamics of the Feldspar Solvus: Spinodal Decomposition & Nucleation

At elevated magmatic temperatures ($T > 800\text{--}900^\circ\text{C}$), alkali feldspars and ternary feldspars form a complete, continuous solid solution because thermal kinetic energy overcomes the strain caused by the size mismatch between the large potassium ion ($r_{\text{K}^+} = 1.38\text{ \AA}$) and smaller sodium ($r_{\text{Na}^+} = 1.02\text{ \AA}$) and calcium ($r_{\text{Ca}^{2+}} = 1.00\text{ \AA}$) ions.

Subsolidus Phase Separation Across the Miscibility Gap

As the crystalline rock cools below the solvus temperature ($T < 650\text{--}700^\circ\text{C}$), the excess Gibbs free energy of mixing ($\Delta G_{\text{mix}} = \Delta H_{\text{mix}} - T\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$) becomes positive due to the high enthalpy of lattice strain ($\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$). The single homogeneous solid solution becomes thermodynamically unstable and unmixes:

  • Binodal (Solvus Boundary): The equilibrium boundary where two distinct coexisting feldspar phases are in thermodynamic equilibrium ($\mu_i^{\text{plag}} = \mu_i^{\text{Kfs}}$).
  • Spinodal Boundary ($\frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial X^2} = 0$): Inside the chemical spinodal, there is no activation energy barrier to phase separation. The homogeneous lattice spontaneously breaks down via uphill diffusion (spinodal decomposition), producing ultrafine, periodic, coherent exsolution lamellae (cryptoperthites).
  • Nucleation and Growth: In the metastable region between the binodal and spinodal ($\frac{\partial^2 G}{\partial X^2} > 0$), unmixing requires overcoming an activation energy barrier, producing discrete, isolated blebs or patches of K-feldspar within plagioclase—the classic patchy antiperthite.
3. Petrologic Environments & Geothermobarometry of Antiperthite

Antiperthitic plagioclase is not ubiquitous; its presence serves as a diagnostic fingerprint of specific, extreme high-temperature and water-undersaturated geological environments:

  • Charnockite and Granulite Terrains: In granulite facies high-grade metamorphic complexes (e.g., Eastern Ghats, Southern Granulite Terrain of India), anhydrous conditions and high temperatures ($750\text{--}900^\circ\text{C}$) permit substantial substitution of potassium into plagioclase at peak conditions. Subsequent slow cooling yields spectacular antiperthitic andesine in enderbites and acid charnockites.
  • Proterozoic Anorthosite Massifs: Massive, plagioclase-dominated cumulates of massif-type anorthosites (e.g., Chilka Lake anorthosite, Odisha) typically contain coarse antiperthitic labradorite/andesine formed by slow subsolidus cooling of dry, mantle-derived parent magmas.
  • Two-Feldspar Geothermometry: The partitioning of albite component between coexisting perthitic K-feldspar and antiperthitic plagioclase forms the basis of the famous Two-Feldspar Geothermometer (Stormer, 1975; Fuhrman & Lindsley, 1988), allowing quantitative derivation of peak metamorphic and magmatic temperatures.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 81
An inter-growth texture in which plagioclase contains inclusions of potash feldspar is known as :
(A) Antiperthite
(B) Perthite
(C) Graphic texture
(D) Ophitic
CORRECT ANSWER: (A)
Antiperthite: A subsolidus exsolution texture where a host crystal of plagioclase feldspar contains lamellae, blebs, or irregular inclusions of exsolved potassium feldspar.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Antiperthite — CORRECT

Antiperthite is the exact, universally accepted petrographic definition for an intergrowth where plagioclase acts as the host mineral containing exsolved inclusions, blebs, or lamellae of potassium feldspar. It is commonly observed in high-grade granulite-facies rocks, charnockites (especially enderbite), and massif-type anorthosites (Winter, 2014, p. 95; Mahapatra, p. 119; Deer, Howie & Zussman, p. 390).

(B) Perthite — INCORRECT

Perthite is the inverse texture: the host crystal is potassium feldspar (microcline or orthoclase), which contains exsolved lamellae, strings, or blebs of sodic plagioclase (albite). Mixing up perthite and antiperthite is one of the most common errors in optical mineralogy.

(C) Graphic texture — INCORRECT

Graphic texture is a primary cotectic magmatic intergrowth consisting of angular, cuneiform, runic prisms of quartz embedded within a potassium feldspar host in granitic pegmatites. It does not involve a plagioclase-potash feldspar exsolution relationship.

(D) Ophitic — INCORRECT

Ophitic texture is a magmatic crystallization texture characteristic of hypabyssal dolerite/diabase, where laths of plagioclase are completely enclosed poikilitically within large plates of clinopyroxene (augite).

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Ternary Feldspar Modal Reconstitution to Homogeneous Protolith

Microprobe analysis of an antiperthitic feldspar grain in an enderbite from the Eastern Ghats yields a plagioclase host of composition $\text{Ab}_{68}\text{An}_{30}\text{Or}_2$ occupying $85\text{ vol}\%$, and exsolved K-feldspar blebs of composition $\text{Or}_{92}\text{Ab}_7\text{An}_1$ occupying $15\text{ vol}\%$. Assuming identical molar densities, calculate the bulk ternary composition of the original homogeneous high-temperature feldspar prior to subsolidus unmixing.

Step-by-Step Mass Balance Calculation:
Bulk mole fraction of each end-member component is given by: $$X_i^{\text{bulk}} = (0.85 \times X_i^{\text{host}}) + (0.15 \times X_i^{\text{exsolved}})$$
1. Orthoclase ($\text{Or}$) Component: $$X_{\text{Or}}^{\text{bulk}} = (0.85 \times 0.02) + (0.15 \times 0.92) = 0.017 + 0.138 = \mathbf{0.155} \implies \mathbf{15.5\text{ mol}\%}$$
2. Albite ($\text{Ab}$) Component: $$X_{\text{Ab}}^{\text{bulk}} = (0.85 \times 0.68) + (0.15 \times 0.07) = 0.578 + 0.0105 = \mathbf{0.5885} \implies \mathbf{58.85\text{ mol}\%}$$
3. Anorthite ($\text{An}$) Component: $$X_{\text{An}}^{\text{bulk}} = (0.85 \times 0.30) + (0.15 \times 0.01) = 0.255 + 0.0015 = \mathbf{0.2565} \implies \mathbf{25.65\text{ mol}\%}$$
Conclusion: The original peak metamorphic feldspar had a homogeneous ternary composition of $\mathbf{Ab_{58.8}An_{25.7}Or_{15.5}}$, confirming crystallization above the ternary solvus at $T > 850^\circ\text{C}$.
Problem 2: Size Scale Classification of Perthitic Intergrowths

Define the boundaries between: (a) Macroperthite; (b) Microperthite; and (c) Cryptoperthite, and state the analytical technique required to resolve each variety.

Dimensional Classification:
- (a) Macroperthite: Exsolution lamellae are thick ($> 0.1\text{ mm}$), coarse, and distinct enough to be seen with the naked eye or hand lens without optical magnification.
- (b) Microperthite: Exsolution lamellae range from $1\text{ to } 100\ \mu\text{m}$, invisible to the naked eye but beautifully resolved under the standard petrographic polarizing light microscope (PLM).
- (c) Cryptoperthite: Submicroscopic exsolution lamellae on the nanometer scale ($< 1\ \mu\text{m}$, typically $10\text{--}100\text{ nm}$). Completely invisible under optical microscopy; can only be detected via Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) or single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD). Cryptoperthite causes light diffraction producing the bluish iridescence known as moonstone (schiller effect).
Problem 3: Crystallographic Preferred Orientation of Exsolution Lamellae

Why do perthite and antiperthite exsolution lamellae align preferentially parallel to the $(6\bar{0}1)$ or $(\bar{6}01)$ crystallographic lattice planes rather than along random directions?

Lattice Strain Minimization (Willaime & Brown, 1974):
- During coherent subsolidus exsolution, the lattices of the two unmixing feldspars remain continuous across the phase interface.
- Because $K^+$ and $Na^+$ have different ionic radii, lattice dimensions differ ($a_{\text{Kfs}} = 8.6\text{ \AA}$ vs $a_{\text{Albite}} = 8.1\text{ \AA}$), introducing significant elastic strain energy ($\Delta G_{\text{elastic}}$).
- The crystallographic orientation that minimizes total coherent elastic strain energy between potassium feldspar and sodic plagioclase is the irrational plane oriented close to $(6\bar{0}1)$, inclined at $\sim 73^\circ$ to the $(001)$ cleavage. Aligning along this plane minimizes interfacial lattice mismatch, making phase separation thermodynamically spontaneous.
Problem 4: Hypersolvus vs. Subsolvus Granites and Perthite Formation

Compare the feldspar mineralogy of: (a) a Hypersolvus Granite crystallized at shallow crustal depth under low $P_{H_2O}$; and (b) a Subsolvus Granite crystallized at deep crustal levels under high $P_{H_2O}$.

Petrogenetic Phase Boundary Analysis:
- (a) Hypersolvus Granite (One-Feldspar Granite): Under dry, low $P_{H_2O}$ conditions, the granite solidus lies above the feldspar solvus ($T_{\text{solidus}} > T_{\text{solvus}}$). The magma crystallizes a single, homogeneous ternary alkali feldspar. Upon subsolidus cooling across the solvus, this single feldspar unmixes into spectacular perthite or mesoperthite.
- (b) Subsolvus Granite (Two-Feldspar Granite): Under high $P_{H_2O}$, dissolved water depresses the silicate solidus until it intersects the solvus ($T_{\text{solidus}} < T_{\text{solvus}}$). The magma crystallizes two separate primary magmatic feldspars directly from the melt: an independent potassium feldspar and an independent plagioclase feldspar.
Problem 5: Incoherent vs. Coherent Exsolution Microstructures

Distinguish between coherent and incoherent exsolution in feldspars. Which mechanism governs the formation of coarse patchy antiperthite?

Exsolution Physics:
- Coherent Exsolution: Crystal lattice planes are continuous across the boundary between the host and exsolved phase with zero bond breakage, accommodated entirely by elastic strain. Common in cryptoperthites formed by rapid cooling.
- Incoherent Exsolution: The lattice mismatch is relieved by edge dislocations, lattice severance, and recrystallization. The phase boundary is a true incoherent grain boundary with no continuous lattice planes.
- Patchy Antiperthite: Coarse patchy antiperthite in granulites and charnockites is formed by incoherent exsolution accompanied by fluid-enhanced recrystallization, allowing potassium feldspar to coalesce into large, irregular, isolated blebs within the plagioclase host.
Problem 6: Two-Feldspar Geothermometer Principles

Explain how the thermodynamic exchange of the albite ($Ab$) component between coexisting plagioclase and alkali feldspar is calibrated to calculate metamorphic equilibration temperatures.

Thermodynamic Exchange Derivation:
The exchange equilibrium of albite between coexisting plagioclase ($pl$) and alkali feldspar ($af$) is: $$\text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_{8\ (\text{in alkali feldspar})} \rightleftharpoons \text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_{8\ (\text{in plagioclase})}$$
At thermodynamic equilibrium: $$\mu_{Ab}^{af} = \mu_{Ab}^{pl}$$
Using Margules asymmetric solution parameters ($W_{AbOr}, W_{AbAn}, W_{OrAn}$) to account for non-ideal mixing, the distribution of albite is a sensitive, monotonic function of temperature ($T$) and pressure ($P$). By measuring the chemical compositions of perthite host and antiperthite host via electron microprobe, one can solve for the exact equilibrium temperature ($T_{\text{equilibration}}$).
Problem 7: Massif-Type Anorthosite Plagioclase Mineralogy

In the Chilka Lake anorthosite massif of Odisha, plagioclase megacrysts exhibit antiperthitic texture. What does this reveal about the crystallization temperature and volatile state of the parent magma?

Petrogenetic Interpretation:
1. High Crystallization Temperature: The high solubility of potassium in plagioclase (requiring $> 10\text{--}15\text{ mol}\% Or$ component in the initial plagioclase lattice) proves crystallization occurred at very high temperatures ($T \approx 1050\text{--}1200^\circ\text{C}$).
2. Water-Undersaturated Parent Magma: Massif-type anorthosites crystallized from deep crustal/sub-crustal ponded basaltic melts under essentially anhydrous ($H_2O$-deficient) conditions, precluding early separation of two discrete feldspars and forcing extensive subsolidus antiperthitic exsolution upon prolonged cooling.
Problem 8: Optical Discrimination: Antiperthite vs. Plagioclase Alteration (Sericite)

Under the microscope, fine inclusions inside plagioclase can easily be mistaken for alteration products. How do you optically differentiate true exsolved K-feldspar inclusions (antiperthite) from secondary sericite or saussurite?

Microscopic Criteria:
- Antiperthite (Exsolution): Inclusions are K-feldspar. They have low refractive index ($n < n_{\text{plag}}$), low birefringence ($\delta = 0.006\text{--}0.008$, displaying first-order grey/white interference colors identical to quartz), form crisp, rectangular, optical-crystallographically oriented blebs, and exhibit uniform extinction.
- Sericite (Secondary Alteration): Consists of fine-grained white mica (muscovite/paragonite). Exhibits intense, brilliant high second-to-third order interference colors (pinks, blues, greens) and fibrous/flaky morphology.
- Saussurite: Microcrystalline aggregate of high-relief, high-birefringence epidote/zoisite, calcite, and albite, easily distinguished by its extreme relief and speckled appearance.
