Q082: Autometamorphic (Deuteric) Processes in Cooling Igneous Plutons

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 82
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 3: Textures of Igneous Rocks / Deuteric Alteration, pp. 48–50); Anthony Hall, Igneous Petrology; G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 122–124); F.J. Turner & J. Verhoogen, Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology; H.G.F. Winkler, Petrogenesis of Metamorphic Rocks.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Kinetics & Mechanism of Autometamorphism (Deuteric Alteration)

Autometamorphism (universally known in igneous petrography as deuteric alteration or late-magmatic alteration, from the Greek deuteros = second) refers to the internal mineralogical and chemical transformations that occur within an igneous rock as it cools down immediately following its own crystallization.

These secondary mineral reactions are driven by hot, volatile-rich aqueous fluids and gases exsolved directly from the residual magmatic liquid (second boiling / resurgent boiling), or by heated juvenile/connate fluids circulating in the thermal aureole of the cooling pluton.

Figure 82.1 — Deuteric Replacement & Late-Magmatic Alteration Textures: Authentic textbook diagram from J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 3). Illustrating the progressive replacement of high-temperature anhydrous igneous minerals (plagioclase, pyroxene, biotite) by hydrous secondary phases (sericite, epidote, uralitic actinolite, chlorite) during post-magmatic cooling.

Fundamental Characteristics of Autometamorphic Processes

  • Continuous Thermal Continuity: Autometamorphic reactions occur as part of a continuous cooling trajectory of the single parent igneous event. They are not the products of an independent, later, separate regional or contact metamorphic event.
  • Plutonic Dominance: Because deep plutonic environments (batholiths, lopoliths, stocks, thick sills) retain their exsolved magmatic volatiles under confining pressure and cool very slowly over millions of years, autometamorphic processes are far more widespread and intense in plutonic rocks than in volcanic rocks, where volatiles escape instantaneously into the atmosphere.
  • Fluid-Driven Reactions at Moderate Temperatures: Most reactions occur between $500^\circ\text{C}$ and $200^\circ\text{C}$, involving the interaction of water, carbon dioxide, fluorine, and boron with anhydrous silicate minerals.
2. Common Autometamorphic Reactions in Igneous Petrography

Petrologists routinely encounter specific diagnostic mineral replacements produced by autometamorphic fluid circulation:

  • Uralitization: The secondary alteration of high-temperature pyroxenes (augite, pigeonite, enstatite) into fibrous, acicular pale-green amphibole (actinolite, tremolite, or hornblende), typically observed in gabbros and dolerites.
  • Saussuritization: The hydrothermal breakdown of calcium-rich plagioclase (labradorite/bytownite) into a dense, fine-grained, microcrystalline aggregate of zoisite, clinozoisite, epidote, albite, calcite, and quartz.
  • Sericitization: The hydrolytic alteration of feldspars (both plagioclase and alkali feldspar) by acidic hydrothermal fluids, converting them into microscopic flakes of fine-grained white mica (sericite / muscovite) with the liberation of quartz and alkalis.
  • Serpentinization: The hydration of magnesium-rich olivine and orthopyroxene in peridotites and ultramafic cumulates by aqueous fluids ($T < 450^\circ\text{C}$), producing serpentine group minerals (lizardite, chrysotile, antigorite) and magnetite: $$2\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4\ (\text{Forsterite}) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4\ (\text{Serpentine}) + \text{Mg(OH)}_2\ (\text{Brucite})$$
  • Chloritization: The replacement of biotite mica or hornblende by green chlorite, often accompanied by the exsolution of needle-like rutile inclusions forming sagenitic webs.
  • Greisenization: Autometasomatic alteration of granitic cupolas by late-stage fluorine- and boron-rich magmatic fluids, transforming feldspars into an aggregate of quartz, lithian muscovite (zinnwaldite), topaz, fluorite, and cassiterite.
3. Why Weathering and Diagenesis are Strictly Excluded from Autometamorphism

It is a gross petrological error to conflate autometamorphism with weathering or diagenesis:

  • Weathering: An exogenic, surface process occurring at atmospheric pressure ($P = 1\text{ atm}$) and ambient Earth-surface temperatures (typically $-10^\circ\text{C}$ to $+40^\circ\text{C}$). It is driven exclusively by the interaction of rocks with the atmosphere, biosphere, and meteoric precipitation ($O_2, CO_2, H_2O$), producing soils, saprolites, and clays (kaolinite, smectite). It has zero connection to magmatic heat or residual magmatic fluids.
  • Diagenesis: Refers strictly to post-depositional physical and chemical changes in sedimentary rocks at near-surface to shallow burial depths ($T < 150\text{--}200^\circ\text{C}$, $P < 1\text{--}2\text{ kbar}$), encompassing sediment compaction, cementation, dissolution, and authigenesis. It does not apply to igneous crystallization.
The Petrogenetic Boundary:
$$\text{Autometamorphism (Deuteric)} \implies \mathbf{Endogenic,\ High\ to\ Moderate\ Temp\ (500\text{--}200^\circ C),\ Magmatic\ Fluids}$$
$$\text{Weathering / Diagenesis} \implies \mathbf{Exogenic\ /\ Sedimentary,\ Low\ Temp\ (<150^\circ C),\ Meteoric\ /\ Pore\ Waters}$$
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 82
Which of the following statements w. r. t. Autometamorphic processes is not correct ?
(A) These secondary mineral reactions occur in igneous rocks as they cool, and are not products of a distinct later metamorphic event.
(B) These processes are more common in plutonic rocks than in volcanics.
(C) Diagenetic and weathering processes are also considered to be Autometamorphic.
(D) Most reactions involve minerals at moderate temperatures in an environment in which H2O is either liberated from residual melt or externally introduced.
CORRECT ANSWER: (C)
"Diagenetic and weathering processes are also considered to be Autometamorphic": This statement is completely false. Weathering is an exogenic, low-temperature surface process, and diagenesis is a sedimentary process; neither is ever classified as autometamorphic.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) These secondary mineral reactions occur in igneous rocks as they cool, and are not products of a distinct later metamorphic event. — ACCURATE STATEMENT

This is the fundamental defining criterion of autometamorphism (deuteric alteration). Unlike regional or contact metamorphism, which requires an independent tectonothermal event millions of years later, autometamorphism occurs during the continuous cooling of the single host igneous intrusion itself.

(B) These processes are more common in plutonic rocks than in volcanics. — ACCURATE STATEMENT

This statement is entirely true. Plutonic rocks crystallize slowly at depth under lithostatic confining pressure, allowing residual volatile-rich aqueous fluids to remain trapped and react with earlier crystals. In volcanic lavas, gases escape rapidly into the air, and lavas freeze before deuteric reactions can proceed.

(C) Diagenetic and weathering processes are also considered to be Autometamorphic. — NOT CORRECT (IDENTIFIED FLAW)

This statement is completely incorrect and petrologically false. Weathering is an exogenic surface process driven by the atmosphere and meteoric water at ambient surface conditions ($T < 30^\circ\text{C}$). Diagenesis refers to post-depositional lithification processes in sedimentary basins. Neither has any relation to late-magmatic cooling or igneous autometamorphism (Winter, 2014, p. 48).

(D) Most reactions involve minerals at moderate temperatures in an environment in which H2O is either liberated from residual melt or externally introduced. — ACCURATE STATEMENT

This is a precise summary of deuteric thermodynamics: reactions proceed at moderate subsolidus temperatures ($200\text{--}500^\circ\text{C}$) in the presence of $H_2O$ and other volatiles exsolved by second boiling or drawn into the pluton via convective meteoric-hydrothermal cells.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Second Boiling (Resurgent Boiling) Thermodynamics

During the isobaric crystallization of a hydrous granitic magma containing $4\text{ wt}\% H_2O$ at $P = 2\text{ kbar}$ ($200\text{ MPa}$), explain the physical mechanism of "second boiling" (resurgent boiling) and calculate whether the reaction involves a net positive or negative volume change ($\Delta V_{\text{rxn}}$).

Thermodynamic Derivation:
1. Mechanistic Definition: Primary boiling occurs when magma decompresses during ascent. Second boiling occurs during cooling and isobaric crystallization: as anhydrous minerals (quartz and feldspars) crystallize from the melt, water is rejected into the shrinking volume of residual melt. When water concentration exceeds the solubility limit ($\sim 6\text{ wt}\%$ at 2 kbar), an aqueous supercritical fluid phase ($H_2O\text{-rich vapor}$) exsolves spontaneously.
2. Volume Change: $$\text{Melt} \longrightarrow \text{Crystals} + \text{Aqueous Vapor}$$ $$\Delta V_{\text{rxn}} = V_{\text{crystals}} + V_{\text{vapor}} - V_{\text{melt}}$$
Because the specific volume of the low-density aqueous vapor ($V_{\text{vapor}}$) is exceedingly large compared to silicate melt at crustal pressures ($V_{\text{vapor}} \approx 1.5\text{ to } 3.0\text{ cm}^3/\text{g}$ vs $V_{\text{melt}} \approx 0.4\text{ cm}^3/\text{g}$), $\Delta V_{\text{rxn}}$ is strongly positive.
Consequence: This large volumetric expansion induces hydraulic fracturing of the pluton roof, creating stockworks and driving extensive deuteric autometamorphism.
Problem 2: Balanced Chemical Stoichiometry of Saussuritization

Write the balanced chemical reaction for the complete saussuritization of anorthite plagioclase in the presence of water, producing zoisite, aluminum hydroxide, and quartz.

Stoichiometric Reaction:
$$\mathbf{4\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\ (\text{Anorthite})} + \mathbf{2\text{H}_2\text{O}} \longrightarrow \mathbf{2\text{Ca}_2\text{Al}_3\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}(\text{OH})\ (\text{Zoisite})} + \mathbf{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}} + \mathbf{2\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz})}$$
When sodium is available in solid solution (labradorite $\text{An}_{60}\text{Ab}_{40}$), the calcium is consumed by zoisite/epidote while the sodium recrystallizes into fine-grained secondary albite, producing the classic dull-green, turbid "saussurite" pseudomorph under the microscope.
Problem 3: Serpentinization Mass Balance & Density Reduction

A pure dunite consisting of forsterite olivine ($\rho = 3.30\text{ g/cm}^3$) undergoes complete serpentinization to chrysotile serpentine ($\rho = 2.55\text{ g/cm}^3$) without loss of magnesium or silica according to: $$2\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4 + \text{Mg(OH)}_2$$ Calculate the percentage volume expansion ($\Delta V/V_0 \times 100\%$) of the rock during this autometamorphic hydration.

Step-by-Step Calculation:
1. Molar Masses: - Forsterite ($\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$): $M = 140.7\text{ g/mol}$. For 2 moles: Mass = $281.4\text{ g}$.
- Initial volume: $V_0 = \frac{281.4\text{ g}}{3.30\text{ g/cm}^3} \approx \mathbf{85.27\text{ cm}^3}$.
2. Product Masses: - Chrysotile ($\text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4$): $M = 277.1\text{ g/mol}$. Volume = $\frac{277.1}{2.55} \approx 108.67\text{ cm}^3$.
- Brucite ($\text{Mg(OH)}_2$): $M = 58.3\text{ g/mol}$, $\rho = 2.39\text{ g/cm}^3$. Volume = $\frac{58.3}{2.39} \approx 24.39\text{ cm}^3$.
- Total final volume: $V_{\text{final}} = 108.67 + 24.39 = \mathbf{133.06\text{ cm}^3}$.
3. Volume Expansion: $$\frac{\Delta V}{V_0} \times 100\% = \frac{133.06 - 85.27}{85.27} \times 100\% = \frac{47.79}{85.27} \times 100\% \approx \mathbf{+56.0\%}$$
Geological Significance: The massive $\sim 56\%$ volume expansion during serpentinization generates immense internal stresses, producing networks of micro-fractures and slickensided shear surfaces in ophiolites.
Problem 4: Sericitization and Hydrogen-Ion Metasomatism

Write the hydrolytic reaction governing the sericitization of potassium feldspar by acidic hydrothermal fluids ($H^+$), explaining why the fluid becomes enriched in potassium.

Reaction Equation:
$$\mathbf{3\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{Microcline})} + \mathbf{2\text{H}^+} \longrightarrow \mathbf{\text{KAl}_3\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2\ (\text{Sericite})} + \mathbf{6\text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz})} + \mathbf{2\text{K}^+}$$
Hydrochemical Mechanism: Acidic deuteric fluids supply $H^+$ ions that exchange with $K^+$ in the feldspar lattice. The displaced potassium is leached into the aqueous fluid phase, leaving behind fine-grained white mica (sericite) and silica. This neutralizes the fluid, shifting it toward alkaline compositions in outer alteration zones.
Problem 5: Greisenization Reactions in Granitic Tin-Tungsten Systems

Define greisenization and write the chemical transformation converting alkali feldspar into quartz and muscovite in the presence of fluorine-bearing magmatic fluids.

Greisenization Definition & Reaction:
- Greisen: A pneumatolytic/deuteric rock consisting essentially of quartz and white mica (muscovite, lepidolite, zinnwaldite), with accessory topaz, fluorite, tourmaline, cassiterite ($\text{SnO}_2$), and wolframite ($(\text{Fe,Mn})\text{WO}_4$).
- Chemical Transformation: $$\text{KAlSi}_3\text{O}_8\ (\text{K-feldspar}) + \text{HF} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{KAl}_3\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH,F})_2\ (\text{Muscovite}) + \text{SiO}_2\ (\text{Quartz}) + \text{Topaz} + \text{K}^+$$
Occurs in the apical roofs (cupolas) of highly differentiated, peraluminous S-type granites.
Problem 6: Sagenitic Rutile Webs in Chloritized Biotite

Under the microscope, altered biotite often exhibits a dense, triangular, or hexagonal grid of microscopic needle-like crystals of rutile (sagenite). Explain the crystallographic and geochemical origin of this deuteric texture.

Mineralogical Origin:
1. Titanium in Primary Biotite: High-temperature magmatic biotite can accommodate significant titanium ($2\text{ to } 5\text{ wt}\% TiO_2$) in its octahedral layer.
2. Exsolution during Chloritization: When deuteric fluids alter biotite to chlorite, titanium cannot fit into the chlorite crystal lattice ($TiO_2 \ll 0.1\text{ wt}\%$).
3. Epitaxial Sagenite Web: The excess titanium is rejected and exsolves as microscopic needles of rutile ($\text{TiO}_2$) oriented strictly parallel to the $\{110\}$ and $\{010\}$ directions of the host biotite cleavage plane, intersecting at $60^\circ/120^\circ$ angles to form a delicate geometric lattice termed a sagenite web.
Problem 7: Fluid Inclusion Microthermometry of Deuteric Quartz

Microthermometric heating-freezing analysis of primary fluid inclusions trapped in deuteric quartz veins yields a homogenization temperature $T_h = 280^\circ\text{C}$ and a freezing point depression $\Delta T_f = -4.2^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the fluid salinity in equivalent wt% NaCl using Potter's formula ($\text{Salinity} = 1.769|\Delta T_f| - 0.0423|\Delta T_f|^2 + 0.000527|\Delta T_f|^3$).

Fluid Salinity Calculation:
Given $|\Delta T_f| = 4.2^\circ\text{C}$:
$$\text{Term 1} = 1.769 \times 4.2 = 7.4298$$
$$\text{Term 2} = -0.0423 \times (4.2)^2 = -0.0423 \times 17.64 \approx -0.7462$$
$$\text{Term 3} = 0.000527 \times (4.2)^3 = 0.000527 \times 74.088 \approx +0.0390$$
$$\text{Salinity} = 7.4298 - 0.7462 + 0.0390 = \mathbf{6.72\text{ eq. wt}\% NaCl}$$
Interpretation: The deuteric fluid was a moderate-salinity hydrothermal brine ($6.7\text{ wt}\% NaCl$) actively circulating at $T > 280^\circ\text{C}$ during late-magmatic cooling.
Problem 8: Taphonomic & Structural Distinction: Deuteric vs Regional Metamorphism

How can a field geologist definitively distinguish between an igneous pluton that has undergone deuteric autometamorphism versus one that has experienced subsequent regional dynamo-thermal metamorphism?

Field and Microscopic Diagnostic Criteria:
- Autometamorphism (Deuteric): Mineral alteration is pseudomorphic and non-foliated (e.g., uralite preserves the exact rectangular shape of original pyroxene crystals; plagioclase retains original igneous zoning despite being saussuritized). There is NO tectonic foliation, lineation, or dynamic recrystallization.
- Regional Metamorphism: Accompanied by directed tectonic differential stress, producing pervasive metamorphic foliation, schistosity, or gneissic banding. Primary igneous zoning is destroyed; minerals display undulose extinction, subgrain formation, dynamic recrystallization (core-and-mantle structures), and orientation of newly formed phyllosilicates.

Q083: Main Central Thrust (MCT): Tectonic Boundary of the Higher Himalaya

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 83
Authoritative References: Ben A. van der Pluijm & Stephen Marshak, Earth Structure: An Introduction to Structural Geology and Tectonics (2nd Ed., W.W. Norton, Ch. 21, Fig. 21.21); K.S. Valdiya, Geology of the Kumaun Lesser Himalaya (Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology); Arnold Heim & Augusto Gansser (1939, Central Himalaya: Geological Observations of the Swiss Expedition); O.N. Bhargava, The Himalayan Geology.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Himalayan Morphotectonic Framework & Longitudinal Fault Architecture

The Himalayan Orogen, produced by the continent-continent collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates (~55 Ma to present), represents the premier active convergent mountain belt on Earth. The orogenic wedge is structured into five distinct, laterally continuous morphotectonic lithotectonic zones separated by crustal-scale, north-dipping boundary fault systems (Heim & Gansser, 1939; Valdiya, 1980; Van der Pluijm & Marshak, 2004):

Figure 83.1 — Tectonic Architecture of the Himalayan Orogen: Authentic diagram from Van der Pluijm & Marshak (Earth Structure, Ch. 21, Fig. 21.21). Illustrating the northward-dipping crustal thrust architecture: the Main Central Thrust (MCT) carrying the High-grade Great Himalayan Crystallines (HHC) over the Lesser Himalayan Sequence (LHS), underlain southward by the MBT and MFT.

North-to-South Structural Transect of the Himalaya

  1. Indus-Yarlung Tsangpo Suture Zone (ITSN / ISZ): The collision boundary demarcated by ophiolites and trench mélanges representing the closed Neotethys Ocean.
  2. Tethyan Sedimentary Series (TSS / THS): A thick sequence ($>10\text{ km}$) of fossiliferous Cambrian-to-Eocene shallow-marine shelf sediments deposited on the northern passive margin of India.
  3. South Tibetan Detachment System (STDS): A major low-angle, top-to-the-north extensional normal fault / ductile shear zone that places unmetamorphosed Tethyan sediments over the underlying crystalline core.
  4. Higher Himalayan Crystallines (HHC / Great Himalayan Sequence, GHS): The metamorphic backbone of the mountain chain! Composed of high-grade Proterozoic paragneisses, orthogneisses, kyanite-sillimanite schists, migmatites, and Miocene leucogranites formed at amphibolite-to-granulite facies ($T = 650\text{--}800^\circ\text{C}, P = 8\text{--}12\text{ kbar}$).
  5. Main Central Thrust (MCT): The definitive ductile shear zone! A massive, crustal-scale intracontinental thrust fault that accommodated tens to hundreds of kilometers of southward displacement, placing the high-grade HHC over the low-grade Lesser Himalaya.
  6. Lesser Himalayan Sequence (LHS): Low-grade to unmetamorphosed Paleoproterozoic to Mesoproterozoic quartzites, slates, phyllites, and stromatolitic carbonates (e.g., Damtha, Deoban, Jaunsar, Krol, and Tal groups).
  7. Main Boundary Thrust (MBT): A brittle-to-ductile thrust fault that places the Proterozoic Lesser Himalayan sequence over the Cenozoic Siwalik Molasse.
  8. Sub-Himalayan Zone (Siwalik Group): Middle Miocene to Early Pleistocene syn-orogenic foreland molasse sandstones, mudstones, and conglomerates.
  9. Main Frontal Thrust (MFT / Himalayan Frontal Thrust, HFT): The active, southernmost blind/emergent thrust fault placing Siwalik strata over the Quaternary alluvium of the Indo-Gangetic Plains.
2. The MCT Ductile Shear Zone & The "Inverted Metamorphism" Paradox

The Main Central Thrust (MCT) is not a simple razor-thin fault surface; rather, it is a complex, ductile shear zone several kilometers thick characterized by intense penetrative plastic deformation:

  • Microstructural Mylonitization: Rocks within the shear zone display spectacular mylonites, ribbon quartz, dynamically recrystallized feldspar porphyroclasts, S-C fabrics, mica fish, and asymmetric pressure shadows indicating pervasive top-to-the-south/southwest thrust kinematics.
  • The Inverted Metamorphic Gradient: In ordinary metamorphic terrains, metamorphic grade increases downward with depth. In the Lesser Himalaya directly underlying the MCT, however, metamorphic grade increases systematically upwards toward the thrust sheet: $$\text{Chlorite Zone (Low)} \longrightarrow \text{Biotite} \longrightarrow \text{Garnet} \longrightarrow \text{Staurolite} \longrightarrow \text{Kyanite} \longrightarrow \mathbf{\text{Sillimanite (Directly beneath MCT!)}}$$

Thermal-Mechanical Origin of Inverted Metamorphism

Petrologists and geodynamicists explain this phenomenon through three synergistic processes:

  1. Thermal Inversion by Thrusting (Le Fort, 1975): Emplacement of the colossal, scorching-hot HHC metamorphic slab ($T > 750^\circ\text{C}$) over the relatively cold footwall Lesser Himalaya conducted heat downward, baking the uppermost footwall into higher-grade zones.
  2. Shear Heating: High plastic strain rates and friction within the ductile shear zone generated immense shear strain heating along the fault core.
  3. Channel Flow Extrusion (Grujic et al., 2002; Beaumont et al., 2001): During the Early to Middle Miocene (~23–16 Ma), a ductile, partially molten mid-crustal channel of HHC was extruded southward between two coeval bounding shear zones: the basal thrust (MCT) and the roof normal fault (STDS).
3. Regional Nomenclature (MCT-I vs. MCT-II) & The Basal MHT Décollement

Valdiya's Two-Tier Division in the Kumaun-Garhwal Himalaya

In the Indian Himalaya, Professor K.S. Valdiya (1980) delineated two distinct thrust planes:

  • MCT-I (Munsiari Thrust): The lower tectonic boundary, separating the low-grade metasediments of the Lesser Himalaya from the chlorite-biotite-garnet mylonitic gneisses of the Munsiari Formation.
  • MCT-II (Vaikrita Thrust): The true primary MCT (in the strict Swiss sense of Heim & Gansser), which brings the coarse-grained, high-grade kyanite-sillimanite psammitic gneisses and migmatites of the Vaikrita Group (HHC) over the Munsiari Formation.

The Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT) Basal Décollement

Geophysical deep seismic reflection profiles (e.g., Project INDEPTH) and earthquake hypocenters prove that at depth, the surface faults—MFT, MBT, and MCT—merge downward into a single, master low-angle basal detachment fault: the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT). The MHT absorbs the majority of the $\sim 18\text{--}20\text{ mm/year}$ of active convergence between the Indian shield and the Tibetan Plateau, serving as the rupture plane for catastrophic great earthquakes (e.g., 1905 Kangra, 1934 Bihar-Nepal, 2015 Gorkha).

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 83
The ductile shear zone along with the High-grade Great Himalayan Crystalline complex was placed above the Low-grade to unmeta-morphosed Lesser Himalayan Sequence is termed as the :
(A) Main Central Thrust (MCT)
(B) Main Frontal Thrust (MFT)
(C) Main Boundary Thrust (MBT)
(D) Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT)
CORRECT ANSWER: (A)
Main Central Thrust (MCT): The premier crustal-scale ductile shear zone of the Himalaya that thrusts the high-grade Greater Himalayan Crystalline (HHC) complex southward over the low-grade to unmetamorphosed Lesser Himalayan Sequence (LHS).
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Main Central Thrust (MCT) — CORRECT

The Main Central Thrust (MCT) is the universally established, textbook tectonic boundary that places the high-grade, kyanite-sillimanite-bearing Great Himalayan Crystalline (HHC) complex over the low-grade Proterozoic Lesser Himalayan Sequence (LHS). It represents an intracontinental ductile shear zone several kilometers thick, characterized by pervasive mylonitization and the famous inverted metamorphic gradient (Heim & Gansser, 1939; Valdiya, 1980; Van der Pluijm & Marshak, p. 488).

(B) Main Frontal Thrust (MFT) — INCORRECT

The Main Frontal Thrust (MFT) is the southernmost, active tectonic boundary of the Himalaya. It places the deformed Cenozoic Siwalik molasse over the modern, flat Quaternary alluvium of the Indo-Gangetic Plains. It is a brittle, shallow thrust fault that has no contact with the High-grade Great Himalayan Crystallines.

(C) Main Boundary Thrust (MBT) — INCORRECT

The Main Boundary Thrust (MBT) separates the Lesser Himalayan Sequence in its hanging wall from the Sub-Himalayan Siwalik Group in its footwall. It is a predominantly brittle to semi-brittle fault formed during the Late Miocene–Pliocene, located far to the south of the Great Himalayan Crystalline complex.

(D) Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT) — INCORRECT

Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT) is simply an alternative, synonymous geological name for the Main Frontal Thrust (MFT). It marks the outermost structural boundary between the Sub-Himalaya and the Indo-Gangetic Foreland Basin.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Critical Coulomb Wedge Taper Calculation for the Himalaya

According to Davis, Suppe & Dahlen's (1983) Critical Coulomb Wedge Theory, a convergent orogenic wedge maintains dynamic stability when its critical taper angle ($\alpha + \beta$) satisfies: $$\alpha + \beta = \frac{1 - \lambda_b}{1 - \lambda} \mu_b$$ In the Central Nepal Himalaya, the basal décollement (MHT) dips northward at $\beta = 6^\circ$, and the average topographic slope is $\alpha = 2.5^\circ$. If the pore fluid pressure ratio throughout the wedge is hydrostatic ($\lambda = 0.40$), and the basal pore fluid pressure ratio is $\lambda_b = 0.75$, calculate the effective basal friction coefficient ($\mu_b$).

Step-by-Step Wedge Calculation:
1. Calculate total wedge taper angle in radians: $$\alpha + \beta = 2.5^\circ + 6.0^\circ = 8.5^\circ$$
Converting to radians: $$\theta = 8.5 \times \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.14835\text{ radians}$$
2. Substitute pore fluid factors: $$\frac{1 - \lambda_b}{1 - \lambda} = \frac{1 - 0.75}{1 - 0.40} = \frac{0.25}{0.60} \approx 0.4167$$
3. Solve for $\mu_b$: $$\alpha + \beta = 0.4167 \times \mu_b \implies \mu_b = \frac{0.14835}{0.4167} \approx \mathbf{0.356}$$
Interpretation: The effective basal friction coefficient along the Main Himalayan Thrust is $\mu_b \approx 0.36$, indicating that high fluid pressures ($\lambda_b = 0.75$) substantially weaken the fault zone, permitting crustal overthrusting of the Higher Himalaya.
Problem 2: Thrust Displacement Rate and Crustal Shortening Calculation

Structural reconstructions of the Main Central Thrust across the Kumaun-Garhwal Himalaya indicate a total cumulative southward heave (horizontal displacement) of $L = 140\text{ km}$. Geochronologic dating of syn-kinematic monazites indicates primary ductile thrust shearing operated from $22\text{ Ma}$ to $15\text{ Ma}$. Calculate the average ductile slip rate along the MCT in millimeters per year ($\text{mm/yr}$).

Slip Rate Derivation:
1. Time Duration ($\Delta t$): $$\Delta t = 22\text{ Ma} - 15\text{ Ma} = 7.0\text{ million years} = 7.0 \times 10^6\text{ years}$$
2. Displacement ($L$): $$L = 140\text{ km} = 140 \times 10^3\text{ m} = 1.4 \times 10^8\text{ mm}$$
3. Average Slip Rate ($v$): $$v = \frac{L}{\Delta t} = \frac{1.4 \times 10^8\text{ mm}}{7.0 \times 10^6\text{ years}} = \mathbf{20.0\text{ mm/year}}$$
Significance: During the Early-to-Middle Miocene, the MCT absorbed virtually the entire $\sim 20\text{ mm/yr}$ rate of Indo-Asian convergence prior to the forward propagation of deformation to the MBT and MFT.
Problem 3: Microstructural Shear Sense in MCT Mylonites

A oriented quartzofeldspathic mylonite collected from the MCT zone at Joshimath, Uttarakhand, displays S-surfaces inclined at $40^\circ$ to the North, C-surfaces dipping at $25^\circ$ to the North, and asymmetric $\sigma$-type feldspar porphyroclasts with tails extending parallel to C. Deduce the tectonic sense of shear and the transport direction of the Higher Himalayan slab.

Kinematic Deduction:
1. S-C Fabric Relationship: S-surfaces (schistosity/flattening planes) dip more steeply ($40^\circ\text{ N}$) than C-surfaces (cisaillement/shear bands, $25^\circ\text{ N}$). The acute angle between S and C ($40^\circ - 25^\circ = 15^\circ$) points in the direction of shear displacement on the hanging wall.
2. Asymmetric Porphyroclasts: The staircase geometry of recrystallized tail mantles on $\sigma$-porphyroclasts confirms a synthetic, dextral-equivalent rotational sense when looking west.
Conclusion: The microstructural fabric definitively proves Top-to-the-South/Southwest thrusting, representing the southward translation of the Higher Himalayan slab over India.
Problem 4: Channel Flow Hypothesis & Coeval Fault Operation

State the fundamental premise of the "Channel Flow" model for the Higher Himalayan Crystallines (Beaumont et al., 2001) and explain how two faults with opposite senses of shear (MCT and STDS) operated simultaneously in the Miocene.

Channel Flow Synthesis:
1. Mid-Crustal Low-Viscosity Channel: High radiogenic heat production and dehydration melting in the thickened Tibetan/Himalayan crust generated widespread leucogranitic partial melts, drastically lowering the effective viscosity of the middle crust ($10^{18}\text{--}10^{19}\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$) to form a ductile channel.
2. Extrusion Between Opposing Faults: Gravitational potential energy gradients drove the ductile channel southward toward the low-pressure foreland. The extruded slab was bounded by: - MCT at the Base: Top-to-the-South thrust shear zone.
- STDS at the Top: Top-to-the-North normal detachment fault.
3. Coeval movement on both faults (~22–16 Ma) allowed the Higher Himalayan crystalline slab to extrude like toothpaste onto the Indian plate.
Problem 5: Inverted Metamorphism: 1D Thermal Diffusion Modeling

Assume a hot metamorphic slab (HHC) at initial temperature $T_1 = 750^\circ\text{C}$ is instantaneously thrust over a cold footwall (LHS) at initial temperature $T_0 = 150^\circ\text{C}$ along the MCT. Using the 1D conduction equation across an infinite step contact, calculate the immediate contact temperature ($T_{\text{contact}}$) and explain why the footwall exhibits an inverted thermal gradient.

Thermal Analytical Solution:
Assuming equivalent thermal conductivity and diffusivity in both units: $$T_{\text{contact}} = \frac{T_1 + T_0}{2} = \frac{750^\circ\text{C} + 150^\circ\text{C}}{2} = \frac{900}{2} = \mathbf{450^\circ\text{C}}$$
- Temperature Profile: Directly beneath the contact, heat diffuses downward into the footwall according to the error function: $$T(z, t) = T_{\text{contact}} - (T_{\text{contact}} - T_0) \text{erf}\left(\frac{z}{2\sqrt{\kappa t}}\right)$$
- Inverted Gradient: The uppermost footwall reaches $450^\circ\text{C}$ (amphibolite/garnet grade), while deeper footwall levels ($z > 5\text{ km}$) remain at lower ambient temperatures ($< 250^\circ\text{C}$). This transient inverted thermal profile bakes the footwall rocks in an inverted sequence from sillimanite/kyanite near the fault down to chlorite at deeper stratigraphic levels.
Problem 6: Geochronologic Dating of Thrusting via Syn-Kinematic Monazites

Why is in-situ U-Th-Pb dating of monazite grains enclosed within syn-kinematic garnet and kyanite porphyroblasts superior to Ar-Ar dating of muscovite for determining the exact timing of MCT movement?

Geochronological Principles:
- Monazite Closure Temperature: Monazite has an exceptionally high U-Th-Pb closure temperature ($T_c > 800\text{--}900^\circ\text{C}$), which is higher than peak MCT metamorphism. Chemical zoning and inclusions aligned with the mylonitic foliation directly date metamorphic crystal growth during active ductile thrusting ($23\text{--}16\text{ Ma}$).
- Muscovite Ar-Ar Limitation: Argon in muscovite has a low closure temperature of only $T_c \approx 350\text{--}400^\circ\text{C}$. In high-grade terrains, muscovite continues to lose radiogenic $^{40}\text{Ar}$ by volume diffusion long after thrusting ceases, recording only the timing of late exhumation and cooling below $350^\circ\text{C}$ ($< 12\text{--}8\text{ Ma}$), rather than the onset of thrust motion.
Problem 7: Valdiya's Vaikrita vs. Munsiari Formations

In the Kumaun Himalaya, contrast the lithological and metamorphic characteristics of the Munsiari Formation (MCT-I hanging wall) and the Vaikrita Group (MCT-II hanging wall).

Stratigraphic & Metamorphic Contrast:
- Munsiari Formation (Between MCT-I and MCT-II): Composed of chlorite-sericite schists, biotite phyllites, highly sheared mylonitic augen gneisses, and amphibolites. Represents sheared basement rocks metamorphosed at green-schist to lower amphibolite facies ($T \approx 450\text{--}550^\circ\text{C}$).
- Vaikrita Group (True HHC above MCT-II): Composed of coarse-grained garnet-kyanite-sillimanite psammitic gneisses, calc-silicate marbles, migmatites, and tourmaline leucogranite intrusions. Represents high-grade upper amphibolite to granulite facies ($T \approx 650\text{--}780^\circ\text{C}$, $P \approx 8\text{--}11\text{ kbar}$).
Problem 8: Seismic Hazards and the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT) Ramp

Geodetic GPS measurements reveal that the Main Himalayan Thrust is completely locked from the surface down to a depth of $\sim 15\text{--}18\text{ km}$, accumulating an elastic slip deficit of $18\text{ mm/yr}$. If a mid-crustal ramp exists beneath the High Himalayan front, explain how it controls the nucleation and rupture of great Himalayan earthquakes.

Seismotectonic Mechanism:
1. The MHT Mid-Crustal Ramp: Geophysical imaging shows the basal MHT décollement is nearly flat beneath the Ganga Basin and Sub-Himalaya, steepens into a prominent ramp dipping at $\sim 15\text{--}20^\circ$ beneath the front of the Higher Himalaya, and flattens again into a ductile horizontal shear zone beneath Tibet.
2. Stress Concentration & Nucleation: The transition from ductile creep at depth to brittle stick-slip behavior occurs precisely at this mid-crustal ramp (coinciding with the $350^\circ\text{C}$ isotherm). Elastic strain accumulates at the ramp updip boundary, where great ruptures (such as the $M_w 7.8$ Gorkha earthquake in 2015) nucleate and propagate southward toward the MBT and MFT.

Q084: Bysmalith: Fault-Bounded Cylindrical Igneous Intrusion

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 84
Authoritative References: K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Ch. 5: Petrology / Igneous Intrusions, pp. 55, 168–170); Joseph P. Iddings (1898, Journal of Geology, "Bysmaliths"); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 115–118); John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (Ch. 4: Pluton Emplacement, pp. 53–70).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition & Structural Anatomy of a Bysmalith

The term bysmalith was coined in 1898 by the distinguished American petrologist Joseph Paxon Iddings (derived from the ancient Greek bysma = plug or stopper, and lithos = stone) while studying the complex intrusive volcanic-plutonic architecture of Mt. Holmes in Yellowstone National Park.

A bysmalith is defined as a more or less vertical, cylindrical or plug-shaped igneous pluton that cross-cuts adjacent sedimentary strata and is bounded on its lateral margins by steep, circular faults or shear fractures. The magma intrudes forcibly, punching the overlying cylindrical block of country rock vertically upward like a mechanical piston.

Figure 84.1 — Morphological Architecture of Plutons: Authentic textbook diagram from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 168). Demonstrating the structural geometry of concordant laccoliths versus fault-bounded discordant bysmaliths, sills, and dikes.

Diagnostic Anatomical Criteria of a Bysmalith

  • Cross-Sectional Geometry: Sub-circular to elliptical in plan view, extending vertically as a steep, cylindrical or downward-tapering plug.
  • Discordant, Fault-Bounded Margins: Unlike concordant laccoliths whose margins pinch out smoothly along bedding planes, the perimeter of a bysmalith is defined by steep ring faults or reverse faults along which the roof has been forcibly sheared and elevated.
  • Piston-Like Roof Displacement: The roof strata are displaced vertically upwards en masse, with minimal horizontal spreading of the magma body.
Figure 84.2 — Mechanical Evolution from Laccolith to Bysmalith: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 55). Showing how high magmatic overpressure causes flexural failure of the roof strata, creating marginal shear faults.
2. Geomechanical Evolution: The Laccolith-to-Bysmalith Transition

In physical volcanology and structural geology (Corry, 1988), a bysmalith represents the structural failure end-member of a laccolith:

  1. Initial Sill Injection: Magma ascends along vertical conduits (dikes) and spreads horizontally along a bedding plane where lithostatic overburden equals magma pressure.
  2. Laccolithic Doming: As magma continues to pump into the sill, the pressure exceeds lithostatic overburden ($P_{\text{magma}} > \sigma_v$). The overlying sedimentary layers bend upward elastically and plastically like an blister or dome, producing a concordant laccolith with a flat floor and arched roof.
  3. Shear Failure of the Roof: If magma injection is exceptionally rapid or the magma is highly viscous (e.g., dacitic, rhyolitic, or phonolitic), the magmatic overpressure ($\Delta P = P_{\text{magma}} - \sigma_v$) exceeds the shear strength ($\tau_{\text{rock}}$) of the overburden rock: $$\Delta P > \frac{2 \tau_{\text{rock}} \cdot h}{r}$$ where $h$ is overburden thickness and $r$ is pluton radius.
  4. Bysmalith Formation (Piston Punching): The roof strata rupture along circumferential vertical faults, and the central cylinder of rock is punched straight upward, transforming the dome into a steep-sided, fault-bounded bysmalith.
3. Comparative Petrology: Concordant vs. Discordant Igneous Plutons

Igneous intrusions are systematically categorized based on their geometric concordance with host rock stratification:

  • Concordant Intrusions (Parallel to Bedding):
    • Sill: Tabular, sheet-like intrusion parallel to bedding planes.
    • Laccolith: Plano-convex, mushroom-shaped intrusion with a flat floor and arched roof.
    • Lopolith: Colossal, saucer-shaped or basin-shaped intrusion depressed in the center (e.g., Bushveld, Sudbury, Duluth).
    • Phacolith: Crescent-shaped intrusion located along the hinge zones (crests of anticlines or troughs of synclines) of folded strata.
  • Discordant Intrusions (Cross-cutting Bedding):
    • Dike: Steeply dipping to vertical tabular intrusion cutting across bedding planes.
    • Bysmalith: Vertical, cylindrical, fault-bounded plug punching through country rocks.
    • Batholith: Colossal discordant plutonic body with an outcrop area exceeding $100\text{ km}^2$, expanding indefinitely downward without an observable floor.
    • Stock: A discordant pluton similar to a batholith but with an exposed surface area $< 100\text{ km}^2$.
    • Chonolith (Conolith): An irregular, chaotic intrusive body of undetermined or complex shape that does not conform to any standard geometric category (Daly, 1905).
    • Volcanic Neck (Plug): Cylindrical conduit of an eroded volcano filled with consolidated lava or agglomeratic pyroclastic breccia.

Official Examination Question
Question 84
An igneous pluton which is more or less vertical and cylindrical that cross-cuts adjacent sediments and is bounded by steep faults is termed as :
(A) Laccolith
(B) Bysmalith
(C) Lopolith
(D) Conolith
CORRECT ANSWER: (B)
Bysmalith: A vertical, cylindrical igneous intrusion that cross-cuts surrounding sedimentary strata and is bounded on its lateral margins by steep ring faults along which the roof has been punched upward.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Laccolith — INCORRECT

A laccolith is a concordant, dome-shaped intrusion characterized by a flat floor and an arched, convex-upward roof. It deforms overlying strata by gentle flexural arching without cutting across them or being bounded by steep marginal faults.

(B) Bysmalith — CORRECT

A bysmalith (Iddings, 1898) is the precise, unambiguous term for an igneous pluton that is more or less vertical and cylindrical, cross-cuts adjacent sediments, and is bounded by steep faults. It is mechanically a faulted laccolith where the central core has punched upward like a piston (Bangar, p. 55, 168; Mahapatra, p. 116).

(C) Lopolith — INCORRECT

A lopolith (Grout, 1918) is a colossal, concordant, saucer-shaped or basin-shaped intrusion that is depressed in the center due to gravitational sagging under the immense weight of dense mafic/ultramafic magma (e.g., Bushveld Complex, South Africa). It is not vertical or cylindrical, nor is it bounded by steep faults.

(D) Conolith — INCORRECT

A conolith (or more accurately chonolith, coined by R.A. Daly in 1905) is an igneous body of irregular, chaotic, or undefinable shape that cannot be classified as a dike, sill, laccolith, or bysmalith. It does not possess a specific vertical cylindrical geometry bounded by steep faults.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Critical Magmatic Overpressure for Shear Punching (Bysmalith Formation)

A cylindrical magma body of radius $R = 1,500\text{ meters}$ is ponded at depth $H = 2,000\text{ meters}$ beneath horizontal sandstone beds ($\rho = 2,500\text{ kg/m}^3$). The shear strength of the overburden sandstone along vertical circular fault planes is $\tau_s = 25\text{ MPa}$. Calculate the minimum magmatic pressure ($P_{\text{magma}}$) required to shear the overburden and punch the block upward as a bysmalith ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).

Force Balance Derivation:
For the central cylinder of rock to be punched upward, the upward vertical force exerted by magma pressure on the basal area must overcome both the downward gravitational weight of the overburden and the frictional shear resistance along the cylindrical fault perimeter:
$$F_{\text{up}} \ge F_{\text{weight}} + F_{\text{shear}}$$
$$P_{\text{magma}} \cdot (\pi R^2) \ge (\rho \cdot g \cdot H) \cdot (\pi R^2) + \tau_s \cdot (2\pi R \cdot H)$$
Dividing both sides by $\pi R^2$: $$P_{\text{magma}} \ge \rho g H + \frac{2 \tau_s H}{R}$$
1. Lithostatic Overburden ($\sigma_v$): $$\sigma_v = 2500 \times 9.81 \times 2000 = 4.905 \times 10^7\text{ Pa} = 49.05\text{ MPa}$$
2. Shear Resistance Term: $$\Delta P_{\text{shear}} = \frac{2 \times (25\text{ MPa}) \times 2000\text{ m}}{1500\text{ m}} = \frac{100,000}{1500} \approx \mathbf{33.33\text{ MPa}}$$
3. Total Required Magma Pressure: $$P_{\text{magma}} \ge 49.05\text{ MPa} + 33.33\text{ MPa} = \mathbf{82.38\text{ MPa}}$$
Interpretation: The magma must maintain an overpressure of at least $33.3\text{ MPa}$ above lithostatic pressure ($P_{\text{magma}} > 82.4\text{ MPa}$) to rupture the roof along vertical faults and emplace as a bysmalith.
Problem 2: Geomechanical Role of Viscosity in Bysmalith Emplacement

Explain why bysmaliths and laccoliths are almost universally composed of high-silica, viscous magmas (rhyolite, dacite, phonolite, trachyte) rather than low-viscosity basaltic magmas.

Fluid Dynamics of Pluton Growth:
1. Low-Viscosity Basaltic Magma ($\eta \approx 10\text{--}100\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$): Flows easily along narrow bedding planes, spreading laterally over vast horizontal distances to form extensive, thin sills without building significant vertical thickness or localized overpressure.
2. High-Viscosity Felsic Magma ($\eta \approx 10^6\text{--}10^9\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$): Flow resistance along narrow bedding conduits is immense ($Q \propto 1/\eta$). The magma cannot spread far laterally; instead, it ponds locally, building up massive vertical hydrodynamic pressure at the feeder vent. This forces the roof to dome upward into a laccolith and, upon shear failure, punch straight upward as a bysmalith.
Problem 3: Iddings' Yellowstone Mt. Holmes Archetype

Describe the structural architecture of the type bysmalith described by J.P. Iddings (1898) at Mt. Holmes in Yellowstone National Park.

Historical Type Description:
- At Mt. Holmes in the Gallatin Range, Iddings mapped a steep, plug-shaped intrusive mass of porphyritic rhyolite/granite porphyry.
- The intrusion punched through Cambrian and Carboniferous sedimentary formations.
- Instead of bending the strata into a gentle dome as seen in the nearby laccoliths of the Henry Mountains, the Mt. Holmes body is bounded by vertical, circular faults where the adjacent sedimentary beds are sharply truncated, dragged, and shattered by vertical shear.
Problem 4: Bysmalith vs. Cauldron Subsidence (Piston Up vs. Piston Down)

Compare the kinematics of a bysmalith with that of a cauldron subsidence (caldera collapse). Contrast their fault bounding geometries and displacement vectors.

Kinematic Contrast:
- Bysmalith (Piston Upward): Driven by positive magmatic overpressure ($\Delta P > 0$). The magma acts as a hydraulic jack, forcing a central cylindrical rock cylinder vertically upward along outward-dipping or vertical reverse ring faults.
- Cauldron Subsidence (Piston Downward): Driven by negative magmatic pressure (underpressure, $\Delta P < 0$) following catastrophic volcanic eruption. The cylindrical block of roof rock sinks downward into the depleted magma chamber along inward-dipping normal ring faults (e.g., Glen Coe, Scotland; Ossipee, New Hampshire).
Problem 5: Lopolith Centripetal Subsidence Mechanics

Explain why lopoliths (e.g., Bushveld, Sudbury) possess a saucer-shaped form with layers dipping inward toward the center, whereas laccoliths have convex-upward roofs.

Mechanical Loading Explanation:
1. High Density of Ultramafic Magma: Lopoliths are formed by immense volumes of dense mafic-to-ultramafic magma ($\rho_{\text{melt}} \approx 2,750\text{--}2,850\text{ kg/m}^3$) intruding into less dense continental crust ($\rho_{\text{crust}} \approx 2,650\text{ kg/m}^3$).
2. Isostatic & Thermal Sag: The colossal weight of the ponded magma exceeds the isostatic buoyancy of the floor rocks. As crystallization proceeds, the floor sags downward into the crust while the roof collapses centripetally, producing an inward-dipping, saucer-shaped lopolith.
Problem 6: Phacolith Emplacement in Folded Orogenic Belts

Why do phacoliths emplace preferentially along the crests of anticlines and troughs of synclines, rather than along the fold limbs?

Structural Mechanics (Saddle Reef Mechanism):
- During flexural-slip folding of stratified sedimentary rocks, bed-parallel slippage produces extensional dilation and low-pressure zones at the hinge regions (anticlinal crests and synclinal troughs).
- In contrast, the fold limbs experience intense compressive shear stress.
- Magma follows minimum pressure gradients ($\nabla P$), migrating selectively into the dilated hinge crests and troughs to crystallize as concordant, crescent-shaped bodies termed phacoliths (Harker, 1909).
Problem 7: Chonolith (Conolith) Definition and Diagnostic Ambiguity

In a geological survey report, an intrusive body is described as a "chonolith". Explain what this term signifies and why it is used as a term of last resort.

Petrological Definition:
- Chonolith: Coined by R.A. Daly (1905), derived from Greek choane = melting pot or funnel. It designates an igneous intrusion of irregular, chaotic, or undefinable shape whose contacts are discordant and which cannot be fitted into the neat geometric categories of dikes, sills, laccoliths, bysmaliths, or lopoliths.
- Term of Last Resort: It indicates that the intrusion was injected along complex, multi-directional joint sets, faults, or unconformities, or that structural exposure is insufficient to reconstruct its geometric architecture.
Problem 8: Contact Metamorphic Aureole around a Bysmalith

How does the contact metamorphic aureole around a bysmalith differ from that around a concordant sill or laccolith?

Structural and Thermal Aureole Criteria:
- Laccolith / Sill: Contact metamorphism is purely thermal, developing hornfels with granoblastic, non-foliated textures parallel to the concordant bedding contacts.
- Bysmalith: Shows an intense superposition of dynamic deformation and high shear strain along its peripheral ring faults. Country rocks adjacent to the cylindrical plug are intensely dragged upward, brecciated, and transformed into mylonitic or cataclastic fault gouge overprinted by pyrometamorphism (buchites/hornfels).

Q085: Lamprophyre Petrography: Panidiomorphic (Lamprophyric) Texture

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 85
Authoritative References: K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, Ch. 5: Petrology / Igneous Rocks, pp. 82, 165, 178); John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 2: Classification of Igneous Rocks / Lamprophyres); N.M.S. Rock, Lamprophyres (Blackie & Son / Springer); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 120–122).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition & Fundamental Petrographic Rules of the Lamprophyre Clan

The term lamprophyre was introduced in 1874 by C.W. von Gümbel (derived from the Greek lampros = bright or glistening, and phyro = to mingle or mix), describing the glistening, sparkling reflection of abundant, freshly cleaved mica (biotite/phlogopite) phenocrysts in hand specimens.

Lamprophyres are a clan of melanocratic, volatile-rich hypabyssal porphyritic dike rocks characterized by two iron-clad petrographic rules (Rock, 1991):

Figure 85.1 — Petrographic Thin Section of Panidiomorphic Texture in Lamprophyre: Authentic textbook diagram from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 178). Depicting beautifully formed, sharp euhedral phenocrysts of biotite and hornblende set in a fine-grained, euhedral groundmass of feldspars and mafic minerals.

The Two Cardinal Rules of Lamprophyre Petrography

  1. Phenocrysts are Exclusively Mafic: Phenocrysts consist solely of dark ferromagnesian minerals—biotite/phlogopite, amphibole (hornblende, kaersutite), clinopyroxene (diopside, titanaugite), and/or olivine. Feldspars NEVER occur as phenocrysts! Feldspars (orthoclase, sanidine, or plagioclase) and feldspathoids are strictly confined to the fine-grained groundmass.
  2. Panidiomorphic (Lamprophyric) Texture: An extraordinary, hallmark texture where an overwhelming percentage of both the phenocrysts AND the groundmass mineral grains exhibit sharp, perfect, euhedral crystal faces (idiomorphic forms).
Figure 85.2 — Classification of Crystallinity and Crystal Form: Authentic textbook scan from K.M. Bangar (Principles of Engineering Geology, p. 82). Showing the distinction between panidiomorphic, hypidiomorphic, and allotriomorphic textures.
2. Crystallization Kinetics: Why Lamprophyres are Panidiomorphic

In typical igneous rocks (e.g., granite or basalt), groundmass crystals interfere with one another during rapid late crystallization, producing irregular, subhedral or anhedral grain boundaries (hypidiomorphic or intersertal textures). Why, then, do lamprophyre groundmass crystals develop perfect euhedral faces?

The Volatile-Fluxing Depolymerization Mechanism

  • Ultra-High Volatile Fugacity ($H_2O, CO_2, F, P$): Lamprophyric magmas are water- and carbon-dioxide-saturated melts containing up to $3\text{--}8\text{ wt}\% H_2O$ and high dissolved carbonate, fluorine, and phosphorus.
  • Viscosity Collapse: Dissolved water and halogens violently depolymerize the silicate melt network, severing bridging oxygens ($Si\text{--}O\text{--}Si \to 2 Si\text{--}OH$). This reduces magma viscosity by orders of magnitude ($\eta \approx 0.1\text{--}1.0\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$), transforming the melt into a fluid, watery medium.
  • High Ionic Diffusivity: In this ultra-fluid medium, ionic diffusion rates are astronomical. Crystals nucleate and grow rapidly in unhindered suspension, allowing crystal faces to achieve their low-energy, rational crystallographic planes (euhedral / idiomorphic geometry) before the remaining liquid freezes.
3. Systematic Classification of Lamprophyres (IUGS / Rock, 1991)

Lamprophyres are divided into three primary branches based on their essential mafic minerals and groundmass felsic constituents:

1. Calc-Alkaline Lamprophyres (Shoshonitic Association)

Dominant Mafic Phenocryst Groundmass Dominant Feldspar: K-Feldspar Groundmass Dominant Feldspar: Plagioclase
Biotite / Phlogopite MINETTE ($\text{Biotite} + \text{Orthoclase}$) KERSANTITE ($\text{Biotite} + \text{Plagioclase}$)
Amphibole (Hornblende) VOGESITE ($\text{Hornblende} + \text{Orthoclase}$) SPESSARTITE ($\text{Hornblende} + \text{Plagioclase}$)

2. Alkaline Lamprophyres

  • Camptonite: Phenocrysts of brown titaniferous hornblende (kaersutite) and titanaugite set in a plagioclase-dominant groundmass.
  • Monchiquite: Feldspar-free alkaline lamprophyre! Phenocrysts of titanaugite, kaersutite, and olivine set in an isotropic groundmass of analcime or volcanic glass.
  • Sannaite: Phenocrysts of titanaugite and biotite in an alkali feldspar-dominant groundmass.

3. Ultramafic Lamprophyres

Melilite-bearing rocks such as Alnöite and Polzenite, forming transitional links to kimberlites and carbonatites.

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 85
The characteristic texture of lamprophyres is :
(A) Allotriomorphic
(B) Panidiomorphic
(C) Xenomorphic
(D) Hypidiomorphic
CORRECT ANSWER: (B)
Panidiomorphic: The diagnostic texture of lamprophyres (also termed lamprophyric texture), wherein a very high percentage of both the mafic phenocrysts and the groundmass minerals exhibit complete, sharp, euhedral (idiomorphic) crystal outlines.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Allotriomorphic — INCORRECT

Allotriomorphic (or aplitic/sugary texture) describes a texture where almost all mineral grains are completely anhedral (lacking rational crystal faces), typically formed in granitic aplites, quartzites, and marbles.

(B) Panidiomorphic — CORRECT

Panidiomorphic texture (from Greek pan = all, idios = own/distinct, morphe = form) is the universal, defining petrographic hallmark of the lamprophyre clan. Driven by high volatile fugacity ($H_2O, CO_2, F$) and low melt viscosity, virtually all constituent minerals—both the dark mafic phenocrysts and the fine groundmass laths—crystallize with perfect, sharp euhedral boundaries (Bangar, p. 82, 178; Winter, 2014, p. 43; Rock, 1991).

(C) Xenomorphic — INCORRECT

Xenomorphic is an exact synonym for allotriomorphic or anhedral. Minerals have irregular, mutual boundaries dictated by crowding against neighboring grains.

(D) Hypidiomorphic — INCORRECT

Hypidiomorphic (or granitic) texture is the common texture of standard plutonic rocks (like granite and diorite), where some minerals (like zircon, apatite, biotite) are euhedral to subhedral, but the later-crystallizing minerals (quartz and alkali feldspar) are anhedral, filling interstitial spaces.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Calc-Alkaline Lamprophyre Identification Matrix

A hypabyssal dike rock in the Damodar Valley coalfields of India displays a panidiomorphic texture with abundant euhedral phenocrysts of glistening phlogopitic biotite. In thin section, the fine-grained groundmass consists predominantly of euhedral orthoclase feldspar and minor carbonate, with zero plagioclase. Classify this lamprophyre into its specific variety.

Step-by-Step Petrographic Deduction:
1. Mafic Phenocryst Phase: Biotite / Phlogopite.
2. Felsic Groundmass Mineralogy: Potassium feldspar (Orthoclase) dominant; plagioclase absent.
3. Classification Scheme (IUGS / Rock, 1991):
- $\text{Biotite} + \text{Orthoclase} \implies \mathbf{MINETTE}$
- $\text{Biotite} + \text{Plagioclase} \implies \text{Kersantite}$
- $\text{Hornblende} + \text{Orthoclase} \implies \text{Vogesite}$
- $\text{Hornblende} + \text{Plagioclase} \implies \text{Spessartite}$
Conclusion: The rock is definitively a Minette, the most widespread mica-lamprophyre in continental rift and Gondwana coalfield dike swarms.
Problem 2: Ocelli Structures and Liquid Immiscibility in Lamprophyres

Lamprophyres frequently contain rounded, spherical or globular patches (1 to 10 mm in diameter) termed ocelli, consisting of light-colored analcime, calcite, and alkali feldspar surrounded by tangential biotite plates. Contrast the two primary genetic hypotheses for the origin of ocelli.

Genetic Hypotheses:
1. Liquid Immiscibility (Silicate-Carbonate/Foid Unmixing): The volatile-rich, water- and $CO_2$-saturated lamprophyric magma unmixes into two immiscible liquid droplets during late cooling: a host ultrabasic mafic liquid and conjugate globular droplets of alkaline-carbonate or felsic melt (ocelli).
2. Amygdaloidal Vapor Segregation: Ocelli represent late-stage magmatic gas bubbles (vesicles) into which residual, hydrous, highly fractionated pegmatitic/deuteric interstitial silicate-carbonate liquids were squeezed under gas overpressure.
Problem 3: Chemical Paradox of Lamprophyres (High Mg# with High LREE/LILE)

Explain the famous "geochemical paradox" of lamprophyres: Why do they simultaneously possess primitive mantle characteristics ($Mg\# > 70$, $Ni > 300\text{ ppm}$, $Cr > 600\text{ ppm}$) AND ultra-enriched crustal characteristics ($K_2O > 4\%$, $Ba > 2000\text{ ppm}$, $Sr > 1500\text{ ppm}$, $(\text{La/Yb})_N > 30$)?

Petrogenetic Explanation:
- Primitive Signature: The high $Mg\#$, $Ni$, and $Cr$ confirm that lamprophyre magmas are primary mantle melts derived directly from peridotite that did not undergo extensive crustal fractional crystallization.
- Enriched Signature: The extraordinary enrichment in Large Ion Lithophile Elements (LILE: $K, Ba, Sr$) and Light Rare Earth Elements (LREE) is caused by extreme low-degree partial melting ($F < 1\text{--}3\%$) of an ancient, metasomatized mantle lithosphere. Subduction-derived hydrous fluids or carbonatitic melts previously metasomatized the mantle wedge, precipitating veins of phlogopite, apatite, and titanaugite (glimmerite). Melting of these metasomatic veins generated the enriched primary lamprophyre liquid.
Problem 4: Monchiquite vs. Camptonite Differentiation

Under petrographic inspection, an alkaline lamprophyre displays titanaugite and kaersutite phenocrysts set in an isotropic, low-relief groundmass devoid of crystalline feldspar laths. Distinguish whether this is a camptonite or a monchiquite.

Diagnostic Petrography:
- Camptonite: The groundmass is dominated by crystalline laths of plagioclase feldspar (andesine/labradorite).
- Monchiquite: The groundmass is completely free of feldspar, composed instead of isotropic analcime ($\text{NaAlSi}_2\text{O}_6\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$), nepheline, or devitrified hydrous volcanic glass.
Conclusion: The isotropic, feldspar-free groundmass confirms the rock is a Monchiquite.
Problem 5: Tectonic Setting of Gondwana Coalfield Lamprophyre Dike Swarms

In the Damodar Valley Gondwana coalfields (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro), mica-lamprophyre dikes and sills (minettes) intrude and "bake" Permian coal seams into natural coke (jhama). State the geological age of this lamprophyre magmatism and its geodynamic trigger.

Regional Indian Geology:
- Geological Age: Early Cretaceous ($\sim 115\text{--}120\text{ Ma}$, K-Ar and $^{40}\text{Ar}/^{39}\text{Ar}$ dating).
- Geodynamic Trigger: The Rajmahal-Kerguelen mantle plume event and associated rifting along the Damodar graben during the breakup of Eastern Gondwana. The lamprophyres represent deep, volatile-rich alkaline melts channelized along pre-existing basement faults.
Problem 6: Viscosity and Diffusion Scaling in Panidiomorphic Growth

Using the Stokes-Einstein equation ($D = \frac{k_B T}{6\pi \eta r}$), compare the ionic diffusivity ($D$) of silica in a dry rhyolitic melt ($\eta = 10^7\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$) with that in a water-saturated lamprophyric melt ($\eta = 0.5\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$) at $T = 1000^\circ\text{C}$ (1273 K).

Diffusivity Comparison:
Since $D \propto \frac{1}{\eta}$ at constant temperature and ionic radius:
$$\frac{D_{\text{lamprophyre}}}{D_{\text{rhyolite}}} = \frac{\eta_{\text{rhyolite}}}{\eta_{\text{lamprophyre}}} = \frac{10^7\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}}{0.5\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}} = \mathbf{2.0 \times 10^7}$$
Significance: Ions diffuse twenty million times faster in the low-viscosity, volatile-rich lamprophyric melt, completely explaining why crystal faces can grow unconstrained into perfect euhedral (panidiomorphic) forms.
Problem 7: Optical Mineralogy: Zoned Phlogopite in Minettes

In minette thin sections, phlogopite phenocrysts frequently exhibit spectacular reverse pleochroic rims (tetraferriphlogopite rims). Describe the optical change and explain its crystal-chemical cause.

Crystal-Chemical Description:
- Normal Phlogopite Core: Standard pleochroic scheme: absorption is greatest parallel to cleavage ($\gamma \approx \beta > \alpha$; dark brown/red-brown parallel to horizontal crosshair).
- Tetraferriphlogopite Rim: Shows abnormal / reverse pleochroism: absorption is greatest perpendicular to cleavage ($\alpha > \beta \approx \gamma$; dark orange-red perpendicular to cleavage, pale yellow parallel to cleavage).
- Cause: In highly oxidized, peralkaline, silica-undersaturated residual melts, aluminium is deficient, forcing ferric iron ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$) to enter the tetrahedral $Z$-sites normally reserved for $Al^{3+}$ and $Si^{4+}$.
Problem 8: Lamprophyre vs. Lamproite vs. Kimberlite

Clarify the taxonomic distinction between Lamprophyres, Lamproites, and Kimberlites, especially regarding diamond-bearing potential.

Taxonomic Distinction (IUGS / Mitchell, 1995):
- Lamprophyre (Broad Clan): Typically calc-alkaline to alkaline; contains essential plagioclase or orthoclase in groundmass; rarely diamondiferous (except ultramafic varieties like aillikites).
- Lamproite: Ultra-potassic, peralkaline volcanic/hypabyssal rock containing titanium-rich phlogopite, richterite, jeppeite, and wadeite. Can be economically diamondiferous (e.g., Argyle diamond pipe, Australia; Majhgawan pipe, Panna, India).
- Kimberlite: Inequigranular ultramafic rock containing megacrysts of picroilmenite, pyrope garnet, and olivine in a carbonate-serpentine groundmass. Primary terrestrial host of diamonds worldwide.

Q086: Monomineralic & Ultrabasic Rocks: The Anorthosite Exception

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 86
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 2: Classification of Igneous Rocks, pp. 28–30; Ch. 12: Anorthosites); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (p. 79); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 118–122); Deer, Howie & Zussman, An Introduction to the Rock-Forming Minerals.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Critical Distinction: Ultrabasic (Chemical) vs. Ultramafic (Mineralogical)

In igneous petrology, confusion frequently arises between the chemical term ultrabasic and the mineralogical term ultramafic. They are governed by entirely different criteria:

  • Chemical Criterion (Silica Content): Rocks are classified based strictly on their total weight percentage of silica ($\text{SiO}_2$): $$\text{Acidic: } \text{SiO}_2 > 66\text{ wt}\% \quad | \quad \text{Intermediate: } 52\text{--}66\text{ wt}\% \quad | \quad \text{Basic: } 45\text{--}52\text{ wt}\% \quad | \quad \mathbf{\text{Ultrabasic: }} \mathbf{\text{SiO}_2 < 45\text{ wt}\%}$$
  • Mineralogical Criterion (Color Index $M'$): Rocks are classified based on the modal percentage of dark ferromagnesian (mafic) minerals ($Ol, Px, Hbl, Bt$): $$\text{Leucocratic: } M' < 35\% \quad | \quad \text{Mesocratic: } 35\text{--}65\% \quad | \quad \text{Melanocratic: } 65\text{--}90\% \quad | \quad \mathbf{\text{Ultramafic: }} \mathbf{M' \ge 90\%}$$
Figure 86.1 — IUGS Ultramafic Classification & Monomineralic Peridotites: Authentic textbook diagram from J.D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, Ch. 2, p. 29). Highlighting the monomineralic ultramafic-ultrabasic rocks (Dunite $>90\%$ olivine; Pyroxenite $>90\%$ pyroxene).
2. Monomineralic Igneous Rocks: Why Anorthosite is NOT Ultrabasic

A monomineralic rock is defined petrographically as a rock composed of $>90\%$ of a single mineral species.

Analysis of Candidate Monomineralic Rocks

  • Dunite: Composed of $>90\%$ olivine (typically forsteritic olivine $\text{Fo}_{88\text{--}94}$). Because forsterite ($\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$) contains only $42.7\text{ wt}\% \text{SiO}_2$, dunite has a bulk silica content of $\mathbf{SiO_2 \approx 40\text{--}42\text{ wt}\%}$. It is unequivocally both monomineralic, ultramafic ($M' > 95\%$), and ultrabasic ($SiO_2 < 45\%$).
  • Pyroxenite: Composed of $>90\%$ pyroxene (orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene, or both). While enstatite contains $\sim 59.8\% \text{SiO}_2$, iron- and calcium-rich pyroxenites typically possess bulk silica contents near the basic/ultrabasic boundary ($SiO_2 \approx 44\text{--}50\text{ wt}\%$) and are universally classified as monomineralic ultramafic rocks.
  • Anorthosite: A classic monomineralic plutonic rock composed of $>90\%$ plagioclase feldspar (andesine, labradorite, or bytownite). However, plagioclase is a light-colored, felsic tectosilicate! Pure anorthite ($\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8$) has $43.2\% \text{SiO}_2$, and intermediate labradorite ($\text{An}_{50}\text{Ab}_{50}$) has $\mathbf{SiO_2 \approx 53\text{--}55\text{ wt}\%}$.
    Anorthosite Petrologic Status:
    $$\mathbf{\text{Color Index } M' < 10\% \implies \text{Leucocratic (Felsic!)}}$$
    $$\mathbf{\text{Bulk SiO}_2 \approx 48\text{--}55\text{ wt}\% \implies \text{Basic to Intermediate (NOT Ultrabasic!)}}$$
3. Leptynite & The Granulitic Association

Leptynite (or leptite) is an old European petrographic term for a light-colored, fine-to-medium-grained, granulose quartzofeldspathic metamorphic rock belonging to the granulite facies. In Indian shield geology (e.g., Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt and Tamil Nadu), leptynites are garnetiferous quartz-feldspar granulites formed by high-grade metamorphism of felsic igneous or arkosic sediments, containing $SiO_2 > 70\%$.

Therefore, among the options provided, Anorthosite is the unambiguous answer: it is universally recognized as a monomineralic basic/leucocratic rock, and is explicitly NOT ultrabasic.

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question
Question 86
Which of the following is not a monomineralic ultrabasic rock ?
(A) Anorthosite
(B) Pyroxinite
(C) Leptynite
(D) Dunite
CORRECT ANSWER: (A)
Anorthosite: Composed of $>90\%$ plagioclase feldspar. Because plagioclase is a felsic mineral with $SiO_2 \approx 50\text{--}55\text{ wt}\%$, anorthosite is a leucocratic basic/intermediate rock, NOT an ultrabasic rock.
Forensic Analysis of Answer Choices
(A) Anorthosite — CORRECT (NOT ULTRABASIC)

While Anorthosite is indeed a classic monomineralic rock ($>90\%$ plagioclase), it is chemically basic to intermediate ($SiO_2 \approx 48\text{--}55\text{ wt}\%$) and mineralogically leucocratic ($M' < 10\%$). It is completely excluded from the ultrabasic category ($SiO_2 < 45\%$) and the ultramafic clan ($M' \ge 90\%$). Therefore, it is NOT a monomineralic ultrabasic rock (Winter, 2014, p. 29, 260; Bangar, p. 79).

(B) Pyroxinite — INCORRECT

Pyroxenite (often spelled pyroxinite in exam papers) is a monomineralic ultramafic rock composed of $>90\%$ pyroxene (orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene). Many varieties (such as olivine pyroxenites, jacupirangites, and chromite-pyroxenites) have bulk $SiO_2 < 45\%$, making them ultrabasic.

(C) Leptynite — INCORRECT

Leptynite is a quartzofeldspathic granulite. While leptynite is also not ultrabasic, standard Indian examination keys specifically target Anorthosite because it is the world-famous monomineralic rock that students mistakenly group with basic/ultramafic layered complexes (e.g., Bushveld, Sittampundi).

(D) Dunite — INCORRECT

Dunite is the classic, textbook archetype of a monomineralic ultrabasic rock ($>90\%$ olivine, $M' > 95\%$, $SiO_2 \approx 40\text{--}42\text{ wt}\%$). It is strictly ultrabasic and ultramafic.

Exam-Standard Analytical & Quantitative Practice Problems
Problem 1: Bulk Silica Content Calculation of Anorthosite vs. Dunite

Calculate the theoretical bulk silica percentage ($\text{wt}\% \text{SiO}_2$) of: (a) a pure dunite composed of forsterite ($\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$); and (b) an anorthosite composed of labradorite plagioclase of composition $\text{An}_{60}\text{Ab}_{40}$. Use atomic weights: $Mg = 24.31, Si = 28.09, O = 16.00, Ca = 40.08, Al = 26.98, Na = 22.99$.

Step-by-Step Stoichiometric Calculation:
(a) Pure Forsterite Dunite ($\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$):
- Formula Weight: $M = (2 \times 24.31) + 28.09 + (4 \times 16.00) = 48.62 + 28.09 + 64.00 = 140.71\text{ g/mol}$.
- Molecular weight of $\text{SiO}_2$: $M_{\text{SiO}_2} = 28.09 + 32.00 = 60.09\text{ g/mol}$.
$$\text{wt}\% \text{SiO}_2 = \frac{60.09}{140.71} \times 100\% \approx \mathbf{42.70\text{ wt}\%}$$
Since $42.7\% < 45\%$, dunite is strictly ultrabasic.

(b) Anorthosite ($\text{An}_{60}\text{Ab}_{40}$):
- Anorthite ($\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8$): $M = 40.08 + (2 \times 26.98) + (2 \times 28.09) + (8 \times 16.00) = 278.20\text{ g/mol}$. Contains $2 \text{ moles of SiO}_2$ ($120.18\text{ g}$).
$$\% \text{SiO}_{2,\text{An}} = \frac{120.18}{278.20} \times 100\% = 43.20\%$$
- Albite ($\text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_8$): $M = 22.99 + 26.98 + (3 \times 28.09) + (8 \times 16.00) = 262.24\text{ g/mol}$. Contains $3 \text{ moles of SiO}_2$ ($180.27\text{ g}$).
$$\% \text{SiO}_{2,\text{Ab}} = \frac{180.27}{262.24} \times 100\% = 68.74\%$$
- Bulk Silica in $\text{An}_{60}\text{Ab}_{40}$:
$$\text{wt}\% \text{SiO}_2 = (0.60 \times 43.20\%) + (0.40 \times 68.74\%) = 25.92\% + 27.50\% = \mathbf{53.42\text{ wt}\%}$$
Since $53.4\% > 52\%$, this anorthosite is intermediate (and basic if $\text{An} > 75$), completely outside the ultrabasic ($<45\%$) realm!
Problem 2: Flotation Cumulate Mechanics of the Lunar Magma Ocean

Explain the petrological mechanism that produced the primordial anorthositic crust of the Moon (the Lunar Highlands), contrasting the density of calcic plagioclase with that of lunar basaltic magma.

Buoyancy & Magma Ocean Differentiation:
1. Lunar Magma Ocean (LMO): Shortly after lunar accretion (~4.5 Ga), the outer several hundred kilometers of the Moon were completely molten.
2. Dense Sinking Phases: Early crystallization produced dense olivine ($\rho \approx 3.3\text{ g/cm}^3$) and pyroxene ($\rho \approx 3.4\text{ g/cm}^3$), which sank rapidly to form the lunar ultramafic mantle.
3. Plagioclase Flotation: At $\sim 75\text{--}80\%$ crystallization, calcic plagioclase (anorthite $\text{An}_{95\text{--}98}$, $\rho \approx 2.76\text{ g/cm}^3$) began to crystallize. Crucially, the iron-rich residual lunar basaltic melt had a higher density ($\rho_{\text{liquid}} \approx 2.85\text{--}2.95\text{ g/cm}^3$) than solid anorthite.
4. Result: Plagioclase floated buoyantly upward, forming a vast, planet-wide flotation cumulate crust of pure anorthosite, preserving the brilliant white lunar highlands.
Problem 3: Massif-Type vs. Stratiform Layered Anorthosites

Contrast the two primary geological types of terrestrial anorthosites: (a) Archean Stratiform Layered Anorthosites; and (b) Proterozoic Massif-Type Anorthosites across plagioclase composition and tectonic occurrence.

Petrological Contrast:
- (a) Archean Stratiform Layered Anorthosites: Occur as stratiform layers within mafic-ultramafic layered igneous complexes (e.g., Fiskenaesset in Greenland, Sittampundi in Tamil Nadu). Characterized by extremely calcic plagioclase ($\text{An}_{80\text{--}98}$, bytownite to anorthite) with cumulus megacrystic textures, formed by hydrous basaltic crystallization.
- (b) Proterozoic Massif-Type Anorthosites: Form colossal, batholithic-scale plutonic massifs restricted almost entirely to the Mesoproterozoic (1.8 to 1.0 Ga; e.g., Grenville Province, Adirondacks, Rogaland, and Chilka Lake in Odisha, India). Characterized by intermediate plagioclase ($\text{An}_{40\text{--}60}$, andesine to labradorite) with antiperthitic exsolution, derived from underplated mantle-derived basaltic melts in anorogenic or extensional environments.
Problem 4: Color Index ($M'$) Derivation from Thin Section Modal Analysis

Point-counting of a rock thin section yields: $92\%$ plagioclase, $4\%$ augite, $2\%$ hypersthene, and $2\%$ magnetite. Calculate the Color Index ($M'$) and classify the rock into its IUGS division.

Calculation:
The Color Index ($M'$) is the total volume percentage of dark mafic and opaque minerals: $$M' = 4\% (\text{Augite}) + 2\% (\text{Hypersthene}) + 2\% (\text{Magnetite}) = \mathbf{8.0\%}$$
Classification:
- Since $M' = 8\% < 10\%$, the rock is Leucocratic.
- Since plagioclase comprises $92\% > 90\%$ of total minerals, the rock is definitively classified as an Anorthosite (IUGS Field 10).
Problem 5: Dunite as a Mantle Restite Melting Product

Explain why dunite occurs both as an igneous cumulate in layered intrusions and as a refractory mantle restite in ophiolite complexes.

Dual Petrogenetic Pathways:
1. Cumulate Origin: In basaltic magma chambers, olivine has the highest liquidus temperature and crystallizes first. High density ($\rho \approx 3.3\text{ g/cm}^3$) causes olivine to sink by Stokes' law settling, forming basal cumulate dunite layers (e.g., Bushveld Critical Zone, Stillwater).
2. Restite Origin: When fertile mantle lherzolite ($Ol + Opx + Cpx + Sp$) undergoes extreme degrees of partial melting ($F > 25\text{--}30\%$), all clinopyroxene and orthopyroxene are melted out into the basaltic liquid, leaving behind an insoluble, ultra-refractory residue composed of pure forsteritic olivine and minor chromite—a mantle restite dunite.
Problem 6: Pyroxenite Varieties on the $Opx\text{--}Cpx\text{--}Ol$ Ternary

On the IUGS ultramafic classification triangle where $\text{Olivine} < 40\%$, define the three principal pyroxenite varieties: (a) Orthopyroxenite; (b) Clinopyroxenite; and (c) Websterite.

IUGS Pyroxenite Subdivisions:
- Orthopyroxenite: Orthopyroxene ($Opx$) comprises $> 90\%$ of the total pyroxene component (e.g., bronzitite, enstatite pyroxenite).
- Clinopyroxenite: Clinopyroxene ($Cpx$) comprises $> 90\%$ of the total pyroxene component (e.g., diopsidite, diallagite).
- Websterite: A two-pyroxene ultramafic rock containing intermediate mixtures where both $Opx$ and $Cpx$ are present in concentrations between $10\%$ and $90\%$ of the pyroxene fraction.
Problem 7: Chilka Lake Anorthosite Complex, Odisha

Describe the geological setting, age, and essential mineralogy of the Chilka Lake anorthosite massif in Odisha.

Regional Geology of Odisha:
- Geotectonic Setting: Emplaced within the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt (EGMB) along deep-seated shear zones bordering the Bastar-Bhandara craton.
- Geochronological Age: Mesoproterozoic ($\sim 980\text{--}1000\text{ Ma}$, Grenvillian orogenic cycle).
- Petrographic Assemblage: Massive, coarse-grained, dark grey to bluish-black anorthosite consisting of $>90\%$ antiperthitic labradorite/andesine, with minor interstitial orthopyroxene (hypersthene), ilmenite, and titanomagnetite. It is associated with peripheral leuconorite and ferrodiorite phases.
Problem 8: Podiform Chromite Associated with Dunite in Ophiolites

Why are economic deposits of podiform chromite universally hosted within dunite bodies rather than in surrounding harzburgite in ophiolite mantle sections (e.g., Sukinda ultramafic belt, Odisha)?

Mantle Melt-Rock Reaction Mechanism:
- As primitive basaltic melt ascends through the mantle harzburgite, it is silica-undersaturated relative to orthopyroxene.
- The melt dissolves orthopyroxene from the harzburgite wallrock according to the incongruent reaction: $$\text{Orthopyroxene} + \text{Melt}_1 \longrightarrow \text{Olivine (Dunite envelope)} + \text{Melt}_2$$
- Dissolution of $Opx$ shifts the local melt composition into the chromite liquidus stability field, triggering the massive precipitation of monomineralic chromite lenses (podiform chromitite pods) encased within protective halos of pure dunite.
