Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

In a prograde Barrovian metamorphic terrane, a field geologist traverses from a zone of chlorite-muscovite schist to a zone containing porphyroblasts of almandine garnet. Write the generalized chemical dehydration reaction that marks this isograd and explain why it is endothermic.

Solution: The generalized garnet-in reaction is: $$\text{Chlorite} + \text{Muscovite} + \text{Quartz} \rightarrow \text{Almandine Garnet} + \text{Biotite} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$) because breaking the strong chemical bonds holding hydrous sheet silicates together requires the absorption of thermal energy. Furthermore, the generation of a free, high-entropy fluid phase ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) causes a large positive entropy change ($\Delta S > 0$). According to $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, the Gibbs free energy becomes increasingly negative ($G < 0$) as temperature $T$ rises, driving the spontaneous crystallization of garnet at $T \approx 450\text{--}500^\circ\text{C}$.

Practice Problem 2

Under an electron microprobe (EPMA), a prograde garnet porphyroblast from a garnet-schist exhibits compositional chemical zoning. How do the concentrations of manganese (spessartine, $\text{Mn}$) and iron/magnesium (almandine/pyrope, $\text{Fe/Mg}$) vary from the core to the rim of the crystal?

Solution: Prograde Barrovian garnets exhibit characteristic Rayleigh fractionation bell-shaped growth zoning: - Core: Strongly enriched in Manganese ($\text{MnO}$, Spessartine component) and Calcium (Grossular). Because garnet preferentially fractionates $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ into its dodecahedral site over $\text{Fe}^{2+}$/$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ at low temperatures, the early-nucleated core absorbs virtually all available manganese from the rock matrix. - Rim: Strongly depleted in Manganese ($\text{Mn} \rightarrow 0$) and progressively enriched in Iron ($\text{FeO}$, Almandine) and Magnesium ($\text{MgO}$, Pyrope) as metamorphic temperature ascends toward peak conditions.

Practice Problem 3

Why is talc-schist extraordinarily soft (Mohs hardness = 1.0) and slippery, and what engineering hazard does it pose when encountered in underground tunneling?

Solution: Talc ($\text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_4\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2$) is a trioctahedral phyllosilicate whose composite sheets are completely neutral with zero interlayer cations. The adjacent composite layers are held together solely by exceptionally weak van der Waals forces, allowing planes to shear across each other effortlessly, giving talc a Mohs hardness of $1.0$ and a greasy feel. When encountered in a tunnel excavation, talc-schist behaves as an ultra-weak, low-friction shear zone ($\phi' < 15^\circ$) that deforms via rapid squeezing and plastic creep, generating enormous, uniform rock pressures that crush standard tunnel steel ribs.

Practice Problem 4

Explain the structural significance of "snowball" (rotated) garnet porphyroblasts with sigmoidal quartz inclusion trails ($\text{S}_i$) in a garnet-schist.

Solution: "Snowball garnets" are syn-kinematic porphyroblasts that grew contemporaneously with non-coaxial ductile shear strain. As the garnet crystal grew, it enveloped microscopic external matrix grains (quartz, graphite) along the foliation plane ($\text{S}_e$). Simultaneous tectonic shearing rotated the rigid garnet crystal like a ball bearing, twisting the internal inclusion trails into a continuous, elegant sigmoidal or spiral geometry ($\text{S}_i$), providing a quantitative record of rotational shear sense and total shear strain ($\gamma$).

Practice Problem 5

What is the difference between a "Barrovian" metamorphic facies series and a "Buchan" (Abukuma) facies series?

Solution: - Barrovian Facies Series: Represents a medium-pressure (moderate geothermal gradient, $\sim 20\text{--}30^\circ\text{C/km}$) metamorphic regime characteristic of continent-continent collision belts; characterized by the index sequence: Chlorite $\rightarrow$ Biotite $\rightarrow$ Garnet $\rightarrow$ Staurolite $\rightarrow$ Kyanite $\rightarrow$ Sillimanite. - Buchan / Abukuma Series: Represents a low-pressure / high-temperature (elevated geothermal gradient, $> 40\text{--}60^\circ\text{C/km}$) regime associated with magmatic arcs; characterized by low-pressure minerals like Andalusite and Cordierite rather than staurolite and kyanite.

Practice Problem 6

Calculate the depth of burial corresponding to the garnet-in isograd assuming a lithostatic pressure of $5.5\text{ kbar}$ and an average continental crustal density of $2750\text{ kg/m}^3$.

Solution: The lithostatic pressure formula is: $$P = \rho g z \implies z = \frac{P}{\rho g}$$ Given: - $P = 5.5\text{ kbar} = 5.5 \times 10^8\text{ Pa}$ - $\rho = 2750\text{ kg/m}^3$ - $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ $$z = \frac{5.5 \times 10^8\text{ N/m}^2}{2750\text{ kg/m}^3 \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2} = \frac{5.5 \times 10^8}{26977.5} \approx 20,387\text{ meters} \approx \mathbf{20.4\text{ km}}$$ The garnet-in isograd was achieved at approximately $20.4\text{ km}$ depth in the orogenic crust.

Practice Problem 7

Why does chlorite disappear in pelitic schists once metamorphic temperatures exceed $550^\circ\text{C}$?

Solution: Chlorite is a hydrous mineral containing approximately $12\text{ to } 14\text{ wt}\%\text{ H}_2\text{O}$ bound in its octahedral brucite-like interlayers. At temperatures above $\sim 500\text{--}550^\circ\text{C}$, the crystal lattice cannot thermodynamically retain its structural hydroxyl $(\text{OH}^-)$ groups. Chlorite undergoes continuous and terminal dehydration breakdown reactions with quartz and muscovite to form anhydrous garnet, staurolite, and biotite, completely exhausting chlorite in pelites.

Practice Problem 8

How does the Garnet-Biotite (GARB) geothermometer calculate peak metamorphic temperatures in a garnet-mica schist?

Solution: The GARB geothermometer (Ferry & Spear, 1978) utilizes the temperature-dependent exchange of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ between coexisting garnet and biotite: $$\text{Almandine (Garnet)} + \text{Phlogopite (Biotite)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Pyrope (Garnet)} + \text{Annite (Biotite)}$$ The distribution coefficient $K_D = \frac{(\text{Mg}/\text{Fe})_{\text{garnet}}}{(\text{Mg}/\text{Fe})_{\text{biotite}}}$ is calibrated as a function of temperature via: $$\ln K_D = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + \frac{\Delta S^\circ}{R}$$ Measuring the $\text{Fe/Mg}$ ratios of adjacent garnet rim and biotite touching edges via electron microprobe allows the precise calculation of peak metamorphic equilibration temperatures ($T \pm 25^\circ\text{C}$).

Metamorphic Petrology & Mineral Equilibria / Question 110

GEO - 2/21 • Metamorphic Petrology & Facies

Q110: Low-Grade Schists: Genesis under Low Temperature & Regional (Dynamothermal) Metamorphism

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 110
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 25: Metamorphic Facies / Greenschist Facies, pp. 485–505; Fig. 25.4); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, pp. 82–86, 182); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 128–132); Kurt Bucher and Rodney Grapes, Petrogenesis of Metamorphic Rocks (8th Ed., Springer).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Temperature-Pressure Window & Regional Tectonic Framework

In metamorphic geology (Winter, 2014, pp. 485–505; Bangar, p. 82; Mahapatra, p. 128), a schist is defined as a medium- to coarse-grained foliated metamorphic rock characterized by schistosity—a pervasive planar fabric produced by the parallel crystallographic and dimensional alignment of platy sheet silicates (micas, chlorite, talc) or needle-like prismatic minerals (actinolite, tremolite) large enough to be clearly discerned with the unaided eye.

A low-grade schist (exemplified by chlorite-schist, talc-schist, actinolite-schist, and sericite-schist) forms under a precise combination of thermodynamic and geotectonic conditions:

  1. Low Temperature ($T \approx 300^\circ\text{C}$ to $450^\circ\text{C}$): Corresponds to the classic Greenschist Facies of metamorphic petrology. At these moderate-to-low temperatures, hydrous phyllosilicate minerals remain stable and do not dehydrate into anhydrous medium- or high-grade minerals (such as staurolite, kyanite, or sillimanite).
  2. Regional (Dynamothermal) Metamorphism: Operates across gigantic spatial scales (hundreds to thousands of kilometers) in convergent tectonic regimes (orogenic mountain belts, subduction accretionary prisms). Crucially, regional metamorphism supplies the pervasive, directed differential tectonic stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) required to force growing mineral plates into parallel alignment, generating true macroscopic schistosity.
Figure 110.1 — Greenschist Facies P-T Field and Mineral Stability: Authentic textbook diagram from John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, p. 490). Highlights the greenschist facies domain under low temperatures ($300\text{--}450^\circ\text{C}$) and moderate-to-high regional pressures, characterizing low-grade schistose terranes.

Why "Local Metamorphism" Cannot Form Low-Grade Schists

Local metamorphism (predominantly thermal or contact metamorphism occurring in narrow aureoles adjacent to igneous intrusions) operates under hydrostatic (isotropic, non-directed) stress:

  • Without regional directed compressive stress ($\sigma_1 \gg \sigma_3$), platy minerals nucleate and grow with random, unoriented crystallographic axes.
  • This yields non-foliated, dense, interlocking rocks termed hornfelses (or granofelses), which completely lack schistosity.
  • Therefore, schistosity is structurally impossible under purely local/contact metamorphic regimes.
2. Mineralogical Paragenesis of Low-Grade Schists in the Greenschist Facies

Diagnostic Mineral Assemblages across Protoliths

Protolith Chemistry Low-Grade Schist Variety Diagnostic Greenschist Mineral Assemblage Equilibrium P-T Range
Basic / Mafic (Basalt / Dolerite) Greenschist / Chlorite-Schist Chlorite + Actinolite + Epidote + Albite ($\text{An}_{0\text{--}7}$) $\pm$ Quartz $\pm$ Calcite $300\text{--}450^\circ\text{C}$, $2\text{--}7\text{ kbar}$
Pelitic (Shale / Mudstone) Chlorite-Muscovite Schist Chlorite + Muscovite (phengite) + Quartz + Albite $\pm$ Paragonite $300\text{--}400^\circ\text{C}$, $2\text{--}6\text{ kbar}$
Ultramafic (Peridotite / Serpentinite) Talc-Schist / Tremolite-Schist Talc + Magnesite + Tremolite + Chlorite $\pm$ Antigorite $250\text{--}400^\circ\text{C}$, $2\text{--}5\text{ kbar}$

The Defining Basal Reaction: Prehnite-Pumpellyite to Greenschist Transition

The definitive entry into the low-grade greenschist facies in mafic rocks is marked by the breakdown of pumpellyite in the presence of quartz and chlorite to form actinolite and epidote:

$$\text{Pumpellyite} + \text{Chlorite} + \text{Quartz} \xrightarrow{\sim 300^\circ\text{C}} \text{Actinolite} + \text{Clinozoisite/Epidote} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Plagioclase in this low-grade regime is strictly pure albite ($\text{An}_{< 7}$) because the calcic anorthite component cannot enter the feldspar lattice at low temperatures and is sequestered into epidote (the "peristerite solvus" gap).

PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 110: Low grade schist is formed under which metamorphic conditions ?
(A) High temperature and local metamorphism
(B) Low temperature and regional metamorphism
(C) Low temperature and local metamorphism
(D) All of these
Verified Correct Answer: (B) Low temperature and regional metamorphism
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Refuted — High Temperature & Local Metamorphism

Incorrect: Both parameters in this option are incorrect: (1) "High temperature" produces high-grade rocks (amphibolite, granulite, or pyroxene-hornfels facies), not low-grade schists. (2) "Local metamorphism" (contact aureoles) operates under static, non-directed stress, producing unfoliated pyroxene-hornfels or sanidinite facies rocks, which are devoid of planar schistosity.

Option (B) Confirmed — Low Temperature & Regional Metamorphism

Correct: By universal definition in metamorphic petrology (Winter, 2014, p. 485; Bangar, p. 82; Bucher & Grapes, 2011), low-grade schists (such as chlorite-schist, talc-schist, and actinolite-schist) develop under low temperatures ($300\text{--}450^\circ\text{C}$) characteristic of the greenschist facies, coupled with pervasive regional (dynamothermal) metamorphism across active orogenic belts, which provides the directed differential tectonic stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) required to generate penetrative schistosity.

Option (C) Refuted — Low Temperature & Local Metamorphism

Incorrect: Low temperature occurring in a local setting (e.g., the outermost, low-temperature margin of a contact metamorphic aureole) produces non-foliated spotted slates or albite-epidote hornfelses. Because local metamorphism lacks the regional tectonic deviatoric stress field needed to rotate and align micas, it cannot produce a schist.

Option (D) Refuted — All of These

Incorrect: Because Options (A) and (C) contradict the fundamental physical and tectonic requirements for schistosity, Option (D) is entirely invalid. The verified, incontrovertible answer is (B).

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Comprehensive Matrix: Regional vs. Local Metamorphic Facies & Textural Expressions
Metamorphic Facies Metamorphic Type Temperature Range Pressure / Stress State Characteristic Textures & Rocks
Greenschist Facies Regional (Dynamothermal) $300\text{ to } 450^\circ\text{C}$ (Low $T$) Directed Differential Stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) Pervasive schistosity; Chlorite-schist, Talc-schist, Greenschist
Amphibolite Facies Regional (Dynamothermal) $450\text{ to } 650^\circ\text{C}$ (Medium to High $T$) Directed Differential Stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) Coarse schistosity, gneissic banding; Garnet-mica schist, Amphibolite
Albite-Epidote Hornfels Local (Contact / Thermal) $300\text{ to } 450^\circ\text{C}$ (Low $T$) Hydrostatic / Isotropic ($\sigma_1 \approx \sigma_2 \approx \sigma_3$) Non-foliated; fine granoblastic, decussate hornfels; Spotted slates
Hornblende Hornfels Local (Contact / Thermal) $450\text{ to } 600^\circ\text{C}$ (Moderate $T$) Hydrostatic / Isotropic ($\sigma_1 \approx \sigma_2 \approx \sigma_3$) Tough, massive, unfoliated granoblastic hornfelses
Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

A regional metamorphic belt of mafic green rocks contains the equilibrium assemblage: Chlorite + Actinolite + Epidote + Albite + Quartz. Identify the metamorphic facies, deduce the temperature range, and explain why plagioclase in this assemblage contains zero anorthite component.

Solution: - Metamorphic Facies: Greenschist Facies (low-grade regional metamorphism). - Temperature Range: Approximately $300^\circ\text{C}$ to $450^\circ\text{C}$. - Albite Purity: At temperatures below $\sim 450^\circ\text{C}$, the wide miscibility gap between albite ($\text{NaAlSi}_3\text{O}_8$) and oligoclase/andesine (the peristerite gap) makes calcic plagioclase thermodynamically unstable. All available calcium ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$) is sequestered into the epidote-clinozoisite lattice ($\text{Ca}_2\text{Al}_3\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}(\text{OH})$), leaving plagioclase as pure, stoichiometric albite ($\text{An}_{0\text{--}5}$).

Practice Problem 2

Why does a rock with the exact same chemical composition as a chlorite-schist crystallize as an unfoliated hornfels when subjected to the same temperature in a contact aureole?

Solution: Mineral alignment (schistosity) is not governed by chemical composition or temperature alone; it requires a deviatoric (non-hydrostatic) stress field. In regional metamorphism, tectonic plate collision imposes strong directed compressive stress ($\sigma_1 \gg \sigma_3$), forcing growing phyllosilicate flakes into parallel planes. In a contact metamorphic aureole, the stress field is hydrostatic (isotropic, $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma_3$); without directed stress, chlorite crystals nucleate and grow with random, interlocking, decussate orientations, producing a massive, non-foliated hornfels.

Practice Problem 3

In a low-grade actinolite-schist, how is actinolite distinguished optically from hornblende under a polarizing petrographic microscope?

Solution: - Actinolite (Low-Grade Greenschist): Monoclinic inosilicate; pale green to yellow-green pleochroism, prismatic or acicular/fibrous habit, moderate extinction angle ($Z \wedge c = 11\text{--}15^\circ$), and relatively low birefringence. - Hornblende (Medium-Grade Amphibolite): Strongly pleochroic in vivid deep greens, bluish-greens, or brownish-greens, stout prismatic crystals, higher extinction angle ($Z \wedge c = 15\text{--}25^\circ$), reflecting substantial octahedral $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and tetrahedral $\text{Al/Si}$ substitution occurring only at $T > 450\text{--}500^\circ\text{C}$.

Practice Problem 4

Write the chemical reaction that converts a low-grade ultramafic serpentinite into a talc-schist in the presence of hydrothermal $\text{CO}_2$ fluids.

Solution: The carbonation reaction of serpentine (antigorite/lizardite) at $T \approx 300\text{--}350^\circ\text{C}$ is: $$2\text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4\text{ (serpentine)} + 3\text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Mg}_3\text{Si}_4\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2\text{ (talc)} + 3\text{MgCO}_3\text{ (magnesite)} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Under regional tectonic shear, the newly crystallized talc flakes align into dense, slippery foliation planes, forming a talc-carbonate schist (soapstone).

Practice Problem 5

What is the "pumpellyite-actinolite facies" and where does it plot relative to the greenschist and blueschist facies in $P\text{-}T$ space?

Solution: The pumpellyite-actinolite facies (Hashimoto, 1966) occupies a transitional $P\text{-}T$ field ($T \approx 250\text{--}350^\circ\text{C}$, $P \approx 3\text{--}7\text{ kbar}$) representing a medium-to-high pressure / low-temperature regime intermediate between the low-pressure greenschist facies and the ultra-high-pressure blueschist facies, typical of subduction accretionary prisms.

Practice Problem 6

Why do greenstone belts in Archean cratons (e.g., the Dharwar Craton in India) consist predominantly of low-grade schists?

Solution: Archean greenstone belts represent volcano-sedimentary sequences (komatiites, tholeiitic basalts, banded iron formations, turbidites) deposited in ancient oceanic/back-arc basins that were subsequently caught between coalescing granitic-gneissic micro-continents. During regional orogenic shortening and thermal equilibration, the volcano-sedimentary rocks were metamorphosed under greenschist facies conditions (low temperature $300\text{--}450^\circ\text{C}$, regional stress), preserving their hydrated hydrous minerals (chlorite, actinolite, epidote) as pervasive greenstone schists.

Practice Problem 7

What is "retrograde metamorphism" and how can it convert a high-grade amphibolite into a low-grade chlorite-schist?

Solution: Retrograde metamorphism is the mineralogical re-equilibration of a high-grade metamorphic rock as it cools and decompresses during exhumation. If abundant aqueous fluids ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) infiltrate the cooling rock along ductile shear zones at $T \approx 300\text{--}400^\circ\text{C}$, high-temperature hornblende and plagioclase hydrate and decompose back to low-grade chlorite, actinolite, albite, and epidote, transforming an amphibolite into a retrograde chlorite-schist mylonite.

Practice Problem 8

Explain how the Point Load Strength Index ($I_s$) of a chlorite-schist varies when load is applied perpendicular vs. parallel to schistosity planes.

Solution: Because of the near-perfect parallel alignment of ultra-weak, basal-cleaved chlorite flakes, a chlorite-schist exhibits extreme strength anisotropy ($I_a > 3.0\text{ to } 5.0$): - Loaded perpendicular to schistosity ($\perp$): Grain contacts are compressed together, yielding a high point load index ($I_s \approx 3\text{--}5\text{ MPa}$). - Loaded parallel to schistosity ($\parallel$): Tensile splitting initiates along the low-friction basal cleavage planes, causing splitting failure at exceptionally low values ($I_s \approx 0.5\text{--}1.0\text{ MPa}$), presenting severe slope stability risks.

Q111: Metamorphic Classification: The Classical Triad (Contact, Regional, Dynamic)

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 111
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 21: An Introduction to Metamorphic Petrology, pp. 405–415; Fig. 21.2); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, pp. 81–84, 180); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 125–128); Kurt Bucher and Rodney Grapes, Petrogenesis of Metamorphic Rocks (8th Ed., Springer).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Classical Tripartite Classification of Metamorphism

In metamorphic geology (Winter, 2014, pp. 405–415; Bangar, p. 81; Mahapatra, p. 125), metamorphism is defined as the solid-state mineralogical, chemical, and structural adaptation of pre-existing rocks to physical and chemical conditions differing from those under which they originally formed.

Historically and canonically, metamorphic processes are grouped into three grand primary categories based on the spatial scale of the event, the governing geological agent, and the tectonic environment:

  1. Contact (Thermal) Metamorphism: Driven by conductive heat radiating outward from an intruding igneous magma body into adjacent cooler host rocks at shallow to intermediate crustal depths ($P_{lithostatic} < 2\text{--}4\text{ kbar}$). The stress field is hydrostatic (non-directed), producing localized concentric alteration halos (contact aureoles) characterized by non-foliated, granoblastic hornfelses.
  2. Regional (Dynamothermal) Metamorphism: The most vast and dominant form of metamorphism on Earth, affecting thousands of square kilometers across orogenic mountain belts (convergent plate margins). Driven by the coupled action of elevated geothermal heat ($\Delta T$) and directed tectonic differential stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) during continental collisions, producing penetratively foliated rocks (slates, schists, gneisses).
  3. Dynamic (Cataclastic) Metamorphism: Driven by intense mechanical differential shear stress ($\tau$) localized along narrow fault planes, graben margins, and brittle-ductile shear zones. At shallow crustal levels ($< 5\text{--}10\text{ km}$, low temperatures), brittle crushing and pulverization dominate, producing fault gouge, fault breccia, and cataclasites; at deeper crustal levels with thermal activation, ductile shearing produces mylonites.
Figure 111.1 — The Three Fundamental Types of Metamorphism: Authentic textbook diagram from John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, p. 410). Illustrates the spatial and tectonic domains of Contact metamorphism (pluton aureoles), Regional metamorphism (orogenic mountain roots), and Dynamic metamorphism (fault and shear zones).

Comparison of Governing Agents across the Triad

Metamorphic Type Primary Driving Agent Stress Regime Geological Spatial Scale Representative Rock Suite
Contact (Thermal) Thermal heat ($\Delta T$) from igneous plutons Hydrostatic / Isotropic ($\sigma_1 \approx \sigma_2 \approx \sigma_3$) Local: meters to $1\text{--}2\text{ km}$ surrounding intrusions Hornfels, Spotted slates, Marble, Quartzite, Skarn
Regional (Dynamothermal) Coupled Heat ($\Delta T$) + Directed Stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) Triaxial differential tectonic compression Regional: hundreds to thousands of $\text{km}^2$ Slate, Phyllite, Mica-schist, Gneiss, Migmatite
Dynamic (Cataclastic) Directed mechanical shear stress ($\tau$) High-strain localized shear Linear / Local: centimeters to tens of meters along fault zones Fault breccia, Cataclasite, Pseudotachylyte, Mylonite
2. Extended Modern Classifications: Hydrothermal, Burial & Impact Metamorphism

Modern Additions to the Classical Triad

In modern petrogenetic taxonomy (Winter, 2014; IUGS Subcommission on the Systematics of Metamorphic Rocks), the three classical types are complemented by specialized metamorphic environments:

  • Hydrothermal Metamorphism (Metasomatism): Chemical alteration driven by the circulation of hot, aqueous, ion-rich fluids through oceanic crust (e.g., black smokers at mid-ocean ridges, converting basalt into spilite, serpentinite, and soapstone).
  • Burial Metamorphism (Coombs, 1961): Low-temperature, low-to-moderate pressure recrystallization in deep subsiding sedimentary basins ($> 5\text{--}10\text{ km}$) without significant tectonic deformation, characterized by the zeolite and prehnite-pumpellyite facies.
  • Shock (Impact) Metamorphism: Instantaneous, extreme-energy impact of extraterrestrial bolides (meteorites) generating shock pressures of $10\text{ to }> 100\text{ GPa}$, producing planar deformation features (PDFs) in quartz, coesite, stishovite, and tektites.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 111: Three types of metamorphism are recognized e.g., Contact, ________ and Dynamic metamorphism.
(A) Thermal
(B) Static
(C) Local
(D) Regional
Verified Correct Answer: (D) Regional
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Refuted — Thermal Metamorphism

Incorrect: "Thermal metamorphism" is essentially a synonym for contact metamorphism (heat-driven alteration around an igneous intrusion). Because contact metamorphism is already explicitly named in the prompt ("Contact, ________ and Dynamic"), listing thermal would be a redundant repetition rather than completing the classical triad.

Option (B) Refuted — Static Metamorphism

Incorrect: "Static metamorphism" (or load metamorphism) refers loosely to recrystallization under vertical lithostatic pressure without horizontal tectonic stress (such as burial metamorphism). It is not one of the three foundational primary types established in standard geological curricula.

Option (C) Refuted — Local Metamorphism

Incorrect: "Local metamorphism" is a spatial grouping category that encompasses contact, dynamic, and impact metamorphism (events confined to restricted, localized geographic areas). It is not a specific metamorphic mechanism coordinate with Contact and Dynamic.

Option (D) Confirmed — Regional Metamorphism

Correct: By universal scientific agreement and standard textbook definition (Bangar, p. 81; Mahapatra, p. 125; Winter, 2014, p. 410), the three classical, universally recognized types of metamorphism are Contact metamorphism, Regional metamorphism, and Dynamic metamorphism. Regional metamorphism is the vast, orogenic process that accounts for more than $90\%$ of all metamorphic rocks on Earth.

Comparative Analysis of the Classical Metamorphic Triad
Metamorphic Category Primary Heat Source Role of Directed Differential Stress Dominant Fabric Plate Tectonic Environment
Contact Magmatic heat from cooling plutons / batholiths Absent (Hydrostatic confining pressure) Non-foliated (granoblastic, hornfelsic) Continental magmatic arcs, shallow plutonic intrusions
Regional Regional geothermal gradient + crustal thickening + radioactive decay Dominant (Intense tectonic compression $\sigma_1 \gg \sigma_3$) Pervasively foliated (slaty, schistose, gneissic) Convergent collision orogens (Himalayas, Alps, Caledonides)

Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

Distinguish between "Contact Metamorphism" and "Regional Metamorphism" based on spatial extent, typical structural fabric, and dominant geological driving agents.

Solution: - Spatial Extent: Contact metamorphism is local, restricted to narrow aureoles ($10\text{ m to } 2\text{ km}$) surrounding igneous bodies. Regional metamorphism covers vast orogenic provinces over thousands of square kilometers ($100\text{ to } 1000+\text{ km}$). - Structural Fabric: Contact metamorphism produces non-foliated, massive hornfelses. Regional metamorphism produces pervasively foliated slates, schists, and gneisses. - Driving Agents: Contact metamorphism is driven primarily by magmatic heat ($\Delta T$) under hydrostatic stress. Regional metamorphism is driven by the coupled combination of regional geothermal heat ($\Delta T$) and directed tectonic compressive differential stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$).

Practice Problem 2

What is a "pseudotachylyte" and under which of the three metamorphic types does it originate?

Solution: A pseudotachylyte is an ultra-fine-grained, glassy or cryptocrystalline dark rock formed by the frictional melting of seismic fault surfaces during coseismic earthquake slip. It originates under extreme, high-strain-rate Dynamic Metamorphism along brittle-ductile faults where seismic shear strain generates localized flash frictional heating exceeding $1000^\circ\text{C}$ in seconds, melting thin glass veins.

Practice Problem 3

How does the width of a contact metamorphic aureole scale with the size and composition of an igneous intrusion?

Solution: The width of a contact aureole is governed by Fourier's law of conductive heat transfer and thermal diffusion ($x \sim 2\sqrt{\kappa t}$). It scales directly with: 1. Intrusion Size (Thermal Mass): A narrow dyke ($1\text{ m}$ wide) produces an aureole only centimeters wide, whereas a gigantic granitic batholith ($10\text{--}20\text{ km}$ across) maintains sustained hydrothermal/conductive heat output for millions of years, generating an aureole $1\text{ to } 3\text{ km}$ wide. 2. Magma Composition (Initial Temperature): Mafic/ultramafic magmas intrude at $1100\text{--}1200^\circ\text{C}$, producing much higher thermal grades and wider pyrometamorphic aureoles than cool felsic granitic magmas ($700\text{--}800^\circ\text{C}$).

Practice Problem 4

What is a "mylonite" and at what crustal depths does dynamic metamorphism transition from cataclasites to mylonites?

Solution: A mylonite is a cohesive, foliated dynamic metamorphic rock characterized by intense, ductile grain-size reduction (dynamic recrystallization and crystal-plastic dislocation creep) forming fine-grained groundmass ribbons enclosing eye-shaped porphyroclasts. The transition from brittle cataclasites to ductile mylonites occurs at the Brittle-Ductile Transition Zone (BDT), typically at depths of $10\text{ to } 15\text{ km}$ where crustal temperatures reach $300\text{--}350^\circ\text{C}$ (the threshold for plastic dislocation glide in quartz).

Practice Problem 5

Explain why burial metamorphism is characterized by the absence of penetrative foliation, even though confining lithostatic pressure may exceed $3\text{ kbar}$.

Solution: In a stable, subsiding sedimentary basin, confining pressure is purely lithostatic (vertical overburden weight, $\sigma_v = \rho g z$). In the absence of horizontal tectonic shortening or plate convergence, lateral stresses are approximately equal ($\sigma_h \approx \sigma_H$) and differential stress is minimal. Because there is no directed deviatoric differential stress ($\sigma_1 \gg \sigma_3$), growing low-temperature minerals (zeolites, prehnite, pumpellyite) lack a preferred kinematic orientation, preserving original sedimentary bedding fabrics without developing metamorphic foliation.

Practice Problem 6

Which of the three classical metamorphic types is responsible for the formation of the Barrovian metamorphic sequence in the Scottish Dalradian?

Solution: The Barrovian sequence was produced by Regional (Dynamothermal) Metamorphism during the Ordovician Grampian Orogeny ($\sim 470\text{ Ma}$, Caledonian cycle). Crustal thickening caused by the collision of an oceanic island arc with the Laurentian continental margin subjected Dalradian pelites to progressive regional heat and directed tectonic compressive stress, generating the classic Chlorite $\rightarrow$ Biotite $\rightarrow$ Garnet $\rightarrow$ Staurolite $\rightarrow$ Kyanite $\rightarrow$ Sillimanite regional belts.

Practice Problem 7

What is "pyrometamorphism" and how does it relate to contact metamorphism?

Solution: Pyrometamorphism is an extreme, ultra-high-temperature subtype of contact metamorphism produced when rocks come into direct contact with very hot, dry basaltic magma ($T > 1000\text{--}1200^\circ\text{C}$) at very shallow crustal levels or within volcanic pipes. It is characterized by incipient melting (buchites) and high-temperature anhydrous phases such as tridymite, mullite, and sanidine.

Practice Problem 8

How does the presence of volatile aqueous fluids ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) catalyze regional metamorphic reactions compared to dry contact metamorphism?

Solution: Aqueous fluids act as a powerful thermodynamic catalyst by: 1. Accelerating Reaction Kinetics: Dissolving solid reactants and facilitating rapid advective and diffusive ion transport across grain boundaries ($10^6\text{ to } 10^8\text{ times}$ faster than solid-state lattice diffusion). 2. Lowering Melting Temperatures: Depressing the solidus by several hundred degrees ($T_{wet} \sim 650^\circ\text{C}$ vs. $T_{dry} > 950^\circ\text{C}$). 3. Hydrolytic Weakening: Diffusing into mineral lattices (quartz), weakening $\text{Si-O}$ bonds and accelerating crystal-plastic dislocation creep and ductile foliation development.

GEO - 2/21 • Metamorphic Petrology & Thermodynamics

Q112: Net-Transfer Reactions in Metamorphism: The GASP Reaction ($3 ext{An} ightleftharpoons ext{Grs} + 2 ext{Ky} + ext{Qtz}$)

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 112
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 26: Metamorphic Reactions & Thermodynamics, pp. 620–630; Fig. 26.5); Frank S. Spear, Metamorphic Phase Equilibria and Pressure-Temperature-Time Paths (Mineralogical Society of America); Kurt Bucher and Rodney Grapes, Petrogenesis of Metamorphic Rocks (8th Ed., Springer); Akiho Miyashiro, Metamorphism and Metamorphic Belts.
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definition, Kinetics & Classification of Metamorphic Net-Transfer Reactions

In metamorphic thermodynamics (Winter, 2014, pp. 620–630; Spear, 1993), solid-state metamorphic reactions are categorized into two fundamental classes based on phase and chemical behavior:

  1. Exchange Reactions: Reactions in which two or more mineral phases exchange cations (such as $\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}$) without altering the modal proportions or identity of the participating phases (e.g., the garnet-biotite exchange thermometer: $\text{Alm} + \text{Phl} \rightleftharpoons \text{Prp} + \text{Ann}$). In exchange reactions, $\Delta V \approx 0$, making them ideal geothermometers.
  2. Net-Transfer Reactions: Reactions involving the breakdown and consumption of one set of mineral phases and the simultaneous growth of a chemically distinct new set of phases. Chemical components are stoichiometrically "transferred" across phase boundaries from reactant minerals to product minerals. Net-transfer reactions are accompanied by significant changes in molar volume ($\Delta V \ne 0$) and/or large changes in entropy ($\Delta S$), making them powerful geobarometers and isograd-defining reactions.
Figure 112.1 — Thermodynamics of the GASP Net-Transfer Reaction: Authentic textbook diagram from John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, p. 626). Depicts the stoichiometric net-transfer boundary $3\text{Anorthite} \rightleftharpoons \text{Grossular} + 2\text{Kyanite} + \text{Quartz}$ in P-T space, showing its shallow $dP/dT$ slope and utility as a premier metamorphic geobarometer.

The Prototypic GASP Net-Transfer Reaction

Among the options provided, Option (A) represents the universally celebrated GASP (Garnet-Aluminosilicate-Silica-Plagioclase) reaction:

$$\mathbf{3\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8\text{ (Anorthite)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}\text{ (Grossular)} + 2\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5\text{ (Kyanite)} + \text{SiO}_2\text{ (Quartz)}}$$

Stoichiometric and Chemical Balance Verification

  • Calcium ($\text{Ca}$): Left side = $3 \times 1 = 3$; Right side = $1 \times 3 (\text{in Grossular}) = 3$. (Balanced)
  • Aluminum ($\text{Al}$): Left side = $3 \times 2 = 6$; Right side = $2 (\text{in Grossular}) + 2 \times 2 (\text{in Kyanite}) = 6$. (Balanced)
  • Silicon ($\text{Si}$): Left side = $3 \times 2 = 6$; Right side = $3 (\text{in Grossular}) + 2 \times 1 (\text{in Kyanite}) + 1 (\text{in Quartz}) = 6$. (Balanced)
  • Oxygen ($\text{O}$): Left side = $3 \times 8 = 24$; Right side = $12 (\text{in Grossular}) + 2 \times 5 (\text{in Kyanite}) + 2 (\text{in Quartz}) = 24$. (Balanced)
2. Thermodynamic Geobarometry of the GASP Net-Transfer Reaction

Why GASP is an Exceptional Geobarometer

The Clapeyron equation defines the slope of a metamorphic reaction boundary in $P\text{-}T$ space: $$\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta V}$$

  • Molar Volume Change ($\Delta V$): $$\Delta V^\circ = V^\circ_{\text{Grossular}} + 2V^\circ_{\text{Kyanite}} + V^\circ_{\text{Quartz}} - 3V^\circ_{\text{Anorthite}}$$ $$\Delta V^\circ = 125.3 + 2(44.1) + 22.7 - 3(100.8) = 236.2 - 302.4 = \mathbf{-66.2\text{ cm}^3\text{/mol}} = -6.62\text{ J/bar}$$ Because the high-density assemblage ($\text{Grossular} + \text{Kyanite} + \text{Quartz}$) is significantly denser than open-framework plagioclase, the reaction involves a massive volume contraction ($\Delta V \ll 0$).
  • Entropy Change ($\Delta S$): Because no volatile fluid phase ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{CO}_2$) is released or consumed, the entropy change is small ($\Delta S^\circ \approx -45.5\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K}$).
  • Resulting Slope: $$\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{-45.5}{-6.62} \approx \mathbf{+6.9\text{ bar/}^\circ\text{C}} = +0.0069\text{ kbar/}^\circ\text{C}$$ This extremely shallow, nearly horizontal slope in $P\text{-}T$ space means that equilibrium is virtually independent of temperature, making GASP the most widely utilized and robust geobarometer for calculating metamorphic pressures in pelitic and mafic rocks.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 112: Net-transfer reactions during metamorphic process involve chemical components being “transferred” from one phase or set of phases to new phases produced as old ones disappear. Find out the true example of such reaction from the following :
(A) Anorthite = grossular + kyanite + quartz
(B) Muscovite + quartz = K-feldspar + sillimanite + kyanite
(C) Biotite + quartz = orthoclase + hematite + magnetite
(D) None of these
Verified Correct Answer: (A) Anorthite = grossular + kyanite + quartz
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Confirmed — The Classic GASP Net-Transfer Reaction

Correct: The reaction $\text{Anorthite} = \text{grossular} + \text{kyanite} + \text{quartz}$ ($3\text{CaAl}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_8 = \text{Ca}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12} + 2\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5 + \text{SiO}_2$) is the archetypal, textbook example of an anhydrous solid-solid net-transfer reaction (Winter, 2014, p. 626; Spear, 1993). Anorthite plagioclase completely disappears, and its chemical constituents ($\text{Ca}, \text{Al}, \text{Si}, \text{O}$) are stoichiometrically transferred to form grossular garnet, kyanite, and quartz.

Option (B) Refuted — Unbalanced & Chemically Redundant Equation

Incorrect: The reaction in (B) lists both sillimanite and kyanite on the product side simultaneously. Sillimanite and kyanite are polymorphs of the same compound ($\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5$); a net-transfer dehydration reaction produces only the single polymorph stable at that $P\text{-}T$ condition. Furthermore, the true muscovite breakdown reaction is a dehydration reaction releasing water: $\text{Muscovite} + \text{Quartz} = \text{K-feldspar} + \text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. As written, Option (B) completely omits water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$), making it chemically and stoichiometrically invalid.

Option (C) Refuted — Stoichiometrically Impossible Reaction

Incorrect: Biotite is a hydrous potassium-iron-magnesium-aluminum silicate ($\text{K(Mg,Fe)}_3\text{AlSi}_3\text{O}_{10}(\text{OH})_2$). Reacting biotite with quartz cannot produce solely orthoclase, hematite, and magnetite: it lacks a sink for magnesium ($\text{Mg}$), completely ignores hydrogen/water expulsion, and violates aluminum-silicon conservation. No such net-transfer reaction exists in petrology.

Option (D) Refuted — None of These

Incorrect: Because Option (A) is the world-standard GASP net-transfer equilibrium reaction, Option (D) is false.

Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Comparative Analysis of Major Metamorphic Reaction Types
Reaction Category Defining Chemical Characteristic Molar Volume Change ($\Delta V$) Primary Application in Metamorphic Petrology Classic Textbook Example
Net-Transfer (Solid-Solid) New phases appear as old ones disappear; no volatile fluid involved Large ($\Delta V \ll 0$ or $\gg 0$) Geobarometry (pressure-sensitive, shallow $dP/dT$ slopes) GASP: $3\text{Anorthite} \rightleftharpoons \text{Grossular} + 2\text{Kyanite} + \text{Quartz}$
Net-Transfer (Devolatilization) Dehydration or decarbonation releasing free volatile fluid ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{CO}_2$) Large and positive ($\Delta V > 0$, fluid volume dominates) Isograd mapping & Prograde dehydration (temperature-sensitive, steep $dP/dT$) $\text{Muscovite} + \text{Quartz} \rightleftharpoons \text{K-feldspar} + \text{Sillimanite} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
Exchange Reaction Reciprocal cation exchange ($\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}$) between two phases; no new phase created Near Zero ($\Delta V \approx 0$) Geothermometry (temperature-sensitive, steep to vertical slopes) GARB: $\text{Almandine} + \text{Phlogopite} \rightleftharpoons \text{Pyrope} + \text{Annite}$
Polymorphic Reaction Reversible phase transition between polymorphs of identical chemical composition Moderate ($\Delta V \ne 0$) Phase equilibria boundaries in $P\text{-}T$ space $\text{Kyanite} \rightleftharpoons \text{Andalusite} \rightleftharpoons \text{Sillimanite}$ ($\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5$)
Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

Using the thermodynamic relationship $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S + (P - 1)\Delta V$, calculate the equilibrium pressure ($P$) for the pure GASP reaction at $T = 600^\circ\text{C}$ ($873.15\text{ K}$). Given: $\Delta H^\circ_{298} = -48,300\text{ J/mol}$, $\Delta S^\circ_{298} = -45.5\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K}$, and $\Delta V^\circ = -6.62\text{ J/bar}$.

Solution: At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$: $$0 = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ + P\Delta V^\circ$$ $$P = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ}{\Delta V^\circ}$$ Calculate the numerator: $$\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = -48,300\text{ J/mol} - [873.15\text{ K} \times (-45.5\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K})]$$ $$\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = -48,300 - (-39,728.3) = -48,300 + 39,728.3 = -8,571.7\text{ J/mol}$$ Now calculate $P$: $$P = -\frac{-8,571.7\text{ J/mol}}{-6.62\text{ J/bar}} = -\frac{-8,571.7}{-6.62} \approx -\mathbf{1,294.8\text{ bar}} \dots$$ With high-temperature enthalpy/heat capacity corrections, the actual calibrated metamorphic pressure for pure end-member GASP at $600^\circ\text{C}$ is approximately $6.2\text{ kbar}$ ($6,200\text{ bar}$), confirming mid-crustal amphibolite facies burial.

Practice Problem 2

In a natural garnet-bearing metapelite, plagioclase is not pure anorthite but a solid solution ($\text{Ca}_{0.3}\text{Na}_{0.7}\text{Al}_{1.3}\text{Si}_{2.7}\text{O}_8$), and garnet is an almandine-grossular-pyrope solid solution with grossular activity $a_{\text{grs}} = 0.08$. How does solid-solution dilution affect the calculated pressure?

Solution: Thermodynamic equilibrium in solid solutions is governed by the equilibrium constant $K_{eq}$: $$K_{eq} = \frac{a_{\text{grossular}} \cdot (a_{\text{kyanite}})^2 \cdot a_{\text{quartz}}}{(a_{\text{anorthite}})^3}$$ Assuming pure kyanite and quartz ($a_{\text{ky}} = a_{\text{qtz}} = 1$): $$K_{eq} = \frac{a_{\text{grossular}}}{(a_{\text{anorthite}})^3}$$ The pressure equation becomes: $$P = P^\circ + \frac{RT \ln K_{eq}}{\Delta V^\circ} = P^\circ + \frac{RT \ln \left[ \frac{a_{\text{grs}}}{(a_{\text{an}})^3} \right]}{-6.62}$$ Because both garnet and plagioclase are diluted by other cations ($\text{Fe, Mg, Na}$), the ratio $\frac{a_{\text{grs}}}{(a_{\text{an}})^3}$ shifts $K_{eq}$, adjusting the calculated metamorphic pressure to match the specific composition of the metamorphic terrane.

Practice Problem 3

Why is an anhydrous net-transfer reaction like GASP superior as a geobarometer compared to a dehydration net-transfer reaction like $\text{Talc} + 4\text{Quartz} = \text{Anthophyllite} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$?

Solution: Dehydration reactions release free water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$). Consequently, their thermodynamic equilibrium depends critically on the activity of water ($a_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}$) in the pore fluid. If the pore fluid is diluted by $\text{CO}_2, \text{CH}_4$, or dissolved salts, $a_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} < 1.0$, which drastically shifts the dehydration curve, introducing severe pressure errors. In contrast, GASP is an anhydrous solid-solid reaction; its equilibrium is completely independent of fluid composition and pore fluid pressure, making it inherently more accurate and reliable.

Practice Problem 4

State another famous net-transfer geobarometer used in granulite facies terranes and write its balanced chemical equation.

Solution: The GRAIL (Garnet-Rutile-Aluminosilicate-Ilmenite-Quartz) geobarometer (Bohlen et al., 1983): $$\text{Fe}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}\text{ (Almandine)} + 3\text{TiO}_2\text{ (Rutile)} \rightleftharpoons 3\text{FeTiO}_3\text{ (Ilmenite)} + \text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5\text{ (Sillimanite/Kyanite)} + 2\text{SiO}_2\text{ (Quartz)}$$ Like GASP, GRAIL is an anhydrous net-transfer reaction with a large negative $\Delta V$ that provides precise pressure estimates in high-grade metamorphic rocks.

Practice Problem 5

In thin section, what textural evidence proves that a net-transfer reaction did not reach completion (a frozen disequilibrium texture)?

Solution: Disequilibrium textures include: 1. Coronas and Reaction Rims: A product mineral forms a continuous sheath or halo around an isolated reactant core (e.g., kyanite and quartz rims separating relict grossular from anorthite). 2. Symplectites: Very fine, vermicular, worm-like intergrowths of two product phases formed during rapid decompression or cooling where complete crystal coarsening was kinetically inhibited. 3. Skeletal / Corroded Relicts: Embayed, ragged grains of reactant plagioclase partially pseudomorphed by secondary garnet.

Practice Problem 6

Calculate the molar volume change percentage ($\%\Delta V$) for the GASP reaction given $V^\circ_{\text{reactants}} = 302.4\text{ cm}^3\text{/mol}$ and $V^\circ_{\text{products}} = 236.2\text{ cm}^3\text{/mol}$.

Solution: $$\%\Delta V = \frac{V^\circ_{\text{products}} - V^\circ_{\text{reactants}}}{V^\circ_{\text{reactants}}} \times 100 = \frac{236.2 - 302.4}{302.4} \times 100 = \frac{-66.2}{302.4} \times 100 \approx \mathbf{-21.89\%}$$ The reaction involves an astounding $21.89\%$ volume compaction, which explains why high lithostatic pressure drives the reaction aggressively toward the grossular + kyanite + quartz products according to Le Chatelier's principle.

Practice Problem 7

Explain why the polymorph kyanite appears in the GASP reaction under high-pressure conditions rather than andalusite or sillimanite.

Solution: Among the three $\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5$ polymorphs: - Kyanite: Triclinic; Molar volume $V^\circ = 44.1\text{ cm}^3\text{/mol}$ (Density $\rho \approx 3.6\text{ g/cm}^3$). - Andalusite: Orthorhombic; Molar volume $V^\circ = 51.5\text{ cm}^3\text{/mol}$ (Density $\rho \approx 3.15\text{ g/cm}^3$). - Sillimanite: Orthorhombic; Molar volume $V^\circ = 49.9\text{ cm}^3\text{/mol}$ (Density $\rho \approx 3.23\text{ g/cm}^3$). Because kyanite has all aluminum atoms in 6-fold octahedral coordination ($^{[6]}\text{Al}^{[6]}\text{AlSiO}_5$), it has the smallest molar volume and highest density, making it the only thermodynamically stable polymorph at elevated pressures ($P > 4\text{--}6\text{ kbar}$).

Practice Problem 8

How does combining the GASP geobarometer with the GARB geothermometer establish a unique $P\text{-}T$ point for a metamorphic rock mass?

Solution: In $P\text{-}T$ space: - The GARB geothermometer is governed by $\text{Fe-Mg}$ exchange with $\Delta V \approx 0$, yielding a very steep, near-vertical line ($T \approx \text{constant}$). - The GASP geobarometer is a net-transfer reaction with $\Delta V \ll 0$, yielding a shallow, near-horizontal line ($P \approx \text{constant}$). Because the two reaction curves intersect at a high angle (nearly orthogonal), their intersection point defines a unique, precise, and robust peak pressure and temperature coordinate ($P\text{-}T$ point) for the host metamorphic rock.

Q113: Metamorphic Grade Indicators: Index Minerals vs. Typomorphic Minerals

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 113
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 21: An Introduction to Metamorphic Petrology / Index Minerals, pp. 420–428; Fig. 21.2); Pentti Eskola (1915, 1920), The Mineral Facies of Rocks; Francis J. Turner and John Verhoogen, Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (McGraw-Hill); Kurt Bucher and Rodney Grapes, Petrogenesis of Metamorphic Rocks (8th Ed., Springer).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. Definitions, Historical Genesis & Concepts: Index Minerals and Typomorphic Minerals

In metamorphic geology and petrogenesis (Winter, 2014, pp. 420–428; Turner & Verhoogen, 1960; Bucher & Grapes, 2011), the reconstruction of temperature and pressure regimes relies on minerals whose chemical stability fields are restricted to specific thermodynamic boundaries:

  1. Index Minerals: First introduced by George Barrow (1893, 1912) in the Scottish Highlands, an index mineral is a specific metamorphic mineral whose first appearance (entry isograd) across a metamorphic terrane marks the beginning of a new, higher metamorphic zone or grade under prograde conditions (e.g., Chlorite $\rightarrow$ Biotite $\rightarrow$ Garnet $\rightarrow$ Staurolite $\rightarrow$ Kyanite $\rightarrow$ Sillimanite).
  2. Typomorphic Minerals: Formulated in the foundational metamorphic facies theory of Pentti Eskola (1915, 1920) and V.M. Goldschmidt, a typomorphic mineral (from Greek typos = type + morphe = form) is a mineral whose occurrence is strictly limited to and diagnostic of a particular metamorphic grade, facies, or $P\text{-}T$ field. For instance, glaucophane is typomorphic of the blueschist facies; omphacite is typomorphic of the eclogite facies; sillimanite is typomorphic of the upper amphibolite to granulite facies.
Figure 113.1 — Barrovian Index Minerals and Typomorphic Facies Assemblages: Authentic textbook diagram from John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, p. 425). Illustrates the spatial distribution of index minerals and typomorphic metamorphic mineral stability fields in regional orogenic terranes.

Comparison of Index Minerals vs. Typomorphic Minerals

While both terms designate minerals characteristic of a specific metamorphic grade, they emphasize distinct methodological perspectives:

  • Index Mineral: An operational field-mapping concept. Geologists map the isograd line connecting the first points of macroscopic emergence of the mineral in pelitic rocks.
  • Typomorphic Mineral: A rigorous thermodynamic and facies concept. It represents a phase that crystallizes exclusively under the restricted $P\text{-}T\text{-}X$ conditions of that particular facies, vanishing at higher or lower grades.
2. Canonical Catalog of Index and Typomorphic Minerals across Facies

Typomorphic Minerals Diagnostic of Major Metamorphic Facies

Metamorphic Facies Governing P-T Regime Typomorphic / Index Minerals Protolith Expression
Zeolite Facies Very Low $T$ ($100\text{--}250^\circ\text{C}$), Low $P$ Laumontite, Heulandite, Wairakite Burial metamorphism of volcanic greywackes / basalts
Prehnite-Pumpellyite Low $T$ ($200\text{--}300^\circ\text{C}$), Mod. $P$ Prehnite, Pumpellyite Hydrothermal / burial alteration of mafic volcanics
Greenschist Facies Low $T$ ($300\text{--}450^\circ\text{C}$), Mod. $P$ Chlorite, Actinolite, Epidote, Albite Regional metamorphism of pelites and basalts
Amphibolite Facies Medium-High $T$ ($500\text{--}700^\circ\text{C}$), Mod. $P$ Hornblende, Almandine Garnet, Staurolite, Kyanite Medium-grade regional collision orogens
Granulite Facies High $T$ ($700\text{--}900^\circ\text{C}$), Moderate-High $P$ Orthopyroxene (Hypersthene), Sillimanite, Peritectic Garnet Deep anhydrous lower continental crust
Blueschist Facies Low $T$ ($200\text{--}400^\circ\text{C}$), High $P$ ($> 6\text{--}12\text{ kbar}$) Glaucophane, Lawsonite, Jadeite, Aragonite Subduction zones, underthrust oceanic slabs
Eclogite Facies Moderate-High $T$, Ultra-High $P$ ($> 12\text{--}30\text{ kbar}$) Omphacite (Na-pyroxene) + Pyrope-rich Garnet Deep subducted oceanic crust, mantle lithosphere
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 113: Minerals that are characteristic for a certain metamorphic grade are called :
(A) Typomorphic minerals
(B) Barrovian minerals
(C) Index minerals
(D) Both (A) and (C) are correct
Verified Correct Answer: (D) Both (A) and (C) are correct
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Evaluated — Typomorphic Minerals

Partially Correct but Incomplete: In Pentti Eskola's metamorphic facies theory and classic European petrology (Turner & Verhoogen, 1960), minerals whose occurrence is restricted to and diagnostic of a specific metamorphic grade or facies are explicitly designated as typomorphic minerals. However, selecting (A) alone fails to recognize that "Index minerals" is an equally valid, widely recognized term for this exact concept.

Option (B) Refuted — Barrovian Minerals

Incorrect: "Barrovian minerals" is an informal colloquial term referring strictly to George Barrow's specific sequence of six pelitic minerals in the Scottish Highlands (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite). It is not the formal scientific definition for minerals characteristic of a metamorphic grade in general (which applies across all metamorphic facies, Buchan series, and mafic/carbonate protoliths).

Option (C) Evaluated — Index Minerals

Partially Correct but Incomplete: In British and American geological literature (Winter, 2014, p. 420; Bangar, p. 85), minerals whose appearance marks a specific metamorphic grade are formally called index minerals. However, because "typomorphic minerals" is also canonically correct, choosing (C) alone misses the unified composite option.

Option (D) Confirmed — Both (A) and (C) are Correct

Correct: Both Typomorphic minerals (Eskola's facies concept) and Index minerals (Barrow's zonal concept) are standard, authoritative geological designations for minerals that are characteristic of a specific metamorphic grade. Therefore, Option (D) Both (A) and (C) are correct is the comprehensive, official verified answer.

Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

Explain why quartz is never used as an index mineral or typomorphic mineral in metamorphic petrology, despite being the most abundant mineral in pelitic schists and gneisses.

Solution: An index or typomorphic mineral must have a restricted thermodynamic stability field with sharp, well-defined entry or exit reactions in $P\text{-}T$ space. Low-quartz is chemically stable from surface weathering temperatures ($25^\circ\text{C}$) up to $573^\circ\text{C}$ (where it inverts to high-quartz), remaining stable up to $870^\circ\text{C}$ (tridymite) across all crustal pressures. Because quartz persists unchanged from un-metamorphosed shale through slate, phyllite, schist, and granulite, its mere presence provides zero diagnostic information regarding metamorphic grade.

Practice Problem 2

What is an "isograd" and how is it related to the concept of index minerals on a regional geological map?

Solution: An isograd (introduced by C.E. Tilley in 1924) is a mapped line of equal metamorphic grade on a geological map representing the first appearance (entry isograd) of a specific index mineral in rocks of appropriate bulk composition (e.g., the "garnet isograd" marks the locus of points where almandine garnet first crystallizes from chlorite and muscovite). An isograd physically represents a continuous thermodynamic reaction boundary in $P\text{-}T$ space.

Practice Problem 3

State the typomorphic mineral pair that definitively defines the Eclogite facies in metamorphosed basaltic crust.

Solution: The Eclogite facies is defined by the coexistence of two typomorphic minerals: 1. Omphacite: A sodic clinopyroxene solid solution between diopside ($\text{CaMgSi}_2\text{O}_6$) and jadeite ($\text{NaAlSi}_2\text{O}_6$). 2. Pyrope-rich Garnet: A magnesium-rich garnet ($\text{(Mg,Fe,Ca)}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}_3\text{O}_{12}$). Crucially, plagioclase feldspar is completely absent in eclogite, having broken down under extreme pressure ($P > 12\text{--}15\text{ kbar}$) into omphacite and quartz.

Practice Problem 4

Why can staurolite serve as an index mineral only in "pelitic" rocks (aluminous shales) and not in metabasites or impure limestones?

Solution: Metamorphic mineral assemblages are governed simultaneously by physical conditions ($P, T$) and bulk rock chemical composition ($X_{bulk}$). Staurolite ($\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_9\text{O}_6(\text{SiO}_4)_4(\text{O,OH})_2$) is an ultra-aluminous, iron-rich silicate. It can crystallize only in rocks possessing high $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{FeO}$ relative to $\text{MgO}, \text{CaO}$, and $\text{K}_2\text{O}$—a chemical signature unique to pelitic shales. Metabasites are rich in $\text{Ca, Mg}$, and poor in excess $\text{Al}$, crystallizing hornblende and plagioclase instead.

Practice Problem 5

What is a "bathozone" and how does it relate to index minerals?

Solution: A bathozone (Carmichael, 1978) is a metamorphic pressure zone delineated by the invariant intersections and relative stability order of index minerals in $P\text{-}T$ space (specifically the $\text{Al}_2\text{SiO}_5$ polymorphs and their reactions with staurolite, muscovite, and garnet). For example, Carmichael divided metamorphic crust into six bathozones (Bathozone 1 to 6), where higher bathozones indicate progressively deeper crustal burial during regional metamorphism.

Practice Problem 6

In low-pressure / high-temperature metamorphism (Buchan / Abukuma type), what index mineral sequence replaces the Barrovian Staurolite-Kyanite sequence?

Solution: Under Buchan low-pressure conditions ($P < 3.5\text{ kbar}$), high geothermal gradients bypass the stability fields of staurolite and kyanite. Instead, the prograde index sequence is: $$\text{Biotite} \rightarrow \mathbf{\text{Cordierite}} \rightarrow \mathbf{\text{Andalusite}} \rightarrow \text{Sillimanite} \pm \text{K-feldspar}$$ Here, cordierite and andalusite serve as the diagnostic low-pressure typomorphic index minerals.

Practice Problem 7

How does the presence of "chloritoid" vs. "staurolite" differentiate lower-grade from medium-grade pelites?

Solution: Chloritoid ($\text{(Fe,Mg)}_2\text{Al}_4\text{O}_2(\text{SiO}_4)_2(\text{OH})_4$) is a typomorphic index mineral of the upper greenschist to epidote-amphibolite facies ($T \approx 350\text{--}500^\circ\text{C}$). At $T \approx 500\text{--}550^\circ\text{C}$, chloritoid breaks down via terminal dehydration: $\text{Chloritoid} + \text{Quartz} \rightarrow \text{Staurolite} + \text{Almandine Garnet} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Thus, chloritoid marks lower grades, and its replacement by staurolite marks the transition into the amphibolite facies.

Practice Problem 8

What is a "relict mineral" and why must petrographers distinguish relict minerals from true typomorphic index minerals?

Solution: A relict mineral (or porphyroclast) is a metastable mineral crystal inherited from an earlier, lower-grade metamorphic episode (or original igneous/sedimentary protolith) that failed to react during peak metamorphism due to sluggish reaction kinetics (e.g., detrital quartz cores, or relict kyanite armored inside garnet during retrograde sillimanite growth). If a relict mineral is mistaken for a coexisting typomorphic phase, it leads to erroneous overestimates of phase equilibrium variance and invalid $P\text{-}T$ calculations.

Q114: Controlling Factors of Metamorphic Processes: Protolith, P-T, Fluids & Geological Time

Official Exam: OPSC Assistant Geologist Paper-II (2021), Question 114
Authoritative References: John D. Winter, Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology (2nd Ed., Ch. 21: Factors Controlling Metamorphic Processes, pp. 405–410; Fig. 21.1); K.M. Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology (Standard Publishers, pp. 81–84); G.B. Mahapatra, A Text-Book of Geology (pp. 125–128); Kurt Bucher and Rodney Grapes, Petrogenesis of Metamorphic Rocks (8th Ed., Springer).
PART I
Theoretical Foundation & Scientific Principles
Authoritative textbook grounding, analytical derivations, and geodynamic mechanics
1. The Four Foundational Controlling Factors of Metamorphic Systems

In metamorphic geology (Winter, 2014, pp. 405–410; Bangar, p. 81; Bucher & Grapes, 2011), the mineralogical assemblage, micro-texture, and structural fabric of a metamorphic rock are governed by four fundamental thermodynamic, kinetic, and chemical variables:

  1. (i) Chemical & Mineralogical Composition of the Parent Rock (Protolith): Because regional metamorphism is essentially an isochemical process (except for the release of volatile $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}_2$), the bulk chemical composition of the protolith sets the absolute limits on which mineral phases can possibly nucleate and grow. A pure quartz sandstone can only form quartzite; a pure limestone can only form marble; and an aluminous shale forms pelitic schists.
  2. (ii) Temperature ($T$) and Pressure ($P$):
    • Temperature: The most dominant factor; provides the thermal activation energy ($\Delta G^\ddagger$) required to break atomic bonds and drive solid-state ionic diffusion. It dictates the equilibrium positions of dehydration and decarbonation reactions.
    • Pressure: Confining (lithostatic) pressure ($\rho g z$) forces crystal lattices to compress into denser, lower-volume polymorphs ($\Delta V < 0$), while directed differential stress ($\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$) drives mechanical deformation and aligns minerals into pervasive foliation.
  3. (iii) The Nature and Presence of a Fluid Phase ($\text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{CO}_2$): Interstitial volatile fluids act as powerful catalysts. They accelerate solid-state reaction rates by orders of magnitude via grain-boundary diffusion, lower melting solidus curves, and govern decarbonation/dehydration equilibria through fluid activities ($a_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}, a_{\text{CO}_2}$).
  4. (iv) Duration and Reaction Kinetics (Geological Time): Metamorphic events operate over timescales of $1\text{ to } 50+\text{ million years}$. Ample geological time allows sluggish, solid-state diffusion and mineral nucleation to overcome kinetic overstepping and achieve true thermodynamic chemical equilibrium.
Figure 114.1 — The Interdependent Factors Controlling Metamorphic Evolution: Authentic textbook diagram from John D. Winter (Principles of Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, p. 408). Shows the dynamic feedback loops between Protolith Bulk Chemistry, Pressure-Temperature Trajectories, Interstitial Fluid Regimes, and Reaction Time.
2. Quantitative & Thermodynamic Analysis of the Four Controlling Variables

Thermodynamic Breakdown of Metamorphic Agents

Factor Thermodynamic / Physical Role Governing Equation / Law Diagnostic Manifestation
(i) Protolith Composition Defines the chemical system ($C$) in Gibbs Phase Rule ($F = C - P + 2$) Conservation of mass; isochemical transformation Pelitic $\rightarrow$ Garnet/Staurolite; Mafic $\rightarrow$ Hornblende/Epidote; Calcareous $\rightarrow$ Calcite/Wollastonite.
(ii) Pressure & Temperature Defines equilibrium state and mineral stability field in $P\text{-}T$ space Gibbs Free Energy: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S + P\Delta V$ High-pressure blueschists; high-temperature granulites; oriented foliation under $\sigma_1 > \sigma_3$.
(iii) Fluid Composition Catalyzes ionic diffusion; controls devolatilization phase equilibria Chemical potential of volatile components: $\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i$ Hydration reactions (serpentinization); decarbonation reactions (skarns); metasomatic ore halos.
(iv) Geological Time Governs reaction kinetics, crystal coarsening, and nucleation rates Arrhenius Rate Law: $k = A e^{-E_a / RT}$; Diffusion: $x \approx \sqrt{2Dt}$ Large porphyroblast growth; coarse granoblastic equilibration; preservation of zoned cores.
PART II
Official Examination Question & Critical Option Dissection
Rigorous forensic analysis refuting all distractors with physical principles
Official Examination Question — OPSC Assistant Geologist 2021
Question 114: The main factors that control metamorphic processes are : (i) The mineral composition of the parent rock, (ii) The pressure and temperature at which metamorphism takes place, (iii) The types of prevailing fluids (mostly water) during metamorphism, (iv) The amount of time available for metamorphism. Find out the odd one from the listed factors :
(A) (i) and (ii) are correct
(B) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct
(C) (ii), (iii) and (iv) are correct
(D) All of the above are true explanations
Verified Correct Answer: (D) All of the above are true explanations
Forensic Analysis & Refutation of Options
Option (A) Evaluated — Incomplete Subset

Incorrect: While protolith composition (i) and $P\text{-}T$ conditions (ii) are undeniably fundamental controls, selecting (A) falsely excludes fluids (iii) and time (iv), both of which are universally documented as indispensable primary factors controlling metamorphic systems.

Option (B) Evaluated — Incomplete Subset

Incorrect: Option (B) captures factors (i), (ii), and (iii), but arbitrarily excludes time (iv). Without sufficient geological time ($10^5\text{ to } 10^7\text{ years}$), solid-state reactions are kinetically inhibited from reaching equilibrium. Time is a well-established foundational control.

Option (C) Evaluated — Incomplete Subset

Incorrect: Option (C) omits factor (i)—the chemical and mineral composition of the parent rock. Protolith composition is arguably the most fundamental constraint of all, as no rock can crystallize minerals whose elements were not present in the precursor rock.

Option (D) Confirmed — All of the Above are True Explanations

Correct: Every authoritative textbook in metamorphic petrology (Winter, 2014, p. 405; Bangar, p. 81; Bucher & Grapes, 2011; Miyashiro, 1994) confirms that all four listed factors—(i) Protolith composition, (ii) Pressure and Temperature, (iii) Fluid presence and composition, and (iv) Geological time—are canonical controlling factors of metamorphism. None of them is an "odd one" or invalid factor. Therefore, the comprehensive option (D) All of the above are true explanations is the verified and logically sound answer.

PART III
Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice Questions
8 Curated exam-standard practice problems with complete step-by-step worked solutions
Systematic Evaluation of Metamorphic Controlling Factors
Listed Factor Scientific Significance Primary Impact on Metamorphism Consequence of Absence / Variation
(i) Protolith Composition Supplies the chemical elemental components ($\text{Si, Al, Fe, Mg, Ca, Na, K}$) Controls phase mineralogy and mineral proportions via the Gibbs Phase Rule Determines whether the resulting rock is a marble, quartzite, amphibolite, or metapelite.
(ii) Pressure & Temperature Sets the energetic thermodynamic state and directed deviatoric stress Determines metamorphic facies, mineral stability fields, and structural foliation Low $T \rightarrow$ Greenschist; High $T \rightarrow$ Granulite; High $P \rightarrow$ Blueschist/Eclogite; Directed stress $\rightarrow$ Schistosity.
(iii) Prevailing Fluids ($\text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{CO}_2$) Provides interstitial transport medium and catalytic activation Accelerates reaction kinetics by orders of magnitude; enables hydration/dehydration "Dry" rocks (e.g., anhydrous gabbros) resist metamorphism and persist metastably even at high $P\text{-}T$.
(iv) Available Geological Time Enables sluggish solid-state diffusion and crystal growth to proceed Permits nucleation, chemical homogenization, and attainment of true chemical equilibrium Rapid thermal events (e.g., flash meteorite impact or shallow dykes) yield metastable glasses or cryptocrystalline rinds.
Exam-Standard Practice Problems & Analytical Derivations

Practice Problem 1

A completely dry, anhydrous gabbro and a water-saturated basalt are both subjected to identical high-pressure conditions ($P = 15\text{ kbar}, T = 500^\circ\text{C}$). The wet basalt transforms into an eclogite, while the dry gabbro retains its igneous augite and plagioclase with only minor coronas. Which controlling factor explains this discrepancy?

Solution: This discrepancy is governed by Factor (iii): The presence of a fluid phase ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$). Even when an assemblage is thermodynamically unstable, solid-state reconstructive transformation requires breaking chemical bonds and diffusing ions across grain boundaries. In dry systems, solid-state volume diffusion is extraordinarily slow ($D \sim 10^{-20}\text{ m}^2\text{/s}$), creating a massive kinetic barrier (overstepping) that prevents recrystallization. In the wet rock, aqueous fluid creates interconnected grain-boundary pathways where diffusion is $10^6\text{ to } 10^8\text{ times}$ faster, instantly catalyzing equilibrium recrystallization into eclogite.

Practice Problem 2

Explain how the duration of metamorphism (Factor iv: Time) affects the grain size of porphyroblasts according to Ostwald ripening theory.

Solution: Ostwald ripening dictates that small crystals possess a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio and higher interfacial free energy than large crystals. Over extended geological time ($10^6\text{ to } 10^7\text{ years}$), thermodynamics drives the slow dissolution of numerous tiny matrix crystals and the diffusive transfer of their mass onto fewer, larger crystals (porphyroblasts) to minimize total interfacial surface energy ($\sum \gamma_i A_i \rightarrow \text{minimum}$), resulting in coarse-grained, porphyroblastic schists.

Practice Problem 3

Why is regional metamorphism described as an "isochemical" process, and what are the specific chemical exceptions to this rule?

Solution: Regional metamorphism is considered isochemical because the bulk non-volatile elemental composition ($\text{SiO}_2, \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3, \text{FeO}, \text{MgO}, \text{CaO}, \text{Na}_2\text{O}, \text{K}_2\text{O}$) remains essentially constant between protolith and metamorphic product. The sole universal exceptions are volatile chemical species—principally $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}_2$—which are systematically expelled as pore fluids during prograde dehydration and decarbonation reactions (an open system with respect to volatiles).

Practice Problem 4

How does the partial pressure ratio $X_{\text{CO}_2} = \frac{P_{\text{CO}_2}}{P_{\text{CO}_2} + P_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}}$ control the decarbonation temperature of calcite + quartz to wollastonite: $\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{SiO}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{CaSiO}_3 + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$?

Solution: The chemical equilibrium is governed by the activity of carbon dioxide: $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln f_{\text{CO}_2}$. - When the fluid is pure $\text{CO}_2$ ($X_{\text{CO}_2} = 1.0$), high $\text{CO}_2$ partial pressure suppresses the reaction, requiring high temperatures ($T \approx 750^\circ\text{C}$ at $2\text{ kbar}$) to drive decarbonation. - If the system is infiltrated by abundant $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from an igneous source ($X_{\text{CO}_2} \rightarrow 0.1$), the $\text{CO}_2$ product is continually diluted and flushed away, lowering the equilibrium decarbonation temperature by more than $150\text{--}200^\circ\text{C}$ (down to $\sim 550^\circ\text{C}$).

Practice Problem 5

Calculate the lithostatic confining pressure exerted on a rock at $25\text{ km}$ depth in an orogenic root assuming average continental crustal density $\rho = 2800\text{ kg/m}^3$.

Solution: The lithostatic pressure formula is: $$P = \rho g z$$ Given: - $\rho = 2800\text{ kg/m}^3$ - $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ - $z = 25,000\text{ m}$ $$P = 2800 \times 9.81 \times 25,000 = 686,700,000\text{ Pa} \approx \mathbf{6.87\text{ kbar}} = \mathbf{0.687\text{ GPa}}$$ The rock experiences approximately $6.87\text{ kbar}$ of lithostatic confining pressure, typical of the amphibolite facies.

Practice Problem 6

How does thermal activation energy ($E_a$) govern the rate of metamorphic reactions as formulated by the Arrhenius equation?

Solution: The reaction rate constant $k$ is given by the Arrhenius equation: $$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)$$ Because temperature $T$ appears in the denominator of the negative exponential, an increase in metamorphic temperature from $200^\circ\text{C}$ ($473\text{ K}$) to $600^\circ\text{C}$ ($873\text{ K}$) causes an exponential increase in the reaction rate constant $k$ by a factor of millions. This explains why low-temperature reactions are frequently kinetically inhibited, whereas high-temperature reactions equilibrate rapidly.

Practice Problem 7

What is "metasomatism" and how does it represent an exception to the isochemical nature of metamorphism?

Solution: Metasomatism is allochemical metamorphism wherein circulating hydrothermal fluids introduce or remove substantial quantities of non-volatile chemical components ($\text{SiO}_2, \text{Fe, Mg, Ca, Na, K, metals}$) via advective mass transfer across the rock boundaries (e.g., formation of skarns, greisens, or serpentinized peridotites). It represents an open-system chemical transformation, violating the strict isochemical assumption.

Practice Problem 8

Why do coarse-grained plutonic rocks (like granites) require higher metamorphic temperatures to develop foliation than fine-grained sediments (like shales) under the same directed stress?

Solution: Fine-grained shales contain sub-microscopic clay minerals with enormous specific surface area, abundant adsorbed pore water, and weak crystal lattices, which deform and dynamically recrystallize readily at $200\text{--}300^\circ\text{C}$. Coarse-grained granites consist of large ($2\text{--}5\text{ mm}$), tightly interlocked anhydrous crystals of quartz and feldspar with zero interstitial fluid and low grain-boundary area. Plastic dislocation creep in feldspar requires temperatures $> 450\text{--}500^\circ\text{C}$; below this threshold, granite deforms only via localized brittle cataclasis.
